In addition to discovering the original church's foundation, archaeologists uncovered the graves of 62 community members. DNA tests and bone analyses for three sets of remains linked them back to the African Baptist Meeting House congregation.
But it was oral tradition that served as the first hint in the discovery, where stories of ancestors buried in the area led to a search.
“We knew the building was here, and we knew that there were maybe burials behind it,” said Jennifer Wilkoski, director of architectural preservation and research at Colonial Williamsburg.
When the church’s original structure was discovered in 2021, Davis called it “a rediscovery of the humanity of a people.”

“We were just so elated that those people who had been buried and forgotten, have now been unearthed and given the recognition as human beings, as they should have been,” he said. “It's a wonderful time to shed light on our history in light of the erasure of so many things within our history."

The meeting house reconstruction, built at its original site, honors its original character. Archaeologists and Colonial Williamsburg's construction team modeled the new church out of pine and white oak woods, and recreated details like the original half-round brick steps.
Wilkoski said the materials for the original church demonstrated the resourcefulness of the congregants, who likely included carpenters with the skills necessary to build the church.

Modern renovations include an HVAC system for Virginia's hot summers, a refreshed altar table for sermons, shutters, and handblown glass windows. Last year, Colonial Williamsburg considered glassless windows but has since had to reconsider to build the cooling HVAC system.
“It's not church stained glass, but we call it restoration glass, handmade like they would've had in the 18th and early 19th century,” Wilkoski said.
Finishing touches on the church will wrap in the next few months and will include an ADA- accessible ramp.
Davis, the First Baptist pastor, said the meeting house structure is overdue recognition for "those of us who are still working to make America a more perfect union.”
Nancy Jiang reported from New York.

title: Spaghetti models, rapid intensification, storm surge. Confused? Here's what hurricane terms mean
summary: It can be a confusing time when a hurricane is threatening, and weather officials use terminology that may not be fully understood
story: It can be a confusing time when a hurricane is threatening, and weather officials use terminology that may not be fully understood
It's a confusing time when a hurricane threatens, and some terms used by officials aren't known by everyone, so here's a storm glossary.

Let's start with the broad category of these storms, called tropical cyclones. In the northern hemisphere, a tropical cyclone is a rapidly counterclockwise-rotating storm that forms in Earth's warmer areas that is organized with a center that winds flow out of. Tropical cyclones rotate clockwise in the southern hemisphere.

The strongest tropical cyclones in the Atlantic and eastern and central Pacific oceans are called hurricanes. In the northwest Pacific they are called typhoons and in the south Pacific and Indian oceans they are called cyclones or tropical cyclones.
In the Atlantic, the weakest of these systems are called tropical depressions. They have winds of less than 39 mph (63 kph).
When a tropical depression reaches 39 mph (63 kph) but is weaker than 74 mph (119 kph) they are called tropical storm and receive a name from a pre-established list.

When a tropical storm hits 74 mph (120 kph), it achieves hurricane status. There are five categories of hurricanes based on maximum sustained winds speed in a rating system called the Saffir-Simpson Scale.

The weakest is a Category 1, with winds of 74-95 mph (120-150 kph) and it will have dangerous winds that produce some damage. Tree branches will snap and some will be uprooted. Extensive power damage is likely.
A Category 2 has winds of 96-110 mph (155-175 kph) and can be disastrous, with near-total power loss expected near the center.

When hurricanes sustain winds exceeding 111 mph (180 kph), they get major hurricane status, with devastating consequences. Even well-built homes may be severely damaged by a Category 3 hurricane with winds of 111-129 mph (180-210 kph).
A Category 4 hurricane is considered catastrophic, with winds of 130-156 mph (210-250 kph) that leave entire areas uninhabitable for weeks or months.
The scale tops out at Category 5, when a hurricane's winds exceed 157 mph (250 kph). A high percentage of the homes in the disaster region will be destroyed. Power outages could last for months.

Storm surge is the deadly rise of water generated by a storm that's above and beyond the normal tide. It starts in the ocean but could include rivers and canals. Storm surges once caused nearly half of a hurricane's deaths, but surge-related fatalities have come down with warnings and education to about 11% of all direct deaths. Surges can reach as much as 20 feet or more and that does not include waves, which are on top of storm surge.
Storm tide is storm surge plus tides.

A hurricane's center is called the eye. It is calm inside the eye, but it is crucial to the storm's formation and continuation. It is circular and is usually 20 to 40 miles (30 to 60 km) in diameter, but can be bigger. The smaller the eye is, the stronger the storm. After awhile, a storm can form a new second eyewall around the first in a process called eyewall replacement that temporarily weakens the storm's intensity but enables it to grow larger overall.

The outside of the eye is the eyewall and it is the storm's most dangerous area with the strongest winds. When an area on the ground is hit by the eyewall, it will be buffeted by intense winds, then get a break before being slammed by the other side of the eye in a second round of the storm's strongest winds.

When the eye of a hurricane or tropical storm goes over land, that point is called landfall. But high winds, rain and storm surge can cause all sorts of damage many hours before landfall, and last many hours thereafter. Landfall is not necessarily where the strongest winds are, and the wider swirl of a storm can spread destruction across large areas.

The right front quadrant of a hurricane or northeast part of the eyewall tends to cause the most damage as the strongest winds blow counterclockwise around the center, so this at times is called a storm's dirty side. In the southern hemisphere, it's the left front quadrant that is the dirty side.

There are dozens of computer generated models that forecast changes in each storm's track and intensity. They vary because each one uses different assumptions about how storms operate and some prove better during certain storms and worse during others. Forecasters advise to avoid concentrating on one individual model. When many or all of the models are put on one map, they generally show an overall sense of what will happen. Sometimes they show a lot of lines going in different directions, which can look like cooked spaghetti.

The National Hurricane Center's official forecast is not one specific line, but rather a cone of uncertainty that expands with time, up to five days out. That cone shows the most probable area where the eye of the storm could move over time, but it doesn't mean the storm will be in the center of that cone. It is designed so that 67% of the most likely tracks fall within the cone.

A hurricane or tropical storm watch means conditions are possible within an area during the time specified by the National Weather Service. A hurricane or tropical storm warning means those conditions are no longer just possible, but expected. One way to think about it: A watch is having the ingredients to bake a cake, while a warning comes when the cake is pretty much done.

Wind shear is a change in wind speed or direction, or both, and it can weaken a storm. Crosswinds at high levels, such as 40,000 feet (12,200 meters) above sea level, can often decapitate a storm. Wind shear also can describe when winds up at the top of the storm blow in different directions than at bottom or middle.

When a storm, usually fed by unusually warm water, suddenly gathers a lot of strength, sustaining winds that increase in speed by at least 35 mph (56 kph) in 24 hours, it is called rapid intensification. This is a dangerous situation if it happens close to land.

title: Severe turbulence injures 9 aboard Avianca flight, forcing emergency landing in Miami
summary: Nine people were injured when an Avianca flight encountered severe turbulence and had to make an emergency landing in Miami
story: Nine people were injured when an Avianca flight encountered severe turbulence and had to make an emergency landing in Miami
Nine people were injured when an Avianca flight encountered severe turbulence and had to make an emergency landing in Miami early Friday.

Miami-Dade Fire Rescue said that one person was rushed to a trauma center with severe injuries while seven others were taken to area hospitals in ambulances after the plane landed shortly after 3 a.m. Friday. The airline said nine people — three crew members and six passengers — were affected by the turbulence.
The Federal Aviation Administration said the Avianca flight was en route from Medellin, Colombia, to John F. Kennedy International Airport in New York when the Airbus A320 had to divert to Miami.

Avianca said the unhurt passengers were rebooked on other flights to continue their trip to New York. The airline said “the safety of our customers and employees is, and will remain, the foundation of our operations.”

Serious injuries from in-flight turbulence are rare, but scientists say they may be becoming more common as climate change alters the jet stream. The International Air Transport Association said the number of reports it received about turbulence incidents surged more than 25% last year.

Last summer, 24 people were taken to the hospital after a Delta Air Lines flight encountered turbulence caused by a thunderstorm over Wyoming. The National Transportation Safety Board has said passengers and flight attendants were thrown into the ceiling with enough force to crack some of the interior panels before tossing them back to the floor and then up again. The seat belt sign was off at the time so some passengers were up and drinks were being served when that plane hit the turbulence.
At least 20 passengers have filed lawsuits against Delta over that incident, arguing the airline could have avoided the severe weather.
The FAA recommends that passengers stay buckled whenever possible to protect against unexpected turbulence.

title: Florida execution called off after DeSantis withdraws death warrant for the first time
summary: Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis has withdrawn a death warrant, halting the execution of William Lee Thompson
story: Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis has withdrawn a death warrant, halting the execution of William Lee Thompson

MIAMI -- MIAMI (AP) — Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis has withdrawn a death warrant for the first time since taking office, calling off a man’s execution just days before he was scheduled to die by lethal injection in the nation’s busiest death chamber.

The Republican governor, who has aggressively used the death penalty in his final term, signed a letter Thursday withdrawing the death warrant for William Lee Thompson. The 74-year-old inmate had been set to die Tuesday for the murder and kidnapping of Sally Ivester in 1976.

A second Florida execution scheduled for the same day is still set to take place. James Robertson, 63, pleaded guilty to first-degree murder and waived all appeals in the 2008 strangling of Frank Hart while the men were cellmates at Charlotte Correctional Institution, north of Fort Myers. Robertson told investigators he killed the other man so he could be moved to death row.

DeSantis did not provide a reason in the letter for withdrawing Thompson's death warrant but had temporarily stayed his execution last month pending a psychiatric evaluation. Florida prison officials, however, had still been preparing for Thompson's potential execution next week.
Thompson's attorney, Bri Lacy, said they're relieved by the result.

“Mr. Thompson suffers from dementia and his health is failing — both of which were gravely concerning with an impending execution,” Lacy said in an email. “Now that Mr. Thompson is no longer under a death warrant, we hope FDOC (Florida Department of Corrections) will relocate him to an adequate medical facility and provide the care he needs.”
The move comes at a time of escalating attention on the death penalty in the U.S.

In Tennessee, Christa Pike survived an execution attempt last week despite receiving two lethal doses of pentobarbital. On Thursday, the Pentagon announced that the firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan would be livestreamed.
Thompson will remain on Florida's death row, and a new death warrant could be signed for him in the future.
A spokesperson for DeSantis did not immediately return an email seeking comment.

Florida carried out 19 executions last year, a record in the state since the death penalty was reinstated in 1976. In July, Florida became the first state in nearly a decade to execute two prisoners in one day.

title: FBI arrests suspect in ShinyHunters hack of the bureau's jobs portal
summary: The FBI has arrested an accused co-conspirator of the hacking group ShinyHunters
story: The FBI has arrested an accused co-conspirator of the hacking group ShinyHunters

The FBI has arrested an accused co-conspirator of a criminal hacking group that said last month that it had breached the bureau’s jobs portal and obtained sensitive and personal data on nearly all employees of the law enforcement agency, Director Kash Patel said Friday.

The arrest was the latest targeting ShinyHunters, the group that claimed responsibility for the hack, as the FBI continues a global investigation into the breach of its network, which Patel said “occurred on a platform managed by a third-party vendor.”
“We will continue to work closely with our partners to disrupt what’s left of the ShinyHunters group and their associates, no matter where they operate,” Patel said in a statement.
The identity of the person arrested was not immediately clear, nor what charges they might face.

In a message taking responsibility for the hack and announcing the collection of sensitive information, ShinyHunters said it had taken action over false allegations contained in an FBI public advisory from May that described the organization as a “cyber criminal group specializing in large-scale data breaches and extortion.”

That advisory characterized ShinyHunters as “threat actors” who often “use their real or exaggerated claims of access to sensitive or personal information to prompt payment from victims,” commonly harass or threaten people and “may falsely claim to have sensitive or compromising information, including embarrassing photographs or videos of victims, which frequently do not exist.”

Experts said that although the data that appeared to be compromised was the type of personal information that is routinely accessed during a breach, the hack nonetheless had alarming national security implications given that it could expose agents and their families to extortion, swatting and other harassment and because the identities of spouses were also said to have been obtained.

title: EU and China strike interim trade deal which could cut Chinese hybrid exports by half, EU trade envoy says
summary: EU and China strike interim trade deal which could cut Chinese hybrid exports by half, EU trade envoy says
story: EU and China strike interim trade deal which could cut Chinese hybrid exports by half, EU trade envoy says
HONG KONG -- EU and China strike interim trade deal which could cut Chinese hybrid exports by half, EU trade envoy says.
THIS IS AN APNewsAlert. Check back for updates. AP's earlier story is below.
The top trade envoys for China and the European Union wrapped up two days of talks Friday aimed at calming escalating tensions over growing imbalances between the two giant economies.
China’s commerce ministry said in a statement that both sides had reached “an understanding” on hybrid car trade and agreed to continue exploring the possibility of lower tariffs on some products.
The statement did not specify the details, and the ministry said the two sides would next meet again in January by video conference and then in person in March.
EU trade chief Maros Sefcovic, who traveled to Beijing, said it was crucial that the negotiations deliver “tangible outcomes” in rebalancing trade between China and the 27-nation bloc.
It was unclear, however, if the two sides would find the will to resolve key factors behind China’s growing trade surplus, which hit 360 billion euros ($410 billion) last year.
China is pushing for the EU to stop blocking its imports of advanced computer chipmaking machines, restrictions imposed on national security grounds at Washington's behest.
Sefcovic said the talks this week were the culmination of three months of intensive work. He had set an October deadline for meaningful results on trade rebalancing.
Earlier in the week, the Chinese Commerce Ministry issued a statement urging the EU to avoid protectionist measures, warning that such moves could backfire.
Trade tensions have grown in recent months, with both sides imposing or considering curbs on each other’s imports.

The EU has moved to limit imports of Chinese-made electric vehicles and EV batteries and enacted measures to protect the European steel industry. It also is limiting duty-free imports of e-commerce small parcels, essentially targeting Chinese fast fashion firms.
Last week, China launched an anti-dumping investigation into imports from the EU of p-nitrotoluene, a chemical compound used in dyes and pharmaceuticals.
Chinese officials and businesses have raised concerns over reports some EU members are pushing for new measures to protect local industries.

Worries over surging Chinese exports to Europe and other parts of the world in what some are calling a China shock 2.0 have deepened as the U.S., especially since President Donald Trump returned to the White House, has raised tariffs and enacted other measures to try to reduce its own huge trade deficit with Beijing.
Despite the backlash from some of its trading partners, China's global trade surplus hit $1.2 trillion in 2025 and is forecast to surpass $1 trillion again this year.

The EU's trade deficit with China widened to 103.34 billion euros (about $116 billion) in the April-July quarter, as imports rose to 153.63 billion euros ($172.3 billion), while European exports to China climbed to 50.3 billion euros ($56.4 billion), according to EU statistics.
McNeil reported from Brussels and Kurtenbach reported from Mito, Japan. AP journalists Borg Wong in Beijing and Chan Ho-him in Hong Kong contributed

title: El Niño's storm-killer winds and climate's warming waters in fight over future of Hurricane Isaias
summary: A supersized El Niño’s decapitating winds and the Gulf of Mexico’s hot storm-fueling waters are battling for the core and future of land-approaching Hurricane Isaias and the storm’s tilt and eye show who’s winning
story: A supersized El Niño’s decapitating winds and the Gulf of Mexico’s hot storm-fueling waters are battling for the core and future of land-approaching Hurricane Isaias and the storm’s tilt and eye show who’s winning

A supersized El Niño’s decapitating winds and the Gulf of Mexico’s toasty, storm-fueling waters are battling over the future strength of Hurricane Isaias. And the storm’s tilt and eye show who’s winning.
All Atlantic hurricane season there has been “this battle between shear and just the overall conducive conditions,” said Colorado State University hurricane researcher Phil Klotzbach.

El Niño — the natural temporary warming of parts of the Pacific that warps weather worldwide — dominated. Its wind patterns smothered almost any wisp of a storm from strengthening in the Atlantic, while boosting what will soon be record high levels in the Pacific, Klotzbach said.

It's called wind shear and it pushes the tops and middle of storms around, making them lopsided and keeping them from making a complete circular eyewall, which is when storms can really power up, Klotzbach and University at Albany's Kristen Corbosiero said.

The other ingredients for a storm to turbocharge a storm are pushing back. There is plenty of fuel in warm water and moisture. The Gulf of Mexico is about 2.7 degrees (1.5 degrees Celsius) warmer than normal. The 86 degree waters (30 degrees Celsius) are 100 to 500 times more likely to be that extra hot because of climate change from the burning of coal, oil and gas, said climate scientist Kristina Dahl, vice president of the nonprofit Climate Central, which calculates the boost global warming causes to extreme weather.
“But there’s a certain point where it’s like, I don’t care how hot the waters are and how much moisture you have, if shear gets to a certain point, the shear is gonna win,” Klotzbach said.

The thunderstorm seeds of something bigger earlier in the week grew from circular winds over Central America but often were lopsided and couldn’t quite form a crucial eyewall, all because of El Niño’s high-level strong winds that pushed a would-be storm's top sideways, experts said.

Then a window of moderation opened for just a couple of days, but it was enough, Corbosiero said. It makes sense it was in the Gulf of Mexico and in October, because El Niño has less of an effect in the Gulf than it does in the main Atlantic, she said. And storms often pop up in that region in October because of more northerly storm systems that help foster the right conditions.

Wind shear wasn’t exactly low, but it was a moderate level, when other factors like unusually warm waters and heavy moisture can kick in. Isaias rapidly intensified from 40 mph to 80 mph (64 kph to 129 kph) in a day and by late Wednesday, Isaias became the latest-in-the-season first Atlantic hurricane to form since 1914, Klotzbach said.
“The warm waters and high moisture won,” Klotzbach said. Isaias is likely losing its tilt and straightening and flying right and strong.

For a few hours, the storm is forecast on Friday to flirt with 111 mph (178 kph) winds that could possibly give it major hurricane status, according to Klotzbach and the National Hurricane Center's forecast. But it'll likely be temporary.

Before Isaias comes ashore — forecast for probably somewhere from the Mississippi and Alabama coast to the Florida Panhandle late Friday night or early Saturday — the wind shear will strengthen from moderate levels of around 20 mph (32 kph) to 52 mph (84 kph) and then Isaias will start to struggle, which is good news for coastal residents, Klotzbach said.
It will probably come ashore as a strong Category 1 or weak Category 2 storm, but not a major storm, Klotzbach said. It can still do plenty of damage.

“Once it gets to the coast, we know that the storm surge is going to be deeper and farther reaching because of sea level rise caused by climate change,” Dahl said. “So in this part of the world, there’s been about six and a half inches of sea level rise over the past 100 years or so that’s attributable directly to climate change.”
The National Hurricane Center is calling the surge “life-threatening.”
A warmer atmosphere means storms hold and then dump more rain, worsening flooding, Dahl said. The hurricane center is warning about urban, river and flash flooding in the Southeast this weekend.

“There’s a little bit of a battle here going on, but I think the really important thing to remember is that climate change is like this long-term big kahuna warming everywhere, and El Niño’s like a little icing on the cake,” Dahl said.

title: The FBI has seized tools used by Chinese hackers for cyber operations, officials say
summary: The FBI has seized scanning and phishing tools used by a group of hackers that officials say is associated with the Chinese government and that is responsible for disruptive cyber operations in the United States and abroad, including against the power ...
story: The FBI has seized scanning and phishing tools used by a group of hackers that officials say is associated with the Chinese government and that is responsible for disruptive cyber operations in the United States and abroad, including against the power ...

LOS ANGELES -- The FBI has seized scanning and phishing tools used by a group of hackers that officials say is associated with the Chinese government and responsible for disruptive cyber operations in the United States and abroad, including against the power industry, academia and critical infrastructure.

The seizure of the tools, announced Wednesday by the FBI and Justice Department, represents the latest law enforcement effort in recent years to go after a broad-based hacking campaign known to the private sector as Flax Typhoon.

The tools at issue, called “Microscan” and “FishHub,” were used by the hackers to scan, phish and hack targets that included U.S. and foreign critical infrastructure. The tools were used to target, among other entities, an unnamed power company in the U.S., Japanese and Polish airports, Taiwanese universities, a multinational, nongovernmental organization and Taiwanese critical infrastructure companies.
The latest operation has rendered the tools inoperable in what FBI and Justice Department officials said was a blow to the hacking operation.

“We aim to remove the capability from the threat actors. We target their infrastructure, their money, and their tools,” FBI Cyber Division Deputy Assistant Director Jason Bilnoski told The Associated Press, calling the hacking operation “indiscriminate and reckless.”

The tools were operated by a Chinese-based information security company called Integrity Technology Group, which the FBI has said is closely associated with the Chinese government and is the actual identity of Flax Typhoon.

In September 2024, the FBI announced that it had disrupted a botnet associated with Flax Typhoon that installed malicious software on more than 200,000 consumer devices, including cameras, video recorders and home and office routers, to create a massive botnet — a network of infected computers. The botnet was used to facilitate cyber crimes, such as the theft of sensitive information from victims’ networks.
FBI San Diego Supervisory Special Agent Brett Lally said that the department would continue to monitor for ways that the company might rebuild its infrastructure.
“It’ll be interesting to see what this round of disruption actions have in terms of their ability to operate as a company in China,” Lally said.
Tucker reported from Washington.

title: US newlyweds tour Croatia after fans photobomb their wedding shoot
summary: It began with a hijacked wedding photo shoot and turned into a very unexpected but exciting trip across the world
story: It began with a hijacked wedding photo shoot and turned into a very unexpected but exciting trip across the world
SPLIT, Croatia -- It began with a hijacked wedding photo shoot and turned into a very unexpected but exciting trip across the world.

Ashton and Zachary Smith from Philadelphia are guests in Croatia this week after the couple accidentally celebrated their wedding in June with a crowd of joyful Croatian soccer fans during the FIFA World Cup in the United States.

The Smiths had just gotten married and came out of Philadelphia City Hall to take photos when hundreds of Croats in red-and-white chequered jerseys joined in. Photos and videos of the couple kissing among the fans became popular on social networks and paved the way for a new friendship.

“It was so crazy, we just finished our ceremony, we went outside to take some pictures in front of City Hall,” Ashton Smith recalled. “We were warned that the road was taken over but we’re like, oh, let’s just try it anyway.”
It was “the best decision that we ever could have made” despite the initial shock, she said.

“Everyone stormed us," Ashton Smith added. "At first we were like, oh my gosh I hope everyone is with us. But everyone was there, everyone was celebrating with us and it was just amazing how welcoming they were to complete strangers.”

Months later, the couple received an equally warm welcome in the Croatian town of Split, located on the Adriatic Sea coast. The Croatian National Tourist Board and the Mi Hrvati, or We Croats, fan group invited the Smiths over for a “second honeymoon.”
“I feel amazing,” Ashton said in an interview earlier this week. “We learned a lot of history about Croatia and now the vibes are immaculate.”

Ashton and Zachary joined the fans' march along the city’s waterfront ahead of Croatia’s UEFA Nations League match against Spain on Tuesday. A band played, the fans sang and the couple quickly fitted in. Later in the evening, they also attended the match.
“The fans are so energetic," Ashton said. "They brought the same energy that they did in Philly.”
Daniel Pedisic of the Mi Hrvati association said the spontaneous way Croatian fans reacted to the wedding in Philadelphia showed “the kind of people we are, warm, hospitable people.”
“We were with them that day and now we brought them to Croatia,” Pedisic added, whose association follows the team worldwide and is known for carrying a 100-meter Croatian flag.

The trip also took the Smiths to the coastal town of Sibenik and included a sailing trip and a tour of the stunning Krka National Park. On Friday, the couple will travel to the famous medieval walled city of Dubrovnik in the southern Adriatic, before ending their trip in the capital, Zagreb.

“Technically, this is our second honeymoon because we had a pre-planned one before the wedding," Ashton said. “The first one was laid back and relaxing, and this one is kind of go, go, go, and we absolutely love it.”
Zachary Smith said he had never expected to visit Croatia, which is located in southeastern Europe.
“I knew all about Croatia, where it was, the country obviously," he said. “But (I) never really thought that I would ever make it here, so it’s amazing."

title: Army finds systemic failures behind DC midair collision and calls for safety fixes
summary: A U.S. Army report has highlighted the many systemic breakdowns that led to last year’s midair collision between an American Airlines jet and a Black Hawk helicopter near Washington, D.C. The military has also recommended numerous steps it should take ...
story: A U.S. Army report has highlighted the many systemic breakdowns that led to last year’s midair collision between an American Airlines jet and a Black Hawk helicopter near Washington, D.C. The military has also recommended numerous steps it should take ...

The U.S. Army found many systemic breakdowns that led to last year’s midair collision between an American Airlines jet and a Black Hawk helicopter near Washington, D.C., and recommended numerous steps the military should take to prevent future tragedies.

Families of some of the 67 people who died have been pressuring the Army for months to release the report, which was completed in May. The Associated Press obtained a copy from them Thursday morning, a few hours before the Army made it public.

The deadliest plane crash on U.S. soil in over two decades happened when the helicopter collided with the descending airliner as it approached the runway, sending both plummeting into the icy Potomac River.
The Army report highlighted how the air traffic controller at Reagan National Airport could have prevented the crash, but also acknowledged the military’s own failings and other contributing factors.

Former Army Black Hawk pilot Tim Lilley, whose son Sam Lilley was the first officer on the American Airlines jet, said he needs more details from the military. Some information in the report was redacted and the military assigned responsibility for its shortcomings broadly across the Army.

“The Army owes the families and the American public a full accounting of how these risks were allowed to persist, who was responsible for the decisions that allowed them to persist and what will be done to make sure this never happens again,” said Lilley, who is a commercial jet captain today.
The Army acknowledged that in a statement Thursday afternoon.
“We recognize the families’ need for answers and remain committed to transparency regarding the Army’s review,” the Army said.

While the report largely reinforces the National Transportation Safety Board's conclusions, the civilian investigation was more broad and emphasized years of warning signs missed by the Federal Aviation Administration along with a weak military safety culture.

The Army report recommended that the military look beyond Washington make sure similar risks aren’t present in every major city where its helicopters operate. An Army official said the review of helicopter flights in other cities, including Los Angeles and the Seattle-Tacoma region, is ongoing. The official spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly on the situation.

The lieutenant general who authored the report said “breakdowns across all layers of conflict management caused this accident” but “the most salient contributing factor was the two broken radio transmissions” that contributed to the helicopter crew not identifying Flight 5342 as it was circling to land on the airport's alternate runway. The military pilots were wearing night-vision goggles that limited their field of vision and made it difficult to spot the plane amid the lights of the city.

The poorly designed helicopter route in use at the time of the crash provided only a scant 75 feet (23 meters) of vertical separation between a helicopter and a plane landing on Reagan’s secondary runway, and that was only true if the helicopter stuck to the riverbank. This did not allow enough separation to account for the accepted level of error in a Black Hawk’s altimeter, and the NTSB found the helicopter was flying nearly 100 feet (30 meters) higher than its instruments read.

The NTSB said in a letter to the Army last week that the agency is pleased with the progress being made on seven of the eight recommendations to the Army. That contrasts with the FAA, which the NTSB has faulted for failing to implement roughly one-third of the recommendations to that safety regulator.

The Army report said the controller should have provided the helicopter crew with more details about exactly where the plane was to help the pilots spot it, and the controller should have warned the plane about the helicopter headed toward it. The FAA has prohibited controllers from relying on pilots to maintain visual separation in busy airspace since this crash.

The Army said it strengthened its training for helicopter crews after the crash. Once it became apparent that the ADS-B Out system on the Black Hawk that can broadcast its location was inoperable, all 3,585 affected Army helicopters were inspected and reconfigured. The Army is also working to improve the way it monitors safety concerns and reach an agreement with the FAA to share information about close calls.

The main group of families of passengers on the plane, who were flying from Wichita, Kansas, said the report reinforces their call for Congress to pass aviation safety reforms and require aircraft to be equipped with systems that will help pilots know where traffic in the air is.

“It’s a simple concept anyone can understand: aircraft should be able to see each other in the sky. The technology is proven. All that’s required is the political will to do the right thing,” the Families of Flight 5342 group said in a statement Thursday.

“We have waited long enough. We waited for the NTSB. We waited for the Army. Both investigations are complete, and both make clear that collision avoidance technology must be part of the solution. There is nothing left for Congress to wait for,” they said.
Both the House and Senate passed different aviation safety bills, but lawmakers are still working on a compromise piece of legislation to bring up for a vote in both houses of Congress.
Associated Press Writer Konstantin Toropin in Washington contributed.

title: Curtis Flowers, a Black man whose death sentence was tossed by Supreme Court, dies
summary: Curtis Flowers, a Black man who spent more than 22 years in prison and was on death row in Mississippi before the U.S. Supreme Court threw out his conviction and death sentence, has died
story: Curtis Flowers, a Black man who spent more than 22 years in prison and was on death row in Mississippi before the U.S. Supreme Court threw out his conviction and death sentence, has died
Curtis Flowers, a Black man who spent more than 22 years in prison and was on death row in Mississippi before the U.S. Supreme Court threw out his conviction and death sentence, has died. He was 56.
Flowers' family confirmed that he died Wednesday at his home in Mississippi, attorney Rob McDuff told The Associated Press Thursday.
No cause of death was given, said McDuff, who was part of Flowers' legal team.
Flowers was 26 when he was arrested several months after the July 1996 shooting deaths of four people inside a Winona, Mississippi, furniture store.

At the time, prosecutors described him as a disgruntled former employee who sought revenge against the store’s owner because she fired him and withheld most of his pay to cover the cost of merchandise he damaged. Nearly $300 was found missing after the killings.
Flowers was tried in the killings six times. Justice Brett Kavanaugh wrote in the high court's 7-2 decision in 2019 that the removal of Black prospective jurors deprived Flowers of a fair trial.

During the sixth trial in 2010, Flowers was sentenced to death. There were 11 white jurors and one Black juror who considered the case after District Attorney Doug Evans struck five Black prospective jurors.
Flowers remained in prison for six months after the Supreme Court ruling because he was still under indictment. He finally was released in December 2019 after a judge set bond.
Mississippi dropped charges against Flowers in September 2020.

“Today, I am finally free from the injustice that left me locked in a box for nearly twenty three years,” Flowers said in a statement. “I’ve been asked if I ever thought this day would come. I have been blessed with a family that never gave up on me and with them by my side, I knew it would.”
The legal team that represented Flowers for more than two decades said Thursday in a statement that each member feels “privileged to have called him a client.”

“Later, in the years after his release and exoneration, we felt equally honored to call him a friend,” the legal team said. “No matter where he was — on death row, at home on his parents’ porch with his feet up, singing in church, or fishing in a local pond — Curtis shared his light.”
The trials stretched back more than 20 years. The records showed Evans’ “relentless, determined effort to rid the jury of black individuals,” with the goal of an all-white jury, Kavanaugh wrote.

In the earlier trials, three convictions were tossed out, including one when the prosecutor improperly excluded African Americans from the jury. In the second trial, the judge chided Evans for striking a juror based on race. Two other trials ended when jurors couldn’t reach unanimous verdicts.
Kavanaugh noted that Evans had removed 41 of the 42 prospective Black jurors over the six trials.

Flowers filed a lawsuit in 2021 against Evans and three investigators who worked with the district attorney. The suit claimed Evans and the investigators engaged in misconduct, including “pressuring witnesses to fabricate claims about seeing Mr. Flowers in particular locations on the day of the murders” and ignoring other possible suspects.
Earlier that year, a judge ordered the state of Mississippi to pay Flowers $500,000 for wrongful imprisonment — the maximum under a state law that allows up to $50,000 a year for 10 years.
Evans retired in 2023 after more than 30 years as district attorney. His jury selection tactics had been scrutinized for years.

Flowers' name is “etched into U.S. Supreme Court jurisprudence — about what it means to fight for a fair trial free from racial bias in the selection of jurors,” Flowers' legal team said. “And also for that, but for so many other reasons, his name is etched into our memories, too — professional and personal. We will miss him.”
Williams is a member of AP's Race & Ethnicity team. He reported from Detroit.

title: Family of Mexican father shot dead by ICE in Chicago files claim over 'unlawful' shooting
summary: Attorneys for the family of a man shot dead by an immigration agent in a Chicago suburb said they filed a claim for compensation
story: Attorneys for the family of a man shot dead by an immigration agent in a Chicago suburb said they filed a claim for compensation

CHICAGO -- The family of a man shot dead by an immigration enforcement agent in the Chicago area last year moved to sue the government on Thursday for a shooting they allege was unlawful and could have been prevented, according to attorneys for the family.

Silverio Villegas Gonzalez, a 38-year-old Mexican national who had lived in the U.S. for 18 years, was fatally shot last fall by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent who stopped his car during “Operation Midway Blitz,” the Trump administration's immigration crackdown in Chicago.

The Department of Homeland Security initially said the agent was dragged by Villegas Gonzalez' vehicle and then shot Villegas Gonzalez in self-defense. A coroner’s report determined Villegas Gonzalez was shot from behind, at close range.
“This horrific shooting was unlawful and wholly preventable,” attorneys wrote in the claim.

The claim seeks compensation and gives the federal government six months to respond before a lawsuit can be filed. It comes days after lawyers filed a lawsuit against DHS on behalf of Marimar Martinez, who survived being shot five times in her car by an immigration agent in Chicago, less than a month after Villegas Gonzalez' death. An independent analysis of the shooting found the agent fired at her from behind, contradicting his statements to the FBI that he feared Martinez would drive into him, according to her lawyers.
Federal law does not allow for lawsuits against individual agents.

Jonathan Manes, an attorney for Villegas Gonzalez’ family, declined to share the amount of compensation they are seeking, but told The Associated Press they plan to ask the judge for a “very large amount of damages at trial.”

“The way that the administration has reflexively sought to smear Silverio and call it justified doesn’t suggest to us that they’ll be willing to settle,” Manes said. “We expect that, in six months' time, we’ll be in federal court where the government has to answer for this, where the truth can come out.”
Illinois State Police announced an investigation into the shooting in May.

Villegas Gonzalez, a line cook at a local diner, had just dropped off his two young sons at school and daycare on the morning of Sept. 12, 2025, in the Chicago suburb of Franklin Park, when ICE agents pulled their Jeep in front of his car, according to the claim.

As the two agents stood on either side of his car, leaning on the window frames, Villegas Gonzalez reversed about 50 feet (15.24 meters) and started to drive away into the open traffic lane. Surveillance video captured the sound of gunshots as one agent chased the car, which crashed into a parked delivery truck. The truck driver called 911, and Villegas Gonzalez was pronounced dead at a hospital about an hour later.

A medical examiner found that Villegas Gonzalez was shot downward, through the back of his neck. “The ICE officer was therefore standing alongside the driver’s side of Silverio’s vehicle when he fired the fatal shot, effectively executing Silverio at close range,” attorneys wrote in the complaint.

Immediately after the shooting, DHS said in a news release that Villegas Gonzalez was in the U.S. illegally and had dragged the agent with his car as he tried to flee. The release said the agent was seriously injured and “fearing for his life."
The agent told police who responded to the shooting that his injuries were “nothing major,” according to police body-worn camera footage previously obtained by the AP.
Attorneys wrote in the claim that the agent was not in the path of the vehicle, and chose to hold onto the windows.
Villegas Gonzalez had “no criminal record and only a few minor traffic violations,” it added.

DHS has not identified the agent. Neither of the ICE agents were wearing body-worn cameras when Villegas Gonzalez was shot. The Department did not respond to a request for comment. It was not immediately clear if DHS had received the claim.

Martinez and Villegas Gonzalez are among a growing number of people shot in their cars by federal agents across the country amid the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement sweeps. DHS has characterized the shootings as self-defense against people using their vehicles as weapons.

Mayes-Osterman is a corps member for The Associated Press/Report for America Statehouse News Initiative. Report for America is a nonprofit national service program that places journalists in local newsrooms to report on undercovered issues.

title: Notable Deaths in 2026
summary: A look back at the esteemed personalities who've left us this year, who'd touched us with their innovation, creativity and humanity.
story: A look back at the esteemed personalities who left us this year, who touched us with their innovation, creativity and humanity.
By CBSNews.com senior producer David Morgan. The Associated Press contributed to this gallery.

NFL Hall of Famer Mike Ditka (Oct. 18, 1939-Oct. 9, 2026) became a tough and fiery symbol of Chicago as both a player and coach of the Super Bowl-winning Bears. Nicknamed "Iron Mike," Ditka helped revolutionize the tight end position, then – as Chicago's coach – led his team to the championship with one of the game's most dominant defenses ever (and a lineup that was even featured in a rap video, "The Super Bowl Shuffle").

Born in Carnegie, Pa., the son of a welder, he was a talented three-sport athlete and All-American at Pitt. Selected by Chicago in the 1961 draft, Ditka earned Rookie of the Year honors, and multiple trips to the Pro Bowl. In 1963 the Bears won the NFL Championship. After six seasons in Chicago, Ditka played for the Philadelphia Eagles, and then the Dallas Cowboys. He moved to the sidelines as an assistant to coach Tom Landry (as the Cowboys won three NFC championships and a Super Bowl), before becoming Chicago's head coach in 1982.

His 10 years leading the Bears brought Ditka five straight NFC Central titles and a Super Bowl ring – as well as a DUI conviction, a heart attack, a long-running feud with defensive coordinator Buddy Ryan, and a new nickname: "Da Coach."

After several years in the NBC booth, Ditka returned to coaching the Philadelphia Eagles and the New Orleans Saints, leaving the game behind after the 1999 season. After retiring as a coach, Ditka became an NFL analyst and color commentator at CBS and ESPN, as well as a restaurateur and TV pitchman. He also made appearances as himself on such shows and films as "L.A. Law," "Cheers," "3rd Rock From the Sun," "Entourage" and "Kicking & Screaming." He was also a forceful advocate for improved medical and retirement benefits for former players.

Unafraid to share his opinions about the game, in 1987, Ditka told "Sunday Morning" that he was against playing football in climate-controlled domed stadiums. "Domes have no place in sport, none," he said. "Unfortunately, people waste a lot of money building them … indoor domes should be used for roller rinks."

title: "Star Wars" lightsaber used in "I am your father" duel could sell for $1 million
summary: More than two dozen lightsaber props are up for auction, including ones wielded by Ewan McGregor's Obi-Wan Kenobi and Hayden Christensen's Anakin Skywalker in "Revenge of the Sith."
story: The lightsaber used by Darth Vader in the climactic duel against Luke Skywalker in "The Empire Strikes Back" is going up for auction next month.

The "Star Wars" prop was used in the duel in Cloud City where Vader tells Skywalker, "I am your father," in the second film of the original trilogy franchise. It is expected to fetch at least $1 million in the Ultimate Star Wars Auction to be held by Heritage Auctions on Nov. 12.

More than two dozen lightsaber props are up for auction, including ones wielded by Ewan McGregor's Obi-Wan Kenobi and Hayden Christensen's Anakin Skywalker in "Revenge of the Sith." Those two lightsabers are expected to go for at least $10,000 apiece.
The lot also includes an EE-3 carbine blaster wielded by villain Boba Fett throughout "The Empire Strikes Back" that is estimated to fetch more than $100,000.
A Hero Rebel DH-17 Pistol carried by Rebel Alliance troops in "The Empire Strikes Back" is expected to be sold for more than $10,000.

Also included are a Yoda puppet hand used by Frank Oz in the character's original appearance in "The Empire Strikes Back," C-3PO actor Anthony Daniels' signed, personal third-draft screenplay for the original 1977 "Star Wars," and a TIE Fighter pilot helmet from "Rogue One: A Star Wars Story."
A miniature snowspeeder that used to be part of Carrie Fisher's private collection and used in filming could fetch more than $10,000.

In July, a lightsaber with Luke Skywalker's severed hand from "The Empire Strikes Back" sold for $3.75 million at auction, the highest price ever fetched for a prop used in a "Star Wars" film, according to the auction house.

title: Paramount closes $110 billion deal to acquire Warner Bros. Discovery
summary: The merger unites two major movie studios, news operations CBS News and CNN and cable networks including Comedy Central and TNT.
story: Paramount Skydance on Tuesday completed its $110 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, uniting the movie studios behind "The Godfather" and the "Harry Potter" films into a media colossus rebranded as Skydance.
The merger also brings together the news outlets CBS News and CNN, major cable networks such as Comedy Central, Nickelodeon, TBS and TNT and the streaming services Paramount+ and HBO Max.
David Ellison, who orchestrated the merger as CEO of Paramount Skydance, will lead the new company along with co-CEO Ynon Kreiz, who was previously CEO of toy company Mattel.
In an email to employees, Ellison and Kreiz said the merger will allow the company to create a "stronger competitor, one with the scale to take on the biggest players in our industry."
"Today is a historic day, not just for Skydance but for our entire industry," Ellison said in a separate statement from Skydance.
As part of the deal, Warner Bros. shareholders will receive the cash equivalent of roughly $31 per share, the company said.

The deal came together after Paramount settled a July lawsuit from a coalition of 12 state attorneys general and a separate lawsuit from the Writers Guild of America (WGA). Both had sued to block it on antitrust grounds.

Under the settlement agreement, Paramount pledged to produce 30 films in each of the first two years after the merger and is barred from selling or closing the Paramount or Warner Bros. studio lots in Los Angeles for at least five years.

Paramount has also agreed to establish an editorial board to "help CNN and CBS maintain editorial independence," according to California Attorney General Rob Bonta's office. WGA agreed to settle its lawsuit after Paramount reached a deal with the states.
Ellison and Kreiz said the company is targeting $6 billion in cost savings, a move that some in the media industry are concerned could lead to job losses.
"Integrating two companies will bring change, including difficult decisions that affect our workforce," the co-CEOs said in the email to Skydance employees.

title: Eva Marie Saint, "North by Northwest" star, dies at 102
summary: Eva Marie Saint won an Oscar for her film debut opposite Marlon Brando in "On the Waterfront." She bucked many Hollywood conventions throughout her lengthy career.
story: Academy Award-winning actor Eva Marie Saint, who starred in such classics as "On the Waterfront" and "North by Northwest," but also bucked Hollywood conventions throughout her lengthy career, has died. She was 102.
Her publicist, Jeff Sanderson, said she died of natural causes at her home in Los Angeles, surrounded by family and loved ones.

A regal-looking blonde who ricocheted from playing sultry spies to Southern belles and Superman's stepmother, Saint made her motion picture debut opposite Marlon Brando in Elia Kazan's "On the Waterfront" (1954). Saint played Edie Doyle, whose brother was murdered by thugs working for a mob boss running a longshoremen's union; her character becomes involved with Brando's pugilistic dockworker Terry Malloy.

Her performance earned Saint one of the film's eight Academy Awards. (She was only the fourth person to win a best supporting actress Oscar for their film debut.) On the night she received her award, she was visibly pregnant. "I may have the baby right here!" she said. (Her son, Darrell, was born two days later.)

Saint married director-producer Jeffrey Hayden in 1951, and the couple stayed together for 65 years until his death in 2016. They had two children. Saint had made it clear that family was more important to her than her career.

"I had an agent once who wanted me to make many more movies," she told CBS' "Sunday Morning" in 2014. "I said, 'I can't. I can only do one a year, if that. I have children, young children.' And he said, 'Well, I guess you won't be a superstar.' And I said, 'Well, I guess not.'"
And what happened to that agent? "Fired him," she said.

She kept up her self-imposed limit on films; she also brought her extended family to the set of Otto Preminger's "Exodus" while filming in Cyprus and Israel. Despite not cranking out movies, Saint followed her Oscar win by appearing in many prestige projects, including "A Hatful of Rain," "Raintree County," "All Fall Down," "The Russians Are Coming, the Russians Are Coming," "Grand Prix," and the eponymous TV miniseries based on "How the West Was Won." She also received five Emmy nominations, and won for the 1990 TV movie "People Like Us." At age 97, she appeared on a podcast series.

But perhaps her most memorable performance was as Eve Kendall, a mysterious blonde who crosses paths with Cary Grant's Roger Thornhill as he runs from murderous spies in the 1959 Alfred Hitchcock thriller "North by Northwest." Little does Thornhill realize that Kendall herself is a secret agent.
Saint said Hitchcock's direction to her playing a sexy spy was simple: "Three things: Lower your voice. Don't use your hands. And look directly into Cary Grant's eyes at all times," she recalled.

Hitchcock had a reputation for being tough on young female actors, but not Saint. "I found that he was such a wonderful director, gentleman, funny, courteous, but there are other actresses who don't feel the same way. I don't even want to hear stories about him," she said.
Though playing a femme fatale was new to her, Saint said she wasn't surprised upon watching her performance. "No. I don't think actors are surprised," she said. "I mean, that's what we do."
"Too innocent" looking

Born on July 4, 1924, in Newark, New Jersey, Saint grew up in upstate New York, and attended Bowling Green State University in Ohio (where she was "Sweater Queen"). Originally planning to become a teacher, Saint began acting in student productions, and changed her career focus.

Moving to New York City, she trained at the Actors Studio with famed acting coach Lee Strasberg, and was hired for a production of "Mister Roberts" alongside Henry Fonda. But she was let go by director Joshua Logan; she found out it was because she was deemed "too innocent" looking. The actor who took her place was Jocelyn Brando (Marlon's sister).
Crushed, she was nonetheless determined not to let it dissuade her from pursuing an acting career.

When she was starting out, she told Variety in 2021, Saint and a fellow female actor would talk in a made-up language while riding the subway. "We were so frustrated about not getting jobs, so I suggested that we do something so people would notice us," she said. "When we'd start gabbing, we'd get a little audience. People would put down their papers and wonder, what language is that?"

Saint established herself in the early days of live television as a dramatic actor in plays on "Studio One," "Goodyear Television Playhouse," "GE True Theater" and "Philco Television Playhouse." She starred in the first TV production of Horton Foote's "The Trip to Bountiful," and repeated her role on Broadway, where she was spotted by Kazan, the "Waterfront" director.

He asked Saint to audition opposite Brando in an improvised scene. Upon entering the room, Brando put on a radio, and the two started dancing. "He did something to flip my skirt, and I was so embarrassed I cried a little bit afterward," Saint told the Santa Barbara Independent in 2010. "But Kazan saw the chemistry, and he could see that it could work for the movie."
She said Brando was wonderful to work with.

"What was a little scary about him, which worked for me in the movie, was his perception of people that was so keen," she said. "He could look at somebody or talk with them and hone into what that person was all about. And he would mention it about people around us. So sometimes I would sit there and think, 'If he knows that about that person, he must know more about me than I know about myself.' It made me a little self-conscious, but I used that in the movie. He'd been out in the world and I had been at home protected, so I used that."
Following "Waterfont," Saint appeared on TV in a musical version of Thornton Wilder's "Our Town" with Paul Newman and Frank Sinatra, and also appeared onstage numerous theater productions.

But Hollywood beckoned, and the Oscar winner starred opposite such actors as Montgomery Clift and Elizabeth Taylor ("Raintree County"), Paul Newman ("Exodus"), Warren Beatty ("All Fall Down"), James Garner ("36 Hours"), Richard Burton and Taylor ("The Sandpiper"), Yves Montand ("Grand Prix"), Gregory Peck ("The Stalking Moon"), Bob Hope ("That Certain Feeling," "Cancel My Reservation"), and Tom Hanks ("Nothing in Common").
Other film credits included "Because of Winn-Dixie," "Don't Come Knocking" (with Sam Shepard), "Superman Returns" (as Martha Kent), and "Winter's Tale."

On TV she appeared in "The Best Little Girl in the World," "Moonlighting," the two-hander "Taxi!!" (opposite Martin Sheen), "The Last Days of Patton" (with George C. Scott), "I'll be Home for Christmas," "My Antonia," the 1996 TV miniseries "Titanic," and "Frasier."

And in recent years, Saint podcasted. She played Marisa Tomei's aunt in "The Bus Ride," a short play streamed on "The Pack Podcast." She said the feisty character, written by Eugene Pack, was compelling, calling his work "so honest."
"I've lived long enough to know what's honest and what isn't, and Eugene's plays are," she said. "They're charming, they're positive, but they're not saccharine."
Saint is survived by her two children, Darrell and Laurette, four grandchildren and two great grandchildren, Sanderson's statement said.

title: Jim Bakker, who co-founded "The PTL Club" but fell into disgrace, dies at 86
summary: Jim Bakker, who along with his first wife Tammy Faye built an evangelical empire around "The PTL Club" TV show, only to lose it all over a sex scandal and financial crimes, has died at 86.
story: Branson, Mo. — Jim Bakker, who along with his first wife Tammy Faye built an evangelical empire around the hugely successful "The PTL Club" TV show, only to lose it all over a sex scandal and financial crimes, has died. He was 86.
Bakker died Monday, his second wife, Lori Bakker, said in a statement. His cause of death was not immediately clear.
The pair lived near the Missouri entertainment town of Branson and filmed their TV show, "The Jim Bakker Show," there since it launched in 2003. Bakker suffered a stroke in 2020.

"He was a pioneer of Christian television, but to me, he was my husband, my best friend, and the man I was honored to walk beside through so many seasons of life and ministry," Lori Bakker said in a statement. "Jim loved people deeply. He loved this ministry, and he loved the friends and partners who stood with him throughout the years. Even in his final days, his heart was still for the work of God and for the Gospel to continue reaching the world."

But it was another evangelical program that made Jim and his first wife, Tammy Faye Bakker, cultural icons - so much so that they were often skewered in the 1980s and 1990s by late-night comedians and parodied on "Saturday Night Live." A theatrical movie on their lives, "The Eyes of Tammy Faye," was released in September 2021.

At its peak in the mid-1980s, the Bakkers' ministry included not only the TV show, which drew up to 13 million nightly viewers, but also the Christian-based Heritage USA theme park and hotel in Fort Mill, South Carolina.

Bakker was born in Muskegon, Michigan, and attended North Central Bible College in Minneapolis, where he met Tammy Faye. They married in 1961 and dropped out of college to start their own traveling ministry — he preached, she sang and played the accordion as they crossed the country visiting churches and tent revivals.

They caught the attention of televangelist Pat Robertson, and in 1965 launched a children's show on Robertson's Christian Broadcasting Network. By 1966, he was hosting "The 700 Club," a Christian talk show.
Bakker left CBN in 1972 and two years later formed the PTL Satellite Network. "The PTL Club" — PTL stands for "Praise the Lord" — became its signature show.
In its heyday in the 1980s, "The PTL Club" was drawing millions of viewers - and bringing in millions of dollars annually from followers.

Sort of a Christian version of "The Tonight Show," it featured chats with guests and Christian entertainers. Bakker offered upbeat sermons and Tammy Faye - charismatic and always wearing her trademark heavy mascara - sang. Most episodes were taped at their sprawling complex just south of Charlotte, North Carolina.
The couple was so famous that they were often parodied by TV comedians for their lavish lifestyle and Tammy Faye's abundant makeup.
Jim Bakker gets caught up in scandals

In March 1987, their empire began to crack when Bakker admitted to a sexual encounter with church clerk Jessica Hahn. Bakker was forced to resign from his own empire, turning over operations to pastor and broadcaster Jerry Falwell.
Tammy Faye stuck by Bakker, often with tears running down her mascara, even as many saw his downfall as a fitting symbol of the greed and hypocrisy of the 1980s.
Things only got worse.

In 1988, Bakker was indicted for mail fraud, wire fraud and conspiracy after an investigation of PTL's finances. He was convicted and sentenced to 45 years in federal prison, though the sentence was later reduced to eight years.
At a news conference after Bakker was found guilty, Tammy Faye stood in front of the microphones and sang the hymn, "On Christ the Solid Rock I Stand."

Their marriage crumbled and Tammy Faye divorced Bakker in 1992, just short of their 31st anniversary, while he was still in prison. She later married Roe Messner, a building contractor whose projects included the Heritage USA theme park. Messner was convicted of bankruptcy fraud in 1995 and spent about two years in prison.
Tammy Faye died of colon cancer in 2007.
Bakker was released on parole in 1994. He married his second wife, Lori, in 1998. The couple launched "The Jim Bakker Show" on the PTL Satellite Network five years later.

In June 2021, Bakker and his Morningside Church Productions Inc. settled a lawsuit accusing him of falsely claiming the health supplement Silver Solution could cure COVID-19. The settlement called for $156,000 in refunds to people who paid money or gave contributions to obtain the product in the early days of the pandemic.
The lawsuit said Bakker and a guest made the cure claim during 11 episodes in February and March of 2020.
Bakker and Tammy Faye had two children. He and his second wife adopted five children in 2002.

title: Coco Gauff decries "insane" amount of online racism after China match dispute
summary: Coco Gauff said she received an "insane" amount of racist comments on social media following a controversial point in her China Open match against home player Sun Xinran.
story: Beijing — Coco Gauff said she received an "insane" amount of racist comments on social media following a controversial point in her China Open match against home player Sun Xinran.

Gauff requested a video review, prompting some boos from the crowd, after electronic advertising boards lining the court flickered during a point late in the first set of her 7-5, 6-1 third-round victory over Sun, a 16-year-old who recently won the U.S. Open junior title.

"Hey everyone, you can dislike me or disagree about what happened without being racist," Gauff, who is Black, said in a reply on X. "The amount of racist comments/dms I've received in the last few hours is insane. Lastly, I'm not a cheater or a thief."
Sun appeared about to win the point when Gauff stopped playing. The chair umpire then ordered the point to be replayed.
Gauff, a two-time Grand Slam champion ranked No. 4, went on to take control of the match on Monday.
"Xinran is (an) incredible talent and player, I apologized for the situation at the end of the match and she completely understood," Gauff added in another post.
Sun, who was given a wild card entry by tournament organizers and was making her WTA Tour debut, appeared distraught after the loss.
Gauff, who reached the fourth round of Wimbledon as a 15-year-old in 2019, sympathized with Sun.

"I did not like to see her so emotional as I've been there and I really understand what it is like but this is just the beginning of an incredible career," Gauff said. "It was an honor to share the court in front of her home crowd."

title: Aaron Sorkin on "The Social Reckoning": "Maybe we can't handle the truth"
summary: Sixteen years after "The Social Network," his Oscar-winning film about Mark Zuckerberg, Aaron Sorkin turns from Facebook's origins to its consequences with "The Social Reckoning," about a Facebook whistleblower.
story: Aaron Sorkin offered his remedy for writer's block: "I like to drive around and listen to music, and I try to start arguments with myself, talking out loud. … You're making me sound crazy now!"
But, he adds, that's where some of the best ideas come from. "One out of every 50 times, and I'll take those odds any day," he said.

The odds paid off when Sorkin was working on "The Social Network." Sorkin won an Oscar for screenwriting, and helped define Facebook CEO Mark Zuckerberg – and an entire industry – in the popular imagination.
Sixteen years later, Sorkin wonders about the unintended consequences.

"I remember talking to Jesse Eisenberg, who played Mark Zuckerberg in 'The Social Network,' and how distressed he was that teenage boys were coming up to him; they wanted him to sign business cards that said, 'I'm CEO, bitch,' the way Mark had it," said Sorkin. "Jesse was saying, 'Wait a second, these people think Mark is a hero in this story and not a tragic hero.'
"Of course, I'm responsible," Sorkin said. "It wasn't my intention."
And perhaps that's one reason why Sorkin is revisiting Facebook and Zuckerberg in "The Social Reckoning," out this Friday.

Jeremy Strong plays a grown-up Zuckerberg, still awkward but far more powerful. The film is inspired by the real-life story of Facebook whistleblower Frances Haugen (portrayed by Mikey Madison), who in 2021 leaked thousands of internal documents to Wall Street Journal reporter Jeff Horwitz (played by Jeremy Allen White).
The Facebook Files (Wall Street Journal)
The Facebook Files (Wall Street Journal)

Haugen is still reflecting on Facebook, and Zuckerberg. "When I look at Mark, I view a lot of things about his experience of the world as a tragedy," she said. "Here's a person who rose to power when he was 19 years old, surrounded by yes-men for his entire adult life. He's been able to immediately isolate himself from consequences for 20 years."
The consequences for the rest of us are depicted in "The Social Reckoning": disinformation, extremism and division.

Sorkin says Facebook studied how and why its content was shared. "In 2018, engagement was going down, so they tweaked the algorithm," he said. "That is significant because they knew, they had done plenty of research showing that the things most likely to be reshared are anything that makes you angry – rage bait. That's what they did, and it worked."

On set in Vancouver this past July, we saw Sorkin (who's also directing the film) bring his signature rapid-fire dialogue to life. "I get very nervous when there aren't four walls," he said. "I've written very few exterior scenes in my life. It is mostly people talking in rooms."

Asked what he listens for when directing, Sorkin said, "Well, you used the word 'listen,' which is what I'm doing. I'm very conscious of the music of the language. My parents started taking me to see plays starting from when I was very little. And I loved the sound of dialogue. It sounded like music to me, just these great actors saying words that are crashing against each other. And I wanted to imitate that sound. And so, when I'm writing, what a line of dialogue sounds like is as important to me as what it means."

The movie opens just as Sorkin's first script, "A Few Good Men," returns to Broadway. Made into the 1992 hit film, it similarly examines another large institution wrestling with the truth. Its most famous line – "You can't handle the truth" – also seems to directly apply to "The Social Reckoning."

"I think the theme is you're not getting the truth in 'The Social Reckoning,'" said Sorkin. "I think that we can handle the truth, but ... you know what? I'm going to take that back. Maybe we can't handle the truth, and that the reason why so many people believe things that are flat-out untrue is that the lie is easier to believe.

"For instance, you can tell people 'til you're blue in the face that the undocumented immigrant population commits fewer crimes per capita than citizens; they won't hear that. They will only hear that immigrants are the cause of their problems," he said.
Meta, Facebook's parent company, declined to comment on the film. It's repeatedly said it's working to stop the spread of dangerous or harmful content.

The film arrives as Meta faces billions of dollars in settlements and verdicts over claims its platforms harmed the mental health of young users, with more cases headed to trial. And with Meta now competing in AI, whistleblower Frances Haugen worries. "There have been many whistleblowers that have come out of Meta's AI teams talking about the lack of safety," she said. "I would pause before rushing into giving Mark the level of power that he's trying to seize when it comes to AI."
It's the power Zuckerberg already wields that has kept Aaron Sorkin writing.

Asked what he would say to the Facebook co-founder if he had a moment with him face-to-face, Sorkin replied, "You want to make the world a better place? Don't make the truth up for grabs. Don't be indifferent to the truth. And he can do that."

title: Can GLP-1 drugs help people stop throwing away their money?
summary: Researchers will explore whether weight-loss drugs can deter risky or impulsive financial decisions. "It might be very good financially for the average person," one neuroscientist said.
story: A growing body of research suggests GLP-1 drugs can do more than just help people lose weight by curbing addictive behaviors. Now, experts at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania want to see whether the drugs can benefit people's bank accounts by reducing risky financial decisions, such as gambling or compulsive shopping.

"We believe GLP-1s will ultimately lead to some structural remodeling of the brain, which is where some of those long-term impacts on food choice could show up, but also on financial decision-making," Michael Platt, a neuroscientist and professor at Wharton, told CBS News.
"It might be very good financially for the average person — maybe they're putting more money into savings," he added.

In a first-of-its-kind study, Platt and his fellow researchers will examine how GLP-1s influence the body's reward system, a network of brain structures that reinforces certain behaviors, to see whether the drugs suppress temptations such as luxury purchases, gambling or other activities that people often find hard to control.
If that proves true, GLP-1s could help Americans resist risky financial decisions and potentially develop better spending and saving habits, Platt said.
Risks and rewards

The body's reward system "underlies all consumption decisions," he explained. The researchers posit that GLP-1s could make people more responsible decision-makers through a simple injection, a habit that might otherwise take years to cultivate on their own, Platt said. That hypothesis stems from earlier research by Geoff Cook, the CEO of Noom, a digital health company that is funding the Wharton study.

"There is anecdotal speculation in high-risk professions that dampening reward drive might also dampen appetite for risk and very high returns," Platt said in an overview of the Wharton study, referring to professions such as stock trading. "At the other end of the spectrum, the same shift could potentially help ordinary consumers resist impulsive spending and favor longer-term financial goals."

A 2026 Northwestern Mutual study found that 73% of Americans actively participated in, or considered pursuing, highly speculative activities like sports betting and investing in cryptocurrencies because they believed these methods were more effective at achieving their financial goals than conventional, less risky methods, such as investing in index funds.
How spending lights up your brain
The Wharton team plans to recruit about 180 participants for the study, which will run from mid-October through around March 2027 at the University of Pennsylvania's MindCORE research lab.

Researchers will ask participants basic questions about their demographic background, mental health and GLP-1 use, if applicable, and also to complete a short cognitive exercise. The research subjects will then undergo magnetic resonance imaging while performing four tasks — two focused on food and two on financial decisions.

Scientists will monitor MRI activity for clues about how their brains' reward systems — which process value, reward and decision-making and involve neurotransmitters such as dopamine — respond to that stimulus.

For the first financial task, participants will be shown a series of 14 images of products, services, experiences and spending opportunities such as the Powerball jackpot. The technique, called passive viewing, helps researchers monitor people's spontaneous brain responses to certain images without asking them to take any action. The Wharton researchers said they will avoid showing images featuring recognizable brands or logos to ensure that the person's neural response is not skewed by brand familiarity or preference.
"The passive financial task allows us to compare responses to practical, need-based purchases versus more discretionary and enjoyment-oriented rewards," the researchers wrote in laying out the study.
Can GLP-1s change the need for immediate gratification?

During the second phase of the study, participants will be asked to make a financial decision and indicate their response by pressing a button on the MRI machine. For example, would they prefer $20 now or $50 in two months?
"It's a trade-off between immediate gratification and getting something that you might know is actually of higher value, but you'd have to wait for it," Platt told CBS News.

The MRI scan will show changes in blood flow and oxygen levels that indicate which parts of the brain are being activated and how participants value certain financial options in the study compared to others.

"One of our main questions concerns subjective value, meaning how desirable a food or financial option is to a particular person, and whether this valuation differs with GLP-1 use," other researchers involved in the study told CBS News in an email.

After the MRI, the participants will have to follow through on one of the decisions they made during the study. For example, if they said they would rather receive $50 in two months than $20 immediately, they would later receive the larger sum.
"That ensures that you are being honest and blind with your preferences," Platt said. "You will have to face the consequences of your decision."
