title: AI leaders lobby Trump health officials in government-run chat room
summary: A Slack workspace has served as a war room for AI industry insiders and Trump administration officials to launch a rapid campaign aimed at persuading Americans to manage their healthcare and medical records on apps.
story: A cadre of elite techies, financiers, and high-level Trump administration officials have spent a year quietly charting an extraordinary and rapid campaign to persuade Americans to use apps and other artificial intelligence-powered tools to manage their healthcare and medical records.

As that campaign has unfolded, administration officials have granted tech companies an unusual opportunity to nudge the nation's health department toward a loosely regulated future for AI health apps in which the government reimburses them for services as it does medical professionals.

In February, federal health officials invited those businesses — including tech giants Microsoft, Anthropic, OpenAI, Apple, and Google — to a listening session on conversational AI products for patients, such as chatbots. Representatives from at least 35 industry organizations attended the meeting held by the Food and Drug Administration, which is responsible for regulating health apps as medical devices. Companies were prompted in advance to explain their AI products and how they access patients' sensitive medical information.

But the meeting did not appear on the FDA's public calendar or regulatory notices, nor was the public invited. Rather, the invitation for a select group to help shape federal policy governing AI in healthcare was extended in a chat room on the messaging service Slack.

"This is a great opportunity to support HHS' goals and share your state-of-the-art understanding of safe Conversational AI development and monitoring to help FDA shape future guidance," CMS senior policy adviser Morgan Taylor wrote in the Slack workspace.

The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services has not formally announced the chat room through federal regulatory channels, though CMS officials have talked about it at industry conferences. Legal experts said the chat room resembles a federal advisory panel, which would be required to operate in public view.

KFF Health News reviewed thousands of Slack messages, meeting transcripts, and video recordings that reveal how the Trump administration has granted the industry a direct line to top government officials — including former head of the Department of Government Efficiency Amy Gleason.

The conversation took place behind the scenes as federal health officials publicly worked to integrate AI and other technology into nearly every aspect of healthcare, a plan they've branded the "Health Technology Ecosystem."

"We wanted to give industry a chance to play in the sandbox of government-supported healthcare," CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz said in September at the public launch of an initiative that allows health apps to bill Medicare for AI services such as wearable device tracking. Last week, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. delivered an enthusiastic endorsement of AI in healthcare, claiming it is "much better informed than any doctor in the country."

Meanwhile, HHS staff even promised that a recently launched Medicare App Library would serve as a lucrative pipeline for those businesses to get new users. The library's webpage currently promotes only two dozen commercial apps to millions of American seniors and those with disabilities.
As Trump officials sell it, Americans will get easier access to their medical records so apps can swiftly provide health or wellness advice. In practice, however, so will the tech companies.
Doctors, meanwhile, are increasingly worried about how patients use and share their medical records with the nascent technology.

"Some of these tools just aren't ready for primetime," said John Whyte, CEO of the American Medical Association. "We don't have enough data about them. We don't understand how they work, how they're using the information. There's no liability if these tools get things wrong."
CMS officials declined to answer several questions about the Slack workspace, including about its legality.

"CMS is focused on giving Medicare beneficiaries greater access to their health information and useful digital tools while promoting an open, interoperable healthcare system," Gleason, now chief product officer for the newly created Office of Health Technology and Products at CMS, wrote in an emailed statement. "The Health Technology Ecosystem is an open, voluntary technical collaboration. CMS will continue working with patients, providers, payers, technology organizations, and other stakeholders to make health information more accessible and useful to the Americans it serves."
The FDA did not respond to a request for comment.
The conversation begins
The behind-the-scenes effort to funnel more Americans to AI-powered health apps began in August 2025 in the Slack workspace.
"Welcome all!" Gleason wrote. "Please be sure to read the Code of Conduct and see the Channel list as well to help you find channels that are relevant to you."

Gleason is best known for serving as the acting administrator of Elon Musk's Department of Government Efficiency, as it gained access to millions of Americans' sensitive personal and financial data, including at the Social Security Administration.
As her work with DOGE wound down last year, Gleason welcomed a variety of tech leaders, investors, and entrepreneurs to the chat room.

The Slack workspace's participants include representatives from major digital wellness companies like Oura Health, AI companies like Palantir, and investment outfits like 8VC, a venture capital firm associated with Kennedy's son Finn. While the Slack's member count has ballooned to 1,700 over the past year, only a handful of patient advocates, doctors, and hospital representatives are in it.
The code of conduct Gleason shared on Slack in August 2025 documented that CMS had quietly established a technology working group.

The document also set ground rules for the Slack workspace, noting that the group does not constitute an "advisory committee," nor would it be used "to obtain advice or recommendations for HHS, CMS, or any HHS/CMS officials." The code also advises that federal employees "are prohibited from endorsing any product, service, or enterprise."

Joseph Daval, a former FDA lawyer who is now a research specialist at Harvard Medical School, reviewed messages from the Slack workspace at the request of KFF Health News. He said the chat room in some ways resembles a federal advisory committee — an independent panel that can be formally stood up by an agency head, Congress, or the president to ensure agencies act in the best interest of the public rather than industry.
The law on advisory committees "was passed in part out of a concern about interest group capture, about anticompetitive capture of agency policymaking, about corruption," he said.
Daval said the chat group looks like a committee, with members interacting with one another and building consensus on preferred courses of action.
If it were a formal advisory committee, though, Daval said, it would be subject to certain "membership requirements having to do with independence and fair balance."
A "sales engine"
Over a series of video calls, CMS officials promised tech leaders participating in the Slack workspace that the agency would promote their health apps.

Jacob Shiff, the chief AI and technology officer at CMS' Innovation Center, told industry representatives in a Zoom meeting in February that he hoped the agency's work would be a "sales engine" for the health apps.

"We're going to have a directory of all the organizations," Shiff said in a video recording reviewed by KFF Health News. "The people on this call who hopefully will have amazing solutions that work will be the winners, and you have every incentive to obviously drive down your costs so you can be extremely profitable and scale. So hopefully we're selling — or enabling you guys to thrive."
A recording of the call had been publicly available through a Google Drive link but was made private the day after KFF Health News asked about comments made during the meeting.
CMS did not respond to queries about how the agency has decided which AI-powered health apps appear in the Medicare App Library or why federal employees have promised to promote the products.

Days before publicly launching the Medicare App Library, CMS officials promised AI tech leaders during an informal meeting that the new webpage would become an important distribution channel for health apps because Medicare enrollees would place trust in products listed on the CMS website.

"If medicare.gov is promoting it, for lack of a better word, then yeah, it would be an app that I would trust and explore," CMS' Taylor said during the April 7 meeting, channeling enrollees, according to a transcript of the call.

The Medicare App Library's webpage encourages older and disabled Americans to manage health conditions such as obesity, cancer, or diabetes using two dozen AI-driven apps developed by some of the world's largest corporations, including Microsoft and Google. Many of the apps promise in their product descriptions to give insight, perform analyses, or develop plans that will help patients lose weight or manage diabetes.

CMS officials have suggested to tech representatives during at least two meetings this year that those apps will be prioritized for a new agency program that reimburses companies for AI chatbot advice or wearable device tracking, according to video recordings.
CMS has not publicly divulged all the criteria it uses to decide which apps are listed in its library, but the webpage promotes apps still in their infancy.

Among them is Slothwise, a health app launched this year from a San Francisco apartment by a young, self-described biotech entrepreneur and triple citizen of Russia, Israel, and the U.S. The app says it "knows your whole health" by analyzing medical records and tracking health data for $9.99 a month. It has been reviewed on the Apple and Google app stores only a handful of times.
"I trusted slothwise with my health info because it was endorsed by medicare," one reviewer wrote in a Google review in August. "Connecting info was smooth and I learned a lot about my health."

In a statement, Slothwise CEO Sofia Sigal-Passeck did not answer questions about the size and medical expertise of her current team, nor about the availability of a doctor to consult with patients who use the app. The app, she said, is only "informational" at this time.

"I've spent years building at the intersection of AI and complex biological data," Sigal-Passeck wrote in an email. "A small team is not the same thing as an inexperienced team. Slothwise is built by physicians, PhD researchers and engineers."
"No regulation, no rulemaking"
What's often less clear — and buried deep in lengthy privacy policies — is that these apps are tapping into the intimate details of patients' medical records to fuel their AI-driven analyses.

Tech vendors have lobbied the government to treat these apps, once they are vetted and authorized by a third-party company, like a patient requesting records. That position gives apps sweeping access to pull sensitive health data from the national network through which providers electronically exchange medical records, called the Trusted Exchange Framework and Common Agreement, or TEFCA.

A small but influential group of those tech company executives directly made the case to federal health officials during a formal meeting in May, arguing that when health apps request medical records they should be treated as if they are standing "in the shoes" of a patient.

On Slack, tech vendors have lobbied for a "frictionless pathway" for verified users, after they've consented once, that allows the app to gain limitless access to patients' medical records from the TEFCA network.

Ryan Howells, a healthcare management consultant who lobbies for a Washington, D.C.-based digital health tech organization called the CARIN Alliance, has spearheaded an effort for patients — vis-à-vis apps — to more easily access medical records. He has regularly noted in Slack that health apps accessing TEFCA must be vetted by a third-party organization — one of which he sits on the board of — and agree to a code of conduct, developed by the alliance he lobbies for.

"What more can you do to have trust in these apps?" he wrote in a March Slack message, responding to concerns about how much patient consent is needed for apps to access medical records on the network.
Kristen Valdes, the CEO of b.well, a company that also connects apps to the TEFCA network, made a similar argument.
"My opinion is that we need to stop protecting patients from themselves," she wrote in the same message thread. "Full stop."

Howells did not respond to an emailed list of questions from KFF Health News. In an interview, Valdes told KFF Health News that her comment reflected her frustration at the "paternalism" of the healthcare system, which she said has historically made it difficult for patients to access their records. Although, she said, "there are going to be good and bad apps."
Other tech leaders worried in Slack about the approach.
One startup founder cautioned the group to think about the pitfalls of giving health apps broad leeway to pull medical records.

"We might all be good, honest actors here but security & privacy systems have to be designed around the presence of malicious actors – especially if we want this system to scale up to thousands of apps," wrote Jason Kulatunga, who runs Fasten Health, a medical records management platform.

Gleason, the CMS official, has publicly championed the vision shared by Howells and Valdes. In her speeches, she frequently urges doctors to accept patient medical records directly from apps and calls on them to "Kill the Clipboard," also the title of a 2025 white paper co-authored by Howells that urges doctors' offices to abandon paper records.

Last month, Gleason spoke to a crowd gathered at a swanky hotel in Washington for an event hosted by the MAHA Institute, a think tank that supports Secretary Kennedy's agenda. She laid out her work with tech companies over the past year as she discussed the Trump administration's efforts to make medical records more digitally accessible.
As she told it, more Americans can now download an app and access their medical records.
"Once you've verified your identity you can just click a simple button and say, I'd like my medical records into whatever app I choose," Gleason said.
She continued: "That was all done just — no regulation, no rulemaking — just by challenging industry to work together."

KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF — the independent source for health policy research, polling, and journalism.

title: Can GLP-1 drugs help people stop throwing away their money?
summary: Researchers will explore whether weight-loss drugs can deter risky or impulsive financial decisions. "It might be very good financially for the average person," one neuroscientist said.
story: A growing body of research suggests GLP-1 drugs can do more than just help people lose weight by curbing addictive behaviors. Now, experts at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania want to see whether the drugs can benefit people's bank accounts by reducing risky financial decisions, such as gambling or compulsive shopping.

"We believe GLP-1s will ultimately lead to some structural remodeling of the brain, which is where some of those long-term impacts on food choice could show up, but also on financial decision-making," Michael Platt, a neuroscientist and professor at Wharton, told CBS News.
"It might be very good financially for the average person — maybe they're putting more money into savings," he added.

In a first-of-its-kind study, Platt and his fellow researchers will examine how GLP-1s influence the body's reward system, a network of brain structures that reinforces certain behaviors, to see whether the drugs suppress temptations such as luxury purchases, gambling or other activities that people often find hard to control.
If that proves true, GLP-1s could help Americans resist risky financial decisions and potentially develop better spending and saving habits, Platt said.
Risks and rewards

The body's reward system "underlies all consumption decisions," he explained. The researchers posit that GLP-1s could make people more responsible decision-makers through a simple injection, a habit that might otherwise take years to cultivate on their own, Platt said. That hypothesis stems from earlier research by Geoff Cook, the CEO of Noom, a digital health company that is funding the Wharton study.

"There is anecdotal speculation in high-risk professions that dampening reward drive might also dampen appetite for risk and very high returns," Platt said in an overview of the Wharton study, referring to professions such as stock trading. "At the other end of the spectrum, the same shift could potentially help ordinary consumers resist impulsive spending and favor longer-term financial goals."

A 2026 Northwestern Mutual study found that 73% of Americans actively participated in, or considered pursuing, highly speculative activities like sports betting and investing in cryptocurrencies because they believed these methods were more effective at achieving their financial goals than conventional, less risky methods, such as investing in index funds.
How spending lights up your brain
The Wharton team plans to recruit about 180 participants for the study, which will run from mid-October through around March 2027 at the University of Pennsylvania's MindCORE research lab.

Researchers will ask participants basic questions about their demographic background, mental health and GLP-1 use, if applicable, and also to complete a short cognitive exercise. The research subjects will then undergo magnetic resonance imaging while performing four tasks — two focused on food and two on financial decisions.

Scientists will monitor MRI activity for clues about how their brains' reward systems — which process value, reward and decision-making and involve neurotransmitters such as dopamine — respond to that stimulus.

For the first financial task, participants will be shown a series of 14 images of products, services, experiences and spending opportunities such as the Powerball jackpot. The technique, called passive viewing, helps researchers monitor people's spontaneous brain responses to certain images without asking them to take any action. The Wharton researchers said they will avoid showing images featuring recognizable brands or logos to ensure that the person's neural response is not skewed by brand familiarity or preference.
"The passive financial task allows us to compare responses to practical, need-based purchases versus more discretionary and enjoyment-oriented rewards," the researchers wrote in laying out the study.
Can GLP-1s change the need for immediate gratification?

During the second phase of the study, participants will be asked to make a financial decision and indicate their response by pressing a button on the MRI machine. For example, would they prefer $20 now or $50 in two months?
"It's a trade-off between immediate gratification and getting something that you might know is actually of higher value, but you'd have to wait for it," Platt told CBS News.

The MRI scan will show changes in blood flow and oxygen levels that indicate which parts of the brain are being activated and how participants value certain financial options in the study compared to others.

"One of our main questions concerns subjective value, meaning how desirable a food or financial option is to a particular person, and whether this valuation differs with GLP-1 use," other researchers involved in the study told CBS News in an email.

After the MRI, the participants will have to follow through on one of the decisions they made during the study. For example, if they said they would rather receive $50 in two months than $20 immediately, they would later receive the larger sum.
"That ensures that you are being honest and blind with your preferences," Platt said. "You will have to face the consequences of your decision."

title: Why you just got a $90 Social Security check — and who missed out
summary: Millions of seniors are getting $90 direct deposits from Social Security this week, prompting questions about the source of the money.
story: Millions of seniors are receiving $90 deposits from the Social Security Administration this week, prompting some to question the source of the money. The checks are tied to the Trump administration's announcement that it would send checks to about 20 million Medicare enrollees to lower healthcare costs.

President Trump on Friday announced that the administration would send the money to some participants in the healthcare plan's Part B, which pays for doctor visits, outpatient care and preventive screenings. About one-third of Medicare Part B's 62.9 million enrollees are eligible, with about 40 million not qualifying for the payments.

The payments are funded by the Medicare Improvement Fund, established by Congress to improve and support the original Medicare fee-for-service program. Experts say the $90, while helpful, won't fully offset higher costs facing Medicare recipients.

Premiums for Part B rose by more than $200 annually in 2026 and are projected to increase by nearly $80 in 2027, according to the Medicare trustees' most recent annual report. The standard monthly premium for Part B in 2026 is $202.90, a figure that's expected to rise to $209.50 next year.
Americans of all ages are grappling with rising healthcare costs, which they cite as a top financial concern, according to polling from nonprofit health policy research organization KFF.
Who qualifies for the $90 checks?

Seniors enrolled in Part B under traditional Medicare and who don't pay income-related premiums or receive premium assistance from Medicaid are eligible for the one-time payment. Beneficiaries enrolled in Medicare Advantage are ineligible for the payments.
That leaves more than 20 million Part B enrollees who are eligible, according to a CMS fact sheet.

"People who are paying the income-related premium have higher incomes to begin with, so the thinking is that they may be better able to absorb higher costs and wouldn't benefit as much from the $90 payment as people with lower incomes," Juliette Cubanski, vice president and director of the Program on Medicare Policy at KFF, told CBS News.
Medicare Advantage isn't the same as traditional Medicare, which is likely why those enrollees don't qualify for the payments, she added.
The agency said the initiative improves Medicare and makes coverage more affordable by putting "healthcare dollars back where they belong – in the hands of our Medicare beneficiaries."
How will the money be sent?

Most eligible beneficiaries will receive the $90 rebate through a direct deposit from the Social Security Administration on or around Oct. 8, according to the CMS fact sheet. Some seniors reported receiving the payments or pending deposits on Tuesday, according to social media reports.

Some beneficiaries will receive a $90 paper check from the U.S. Department of the Treasury later in October. It will include the following message: "Medicare Improvement Fund Payment; $90 Payment to Offset October Premium."
Some advocates say the paper payments could go unnoticed by seniors, especially given the volume of mail many receive from insurers during open enrollment season.

Dr. Ed Wu, co-founder of Pinnie, a healthcare advocacy company that helps Medicare recipients navigate their benefits, told CBS News that the checks won't reach many seniors who sorely need assistance affording healthcare, including rising premiums and prescription drug costs.
"While useful, a $90 check is very little compared to what's coming down the pike in terms of continual increase in premiums," he said.

About one-third of the 20,000 patients his group has served over the past years say they are most concerned about high drug costs. He added that roughly one in eight seniors said they put off filling prescriptions for cost-related reasons.

He believes that the roughly $2 billion drawn from the Medicare Improvement Fund for the $90 checks would've been better spent making longer-lasting structural changes to Medicare that help serve more of the program's beneficiaries.
Why are 40 million people left out?
About 40 million Medicare Part B enrollees are ineligible for the $90 payment. They include:
Seniors enrolled in Medicare Advantage plansThose who pay an income-related adjusted premiumPeople who do not live in the U.S.Beneficiaries who receive premium assistance
Seniors enrolled in Medicare Advantage plans
Those who pay an income-related adjusted premium
People who do not live in the U.S.
Beneficiaries who receive premium assistance

Eligible beneficiaries enrolled in Medicare Part B can call 1-800-MEDICARE to determine whether or not they qualify for the one-time check. Beneficiaries who want to check on the status of their payment can call the Social Security Administration at 1-800-772-1213 beginning on Oct. 15.

title: Google unveils Gemini AI agent to handle workplace tasks
summary: The Gemini agent can write and run code, integrate into apps like Gmail, and help workers knock out everyday workplace tasks, Google said.
story: Google on Thursday unveiled a new AI agent tailored for workplace tasks, positioning it to compete with other technology giants racing to offer their own virtual office assistants.

Called Gemini, the AI is a "universal agent" that can write and run code, create images and media and integrate with Google products like Gmail, Docs, Drive and Sheets, as well as third-party apps like Slack and Microsoft 365, Google said in its statement.
Thomas Kurian, the CEO of Google Cloud, shared the new product during a keynote address at Gemini at Work 2026 on Thursday, an annual event where Google showcases its suite of AI technology.

Google said the agent can seamlessly integrate into people's workflow, acting like a co-worker that can carry out tasks autonomously. Workers can delegate tasks to the agent, and it will return a finished product, Kurian said in the company's blog post.

"Gemini can function as your personal assistant or as a team member, where it works on behalf of a group of people, like a project manager within a team, or on behalf of a specific role in an organization, like an analyst in your finance department," he wrote.

To execute on certain tasks, Gemini can create its own "sub-agents," which Google described as "temporary, job-specific agents, each with their own identity," that can work together to accomplish goals over several days.
The AI agent, which runs in the Cloud, is designed to build memory and skills based on the tasks it's assigned and the questions users ask it.
"You never have to re-brief it or wonder which machine you told it to do something on," Kurian wrote in the blog post.

Gemini joins a growing field of AI agents marketed for personal and workplace use. In September, Meta introduced Muse, a personal AI assistant that has been downloaded millions of times. OpenAI followed suit late last month with the introduction of "Dots", an "AI helper" available to ChatGPT users with Pro and Business Premium accounts.

title: "America's Startup" competitors use AI to launch businesses from their dorms
summary: Young entrepreneurs are tapping AI to launch a range of businesses, from analyzing your skin to helping wine growers analyze crop yields.
story: One startup uses artificial intelligence to help winemakers better predict crop yields. Another uses insights gleaned from AI to enable earlier detection of skin cancer, while a third develops a seaweed-based hydrogel fire suppressant that's free of "forever chemicals."

The entrepreneurs behind these tech-forward startups have one thing in common: They started the companies from their college dorm rooms to participate in "America's Startup," a government-backed collegiate innovation competition that's part of America250, the congressional commission behind the U.S.'s 250th anniversary celebration.

America250 chair and the 43rd Treasurer of the U.S., Rosie Rios, who leads America's Startup, told CBS News she expects a wave of innovation led by Generation Z entrepreneurs, who will be the first AI-native cohort of workers to enter the job market upon graduation.

"They really hit the ground running and are not intimidated by it," Rios said. She also thinks AI will help broaden the skills and experience of new entrants to the job market, much as the internet did for millennials.
"It's no longer what they learned at home or in a classroom — it's what they see and have access to," said Rios, adding that AI helps eliminate some of the hurdles to launching companies.
"Idea machines"

Recent research from the Bank of America Institute shows the rate of U.S. business formation is rising, largely driven by Gen Z founders. In June, Gen Z surpassed all other generations in growth in new business registration applications. Researchers concluded that starting a business may be viewed as a desirable pathway to career success as younger workers navigate a challenging labor market.

Additionally, AI can be deployed to perform functions such as bookkeeping or content creation, allowing founders to operate as "solopreneurs" and save on personnel costs, researchers at the Bank of America Institute noted.

"They've been exposed to so much because of their comfort with technology that they are basically idea machines," Rios told CBS News. "AI could be very advantageous for this group, and they have demonstrated their ability to use it for good, so far."

Kayan Shah, a college sophomore and co-founder of Graft Systems, was one of 10 winners of last year's America's Startup competition. He's partnering with vineyards across San Francisco to test and further develop the company's technology, which collects images of plants and combines them with machine-learning models that predict how many grapes they'll yield by analyzing variables such as weather, sunlight and a vineyard's location.
"AI could take over many, many jobs, but this is the status quo, so the only option you have is to make the best of it, and we're using it to help wine growers," Shah said.

While Shah isn't yet 21 and can't legally drink, he said he appreciates wine culture and wants to preserve it, citing a decline in alcohol consumption rates. Americans who say they drink alcohol fell to 54% last year, the lowest level in 90 years, according to an August 2025 Gallup poll.
Skin in the game

Another entrant in last year's startup contest pitched a biotech company that helps people track their exposure to harmful ultraviolet rays and potentially detect skin cancer earlier. Kristina Schiffman, the founder of UV Sense, told CBS News the company uses AI to educate people about their skin, including a tool for analyzing and tracking moles and other conditions.
"We take user inputs, including images and concerns about the skin, and use AI to help people make an informed decision about what they should do," Schiffman said.
"If you have a freckle you're concerned about, you can upload photos and use AI to monitor its shape, size and color, and we can recommend a dermatologist visit," she explained.

Aspiring entrepreneurs can submit their best ideas to America's Startup before applications close on Oct. 8 at 7:59 p.m. EDT. The competition will award a total of $1 million in cash and prizes to a series of winners. Applicant teams can win up to $50,000 each.

An investor council, which will review proposals and have the opportunity to invest, includes some of the nation's most prominent entrepreneurs, such as Apple co-founder Steve Wozniak and Sarah Friar, chief financial officer at ChatGPT developer OpenAI.

title: Congress tried to stop surprise medical bills. It created another problem.
summary: Healthcare providers and middlemen are exploiting a loophole in a 2020 law designed to shield consumers from surprise medical bills.
story: A law designed to protect patients from surprise medical bills succeeded in eliminating unexpected charges, but spawned a lucrative arbitration industry with providers and specialized middlemen extracting payments far above benchmark billing rates.
The practice is ultimately driving up healthcare costs for consumers, a CBS News investigation found.

The arbitration system Congress created to settle disputes between insurers and out-of-network providers allows doctors and resolution specialists acting on their behalf to win payments many times higher than typical rates for medical services. Those costs don't disappear: Much of the money comes from employer-sponsored health plans, meaning workers may ultimately pay through higher premiums or reduced benefits.

Under the arbitration system established by the No Surprises Act, which took effect in 2022, insurers are paying healthcare providers hundreds of dollars for routine lab tests that typically cost between $10 and $30, industry researchers told CBS News. In one instance, a plastic surgeon was awarded more than $400,000 to perform a breast reduction, a procedure the insurer said it had previously paid the doctor between $6,000 and $30,000 to perform.
The plastic surgeon, Dr. Norman Rowe, routinely was awarded around 170 times the benchmark rates for his services under the NSA's arbitration system, a CBS News analysis of public data shows.
A spokesman for Dr. Rowe told CBS News that insurers had manipulated benchmark rates to lowball doctors and create "artificially low reimbursement rates."

"Dr. Rowe uses the widely recognized gold standard FairHealth benchmarks set by the independent nonprofit FairHealth.org using reliable and objective market data. FairHealth data is so reliable that it is incorporated into statutes and regulations around the country and serves as the official data source for many state health programs," the spokesman added.

In addition to the typical benchmark rate arbitrators consider (known as the "qualifying payment amount," or QPA), FairHealth provides another rate that can be used during the dispute resolution process. Medicare rates, meanwhile, may not be considered.

CBS News found that another doctor — Long Island spine surgeon Vadim Lerman — was being awarded an average of 280 times the benchmark rates in arbitration. He declined an interview, but a spokesman for Lerman said that "the suggestion that a physician is receiving 'hundreds of times' above benchmark rates is incorrect. No comparison should be made to the insurer's initial offer — which can be inappropriately low for a complex surgical procedure — and the award given to the physician."
"Baseball-style arbitration"
Insurers have, in many cases, been forced to pay high rates like those Dr. Rowe charges under the law's so-called "baseball-style" or "pendulum" arbitration system.

In an arbitration under the No Surprises Act, insurers and providers each propose a rate for a given service. There's no room for negotiation, as an arbitrator must choose between one of the two parties' suggested figures.

Arbitrators side with providers in more than 85% of the cases, according to Leland Robbins, a product leader at Turquoise Health, a data transparency startup. Some arbitrators – officially called certified Independent Dispute Resolution, or IDR, entities – have track records of siding with providers in an even larger share of cases, according to Robbins' group.
He told CBS News that while patients are no longer being surprised by large medical bills, there is a catch to the new system.

"The transaction didn't go away. It went behind closed doors and has moved into this arbitration process when a payer and a provider can't agree what the fair price should be," Robbins said. "Given that 70% of these awards are being taken out of employer-sponsored health plans, consumers are going to start seeing it when it comes time for open enrollment."
He added, "You know, employers are not able to withstand and absorb these kinds of big fees. They're going to be probably not paying for as much of your premiums."

Last year, 15 government-certified arbitrators earned fees per case, with 17 arbitrators designated to do this work today. Each side in the dispute — the healthcare provider and the insurer — pays into the process prior to the arbitrator making any decision.

During the first six months of 2025, insurers and providers submitted 1.2 million new disputes to the arbitration portal, while federal officials had only expected approximately 17,000 cases per year, research from the Center on Health Insurance Reforms (CHIR) at Georgetown University's McCourt School of Public Policy shows.
However, HaloMD, a company that files cases on behalf of providers, told CBS News that the initial estimates "were objectively flawed in how they calculated expected volume."
Collectively, arbitrators making the decisions have earned more than $2 billion in fees. None agreed to on-camera interviews with CBS News.
New Jersey House Rep. Frank Pallone, a Democrat and the lead sponsor of the No Surprises Act, blames private equity, in part, for breaking the system he helped create.
He said just a few private equity firms – which are increasingly buying up anesthesiology, radiology and emergency room practices — are driving arbitration cases.

Pallone told CBS News that doctors should be paid the equivalent of in-network rates for the services they provide, but said "we had no choice" but to introduce the arbitration system "if we wanted to actually get rid of surprise billing."
"I knew it was not going to go well, but I didn't know it was going to be this bad," he added.
Dispute resolution cottage industry

The law's arbitration provision has also created an opportunity for intermediaries to guide providers through the process and rake in profits by taking a cut of bills that are up to 1,000% above the benchmark rate for a service, CBS News found. Critics argue that such firms demand more money on providers' behalf, leading to the large settlements that drive up everyone's costs.

HaloMD bills itself as "the expert" in arbitration cases brought under the No Surprises Act. Founded by Texas couple Scott and Alla Laroque in 2022, the same year the No Surprises Act took effect, the company is one of the fledgling industry's biggest players.

Private equity firms also sometimes own both physician staffing firms and Independent Dispute Resolution entities, creating a conflict of interest and undermining the law's fairness. HaloMD is not private equity-backed, but Halo and two other groups with investments from buyout firms collectively handled more than 75% of disputes settled in arbitration last year, according to Georgetown University's Center on Health Insurance Reforms.

According to Halo, the firm made more than $1 billion for its clients, routinely earning awards that are nine times the benchmark rates for services. Halo takes a cut of the payouts but has not disclosed the amount.

Halo chief external affairs officer Patrick Velliky told CBS News that insurance companies, not firms like his, are responsible for driving up consumer healthcare costs by either not participating in the arbitration process or submitting ludicrously low offers.

"24% of the time, insurers lose by default. They didn't submit an offer at all. Another 9 1/2% of the time, insurers submit an offer, like a dollar or less," Velliky told CBS News. "So what that actually looks like, a patient goes to the E-D with a heart attack, we go to arbitration and the insurer is offering a total of $1.00."

He also said that insurance companies are offering misleading information about the benchmark rate. "Whatever the actual median in-network rate is, it's not what the insurer presented," Velliky told CBS News. "They're miscalculating it."
A federal court sided with providers on the issue this summer, saying the benchmark rate is "artificially low," pulled down by insurers' $0- or $ 1-reimbursement offers to doctors.
Proposed reforms
Pallone wants to reform the law to gut what he sees as the root of the issues arising from the No Surprises Act: arbitration.

He plans to introduce legislation this week to eliminate the arbitration process and stipulate that providers be paid in-network rates, even if they are out-of-network. Pallone's office also told CBS News that so-called ghost rates, which often drag the benchmark rate down, will be excluded from calculations moving forward.

"Whether it's the hospitals, the doctors, the nurse, they're really trying to care for people. Of course, all of them should have a decent income so they can live," the New Jersey lawmaker said. "But why should these outside investors be making all this money off the backs of, you know, your insurance premiums, essentially?"

title: Trump temporarily expands use of red-dyed diesel. Will it lower costs?
summary: Experts say the new executive order will have a limited impact on farmers and truckers who rely on diesel.
story: President Trump's new executive order allowing the use of red-dyed diesel on highways is aimed at lowering costs for truckers and farmers grappling with diesel prices that remain near record highs. But experts say they are skeptical that the order could deliver sweeping savings.
"It might lead to savings for some, but there are a lot of details that will prevent this from having widespread relief," Patrick De Haan, a petroleum expert at GasBuddy, told CBS News.

Mr. Trump announced the executive order on Tuesday during a midterm rally in Nebraska, saying the move will "officially waive the off-road requirement and allow anyone to purchase tax-free red-dye diesel for any reason."
Before the EO passed, farmers had to buy regular diesel for their trucks and on-road vehicles, which is subject to excise taxes, a White House official told CBS News in an email.
Now, they can use red-dyed diesel, which is exempt from the federal tax of 24.4 cents a gallon that applies to regular diesel.

The EO comes as diesel prices remain high, although they've eased slightly after reaching a record high last month of $6.53 a gallon. High diesel prices are placing financial strains on the nation's transportation, construction and agricultural industries, which rely heavily on the fuel to move goods and power equipment.
On Tuesday, the national average for a gallon of diesel stood at $6.32, according to AAA, compared to $3.76 before the war in Iran started.
Read on to learn more about red-dyed diesel.
What is red-dyed diesel?
Red-dyed diesel is tax-free diesel intended for off-road vehicles, including farm and construction equipment.

The fuel is dyed red because it allows state law enforcement to easily spot it if drivers are using it on roads and highways in an effort to skirt taxes. Violators may face large fines or penalties, including tax evasion.

Mr. Trump's executive order temporarily removes the limits on red-dyed diesel, allowing all drivers to use it without incurring taxes or penalties. However, it doesn't entirely eliminate taxes on red-dyed diesel.

Instead, it defers the federal excise tax for the remainder of 2026 and directs the Treasury secretary to explore ways to eliminate the requirement to pay the taxes, according to the White House. That means drivers could potentially be on the hook for a payment down the road, experts said.
"Whether anyone who makes the switch to dyed diesel suddenly gets a tax bill is the most unanswered question I have," De Haan said in a post on X.
The White House official said drivers will be liable for the deferred tax only if the Internal Revenue Service, at the direction of the Secretary of the Treasury, takes action to enforce it.
Will the Trump administration's EO lead to cost savings?
According to a White House fact sheet on the executive order, drivers who rely on diesel could save more than $100 each time they fill up.
However, many states also have bans on using red-dyed diesel on roads and highways. The White House said it is working with states to encourage them to also waive the ban.

But if some states don't waive their bans, it could lead to a "convoluted patchwork" of enforcement, which may ultimately deter trucks that need to cross state lines from using red-dyed diesel, De Haan added.

"If one state is enforcing red-dyed diesel and a trucker crosses over with dyed diesel, that could spell trouble, and [lead to] enforcement issues," he said. "Most of the large end users that could stand to benefit from lower prices probably won't get much of the benefit behind this."
The impact on farmers will also be muted, given that they already get tax-free diesel in most states, De Haan noted.
"Most of them have thousands of liters that they've been buying at tax-free, at scheduled intervals, I should say, and so it's not really any huge advantage," he told CBS News.

The EO will allow farmers to use red-dyed diesel in personal vehicles, but it will yield only minimal savings, he added. "I don't think that any farmer is going to be jumping for joy at the prospect of saving, you know, 50 or 60 cents a gallon on their personal vehicle."
Fails to address the supply issue
Experts noted that the EO doesn't address the lack of diesel supply, the key issue keeping prices elevated.
"The U.S. has about 105 million barrels of diesel in  inventory," Tom Kloza, chief energy adviser for Gulf Oil, told CBS News in an email. "This move doesn't increase or decrease that level."
In theory, the EO should still put downward pressure on diesel prices; however, swings in the diesel market could blunt progress toward lower prices, Kloza added.
Lowering prices without increasing supply could also stimulate demand, which could have the unintended consequence of driving up costs, De Haan pointed out.
"Part of the reason why we have these high prices is because economics is telling us that there are imbalances," he said. "So to ignore them and go ahead with this risks exacerbating the issue."

title: Paramount closes $110 billion deal to acquire Warner Bros. Discovery
summary: The merger unites two major movie studios, news operations CBS News and CNN and cable networks including Comedy Central and TNT.
story: Paramount Skydance on Tuesday completed its $110 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, uniting the movie studios behind "The Godfather" and the "Harry Potter" films into a media colossus rebranded as Skydance.
The merger also brings together the news outlets CBS News and CNN, major cable networks such as Comedy Central, Nickelodeon, TBS and TNT and the streaming services Paramount+ and HBO Max.
David Ellison, who orchestrated the merger as CEO of Paramount Skydance, will lead the new company along with co-CEO Ynon Kreiz, who was previously CEO of toy company Mattel.
In an email to employees, Ellison and Kreiz said the merger will allow the company to create a "stronger competitor, one with the scale to take on the biggest players in our industry."
"Today is a historic day, not just for Skydance but for our entire industry," Ellison said in a separate statement from Skydance.
As part of the deal, Warner Bros. shareholders will receive the cash equivalent of roughly $31 per share, the company said.

The deal came together after Paramount settled a July lawsuit from a coalition of 12 state attorneys general and a separate lawsuit from the Writers Guild of America (WGA). Both had sued to block it on antitrust grounds.

Under the settlement agreement, Paramount pledged to produce 30 films in each of the first two years after the merger and is barred from selling or closing the Paramount or Warner Bros. studio lots in Los Angeles for at least five years.

Paramount has also agreed to establish an editorial board to "help CNN and CBS maintain editorial independence," according to California Attorney General Rob Bonta's office. WGA agreed to settle its lawsuit after Paramount reached a deal with the states.
Ellison and Kreiz said the company is targeting $6 billion in cost savings, a move that some in the media industry are concerned could lead to job losses.
"Integrating two companies will bring change, including difficult decisions that affect our workforce," the co-CEOs said in the email to Skydance employees.

title: Coca-Cola reveals new flavors for Coke, Powerade and other brands
summary: Coca-Cola said it will roll out the new flavors, all fruit-inspired, in 2027. Here's what the beverage giant is planning.
story: Coca-Cola is refreshing its beverage lineup with a series of new fruit flavors.

The company said Monday that it will roll out "innovations" for its Coca-Cola, Fairlife, Mr. Pibb, Powerade and Topo Chico brands starting in 2027. Coca-Cola will showcase the new products at the National Association of Convenience Stores event in Las Vegas, Nevada, this week.

A Coca-Cola spokesperson said the company is also testing several new products in New York, New Jersey and Pennsylvania to gauge consumer interest in a prebiotic version of Coca-Cola Zero Sugar, Sprite Zero Sugar and Fresca.
Coca-Cola fans will have two new flavors to try next year: Coca-Cola Cherry Lime is scheduled to debut in February, and Coca-Cola Strawberry Float will make its premiere in the summer.

The cherry lime product is a new spin on Coca-Cola Cherry, while the strawberry float version appears to be a nod to the popular dessert that blends soda and ice cream. Both come in sugar and zero-sugar options.

Other Coca-Cola beverage brands are also set to get a fruit-inspired refresh next year. Powerade will add watermelon and lemon-lime zero-sugar options in January 2027. Mr. Pibb, a spicy cherry soft drink, will debut "Mr. Pibb Black-Current" in the spring, while a "berry-forward" flavor will be offered for a limited time.

Topo Chico, a carbonated mineral water product, will launch a pineapple-coconut flavor in February, building on its existing lineup of fruit flavors, which include raspberry with lemon, passionfruit and tropical mango, among others.

Core Power protein shakes, sold under the Fairlife brand, will be available in banana and strawberry beginning in January, the first new flavors in almost a decade. Both will contain 26 grams of protein, while the banana flavor will also be available in a 42-gram version.

title: Trump sending ACA and Medicare checks, but will they offset costs?
summary: President Trump sent $500 checks to some Affordable Care Act enrollees, while 20 million Medicare recipients will soon get $90 checks. Will they make a difference?
story: President Trump is sending checks to millions of Medicare and Affordable Care Act enrollees, with the White House describing the efforts as helping to "lower costs" for seniors and families. But experts say the payments may do little to offset rapidly rising healthcare expenses.
On Friday, Mr. Trump announced on Truth Social that his administration this month will send checks of about $90 to more than 20 million Medicare participants in the program's Part B plans.

That announcement followed the White House's Sept. 10 statement that $500 checks would be sent to about 1 million people who enrolled in an ACA plan this year through federal exchanges administered by the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services. The payments, described as refunds for overcharges, are for people who didn't receive ACA insurance subsidies.

"President Trump is delivering on his promises to lower costs for American patients by putting them first and taking on the special interests that have used the status quo in Washington to raise healthcare costs for Americans," the White House said in an Oct. 2 statement about the Medicare checks.

While the payments will help defray some of the healthcare costs paid by senior citizens and ACA-enrolled households, the money may not go far enough, health policy experts said. Americans cite healthcare costs as one of their top financial concerns, with almost 30% saying they've skipped or postponed healthcare treatments in the last year because of costs, according to polling from nonprofit health policy research organization KFF.

"A plan to lower healthcare costs is welcome, but President Trump's proposal to provide a one-time $90 payment to some Medicare beneficiaries will likely go unnoticed by most seniors," Max Richtman, CEO of the nonpartisan National Committee to Preserve Social Security & Medicare, told CBS News.
The White House said Mr. Trump is taking action to lower healthcare costs for millions of Americans.

"President Trump is enabling Americans to take control of their health by putting money directly back in the hands of Medicare patients," White House spokeswoman Allison Schuster said in a statement to CBS News. "In addition to guaranteeing discounted prices on prescription drugs through his Most-Favored-Nation drug pricing agreements, distributing $500 Obamacare Refund checks and increasing price transparency across the board, President Trump is delivering on his promise to lower costs for American patients by putting them first and taking on the special interests that have used the status quo in Washington to raise healthcare costs for Americans."

Mr. Trump has also promised $5,000 "dividend" payments to every U.S. adult if Republicans retain electoral control of both the House and Senate after the November midterms. Some economists and other experts have raised doubts about the feasibility of the payments, as they would require Congress to authorize more than $1 trillion in spending and could reignite inflation.
The Trump administration began sending the ACA checks on Sept. 30, while the Medicare checks will be sent starting in early October.
Higher Medicare Part B premiums

Premiums for Medicare Part B, which covers medical services such as doctor visits, outpatient care and preventive screenings, rose by more than $200 annually in 2026, and are forecast to rise by another $79 next year, according to June projections in the Medicare trustees' latest annual report.

That means the $90 check could fall short of covering the increased costs that seniors are already paying this year alone for their Part B plans, according to Juliette Cubanski, vice president and director of the Program on Medicare Policy at KFF.

"Receiving a one-time payment of $90 under this new plan from the Trump administration could be helpful, but it may not stretch very far when people are staring down higher costs for gas, heating their homes this coming winter, putting food on the table, keeping up with their mortgage payments," she said.
Rising ACA costs

Meanwhile, the $500 ACA check isn't likely to cover rising costs for people who get their health insurance through the program's marketplaces, said Cynthia Cox, senior vice president and director of the ACA program at KFF.
The average premium for enrollees rose by $780 this year, up 58% from 2025, according to a KFF analysis.

ACA plan costs have risen sharply in 2026, partly due to the expiration of enhanced premium tax credits, which Congress allowed to lapse in December. Those tax breaks had helped lower premium costs for millions of middle-class Americans.

"People this year are paying significantly more than they were paying last year for health insurance on the individual market," Cox told CBS News. "It's going to help some people, certainly — getting a $500 check is better than not getting a $500 check — but for most people it won't cover their full increased costs."

A more effective method to lower healthcare costs would be to restore the enhanced ACA premium tax credits, Brian Keyser and Natasha Murphy of the Center for American Progress, a liberal-leaning think tank that supports the ACA, wrote in a Sept. 17 blog post.
Millions left out
About 40 million Medicare Part B recipients don't qualify for the $90 payment, while about 18 million ACA enrollees won't get a $500 check, enrollment data for the programs shows.

The $90 checks will go to seniors enrolled in Part B under traditional Medicare who don't pay income-related premiums or receive premium assistance from Medicaid. Seniors who are enrolled in Medicare Advantage plans are also excluded from the checks, according to the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services.
The Medicare check is reminiscent of President Trump's proposal to send a $200 drug card to help seniors with out-of-pocket drug costs before the 2020 presidential election, Cubanski said.

While that plan never got off the ground, it was also timed just before an important election. The new Medicare payments, to be disbursed by direct deposit, are set to arrive only weeks before the Nov. 3 midterm elections.

Sen. Ron Wyden, a Democrat from Oregon and ranking member on the Senate Finance Committee, on Saturday called the $90 checks an "attempt to bribe the American public." But experts said the payments may barely register for some seniors.

"There's a question whether many of these payments might go unnoticed," Cubanski added. "People with Medicare get lots of mail from insurance companies and others trying to market plans during the open enrollment season, so this letter might get caught up in all the other mail that people are receiving."

title: When to book Thanksgiving and Christmas flights for the best deals
summary: Knowing when to buy plane tickets for holiday season travel can save you money. Here's the optimal time to book this year as airfares rise.
story: In trying to score the cheapest airfares for the holidays, when you book a flight often matters just as much as your travel dates. And this year, booking early is particularly important as airfares creep higher, new Google data shows.
Flights for travel around Thanksgiving will be cheapest in October, while people traveling around Christmas should lock in their itineraries by around Halloween, according to Google Flights.
When to book flights for optimal deals

It's best to book as early as possible when your travel dates are relatively fixed. For Thanksgiving, consumers will find the lowest fares 34 days before departure, according to Google Flights, which based its findings on five years of flight data. Thanksgiving is on Nov. 26, making Oct. 22 the best day to book travel for the Wednesday before the holiday. For the lowest fares on Turkey Day trips, travelers should aim to purchase tickets between 57 and 21 days before departure.

For flights around Christmas, the lowest fares will be available 56 days before departure. Travelers can land better deals between 33 and 67 days before their trips, according to Google Flights (as of Oct. 5, there are roughly 80 days before Christmas). The best flight deals will emerge between late October and mid-November, according to Google.
Other ways to save

To save money on flights, experts also recommend traveling off-peak, when fewer people will swarm the nation's airports. Data from the fare aggregator Hopper shows that traveling on Monday or Tuesday before Thanksgiving, rather than on Wednesday, can yield savings. Avoid returning on Sunday, Nov. 29, the company said.
The same advice applies around Christmas. Hopper advises avoiding flying on Dec. 18, 19 and 20 and on Dec. 27, the Sunday after Christmas Day.

Americans should expect higher-than-usual flight prices due to the Iran war, which has raised oil and jet fuel prices, the largest expense for airlines after personnel. Before the Middle East conflict began in late February, jet fuel averaged $99 per barrel globally, according to the International Air Transport Association. It peaked at $209 in April and hit $195 a barrel in mid-September, IATA said, citing data from S&P Global Energy Platts.
Hopper data shows that domestic round-trip airfares for Thanksgiving are averaging $402, up 31% from last year. Domestic round-trip Christmas flights are averaging $452, up 23%  from last year.

title: Gatorade sold in dozens of states recalled due to undeclared dyes
summary: Recalled Gatorade sold in 37 states could cause temporary "adverse health consequences," a federal regulatory agency says.
story: PepsiCo has recalled roughly 122,000 cases of Gatorade sold across the U.S. because the product contains undeclared dyes, the Food and Drug Administration said in a notice.

The recall affects cases with 28-ounce bottles of Gatorade Lemon Lime, Gatorade Lemon Lime Zero, Gatorade Orange and Gatorade Orange Zero that were sold in 37 states. The FDA said the beverages contain undeclared Yellow No. 6 and/or Yellow No. 5, artificial dyes that affect the product's color.

PepsiCo initiated the recall on Sept. 25. On Oct. 2, the FDA updated the recall to Class II, which means that exposure to the product "may cause temporary or medically reversible adverse health consequences," according to the regulatory agency.

The cases of Gatorade were sold in Alaska, Alabama, Arkansas, Arizona, California, Colorado, Florida, Georgia, Hawaii, Iowa, Idaho, Illinois, Indiana, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Michigan, Minnesota, Missouri, Mississippi, North Carolina, North Dakota, Nebraska, New Jersey, New Mexico, Nevada, New York, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, Washington and Wisconsin.
The recall number is H-0009-2027.
PepsiCo did not immediately respond to a request for comment on whether customers who bought the recalled Gatorade are eligible for a refund.

title: Trump says Russia will release millions of tons of diesel to help with costs
summary: Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed to release 300,000 tons of diesel immediately and millions more over the coming months.
story: President Trump announced Russia has agreed to provide the world with millions of tons of diesel fuel over the next several months in a bid to decrease skyrocketing global prices.

In a Truth Social post, the president said he had just gotten off the phone with Russian President Vladimir Putin, who had agreed to release 300,000 tons of diesel immediately. He said another 500,000 tons of diesel would be released in November, followed by 1 million tons in December.
"Additionally, based on the condition of their Diesel Refineries, Russia will then deliver, within a short period of time, 3,000,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel," Mr. Trump continued.
The Treasury Department also announced Friday that it would temporarily waive sanctions on Russia's energy sector to "allow the supply of Russian diesel to the global market."

In a statement from the Kremlin later Friday, Putin confirmed he and Mr. Trump spoke on the phone and that "Russia confirmed its readiness to supply oil and petroleum products to the American and global markets," and he was "confident this will have a positive impact on the entire global economy."

"An agreement was confirmed to continue personal contacts between the presidents of the two countries, as well as cooperation between the presidential administrations, special services, and other agencies," Putin's statement added.
The statement said Putin and Mr. Trump's call touched on "the prospects for resolving the Ukrainian crisis, and the situation surrounding Iran and various aspects of bilateral relations."
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy blasted the deal in a social media post, saying any easing of sanctions against Russia is a "weakness."

"Gifts to Putin will not bring peace or any benefit to the civilized world," Zelenskyy said in the post. "Russia will 'repay' the diesel with further terror and perfidy. Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged. What is needed is real de-escalation with Russia on a reciprocal basis."

The moves by the Trump administration mark a reversal of the tight sanctions that have constrained Russia's economy since Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Last month, Mr. Trump signed a bill designed to make it even harder for Russia to profit off oil and gas exports by imposing steep tariffs on the largest buyers of Russian energy.

Mr. Trump had earlier teased a "big announcement coming up on diesel" during remarks Friday at a Columbus Day celebration, but offered little information to speculate on what the announcement would be about.
Mr. Trump pointed out Energy Secretary Chris Wright and said he was "doing a great job."

"We have, I think, some big news on that diesel situation," the president said. "We're gonna be knocking the hell out of it. And remember, what have we done? We stopped Iran from having a nuclear weapon. That's big time. And the prices — the prices will come tumbling."
Diesel prices have skyrocketed in recent months amid the war with Iran. The average price of a gallon of diesel is $6.28, according to AAA, which is up from $5.94 a month ago and $3.68 a year ago.

Diesel had never previously crossed $6 a gallon until just before Labor Day weekend. The record, hit on Sept. 22, was $6.53 per gallon. Diesel is widely used in the trucking, agriculture and construction sectors, so it's a factor for nearly every type of good, including groceries.

The Trump administration has looked into several ways to lower diesel prices, most recently signing an executive order this week allowing the use of red-dyed diesel on highways. Red-dyed diesel is exempt from the federal tax of 24.4 cents a gallon that applies to regular diesel.

The president also argued Thursday that the U.S. has "TOTAL CONTROL" over the Strait of Hormuz, as American forces escort millions of barrels of crude oil through the waterway every night. Iran has continued to target some of those ships, however, including one earlier on Friday.

"Between our TOTAL CONTROL of the Strait of Hormuz, and this great announcement on Russian Energy, Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!" Mr. Trump wrote on Truth Social. "Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority. This is a very big and important announcement."

title: Katie Bailey tapped as new White House legislative director, sources say
summary: Katie Bailey currently serves as both special assistant to the president and deputy director of legislative affairs.
story: The White House has a new chief liaison to Congress as midterms approach and control of the legislative branch is in the balance.
President Trump offered Katie Bailey the position of director of the Office of Legislative Affairs on Friday, and she accepted, according to multiple sources.

Bailey will replace James Braid, who stepped down last month, as announced by Vice President JD Vance. Braid had "one of the toughest jobs in the entire Administration as White House Legislative Director," Vance said.

"He played a critical role in all of the administration's achievements in Congress: largest tax cut ever, resources to carry out President Trump's historic immigration agenda and finish the border wall, defeating two Democratic shutdowns, a landmark first crypto bill, the fastest confirmation of the cabinet in decades and much more," Vance added.
Bailey's job might be even harder.
She accepts the role less than a month before midterm elections. Both the House and Senate, currently controlled in a slim majority by Republicans, could fall into Democratic hands.
Bailey does have experience in the current White House, though. She currently serves as both special assistant to the president and deputy director of legislative affairs.
She previously served as legislative director for Indiana Republican Sen. Mike Braun during his six-year term in office, ending in January 2025 when he won election as the state's governor.

title: Blanche, other DOJ appointees can take part in campaigns, memo says
summary: The Justice Department has loosened the guidelines for the attorney general and other senior ​political appointees, allowing them to participate in political activities.
story: The Justice Department has loosened the guidelines for the attorney general and other senior political appointees, allowing them to participate in political activities.

A memo sent this week by Assistant Attorney General Jolene Ann Laurie relaxes ethics restrictions on Senate-confirmed presidential appointees such that they can speak at rallies, canvass for votes and even serve as delegates or officers of a national political party as long as those activities are conducted in their personal capacities.
The guidance applies to the attorney general, the deputy attorney general, assistant attorneys general, the FBI director, U.S. attorneys and others.
Former Attorney General Pam Bondi had loosened the regulations somewhat during her tenure by allowing political appointees to attend rallies and fundraisers. The new memo goes a step further.

It specifically states that presidentially appointed, Senate-confirmed Justice Department employees are exempt from the more stringent guidelines imposed on some other DOJ employees, such as administrative law judges and those in the Criminal Division.

Attorney General Todd Blanche addressed the Republican midterm convention in September and attended a rally for a North Carolina Republican Senate candidate, drawing criticism that he violated long-standing Justice Department norms intended to keep politics independent from the law.
"I am not in any way violating any rule or law," Blanche said about his appearances at these events, adding they were done in his personal capacity.
These moves come after the Biden-era Justice Department clamped down on appointees' political activities.
"Non-career appointees may not attend any partisan political events, even in their personal capacities," a 2024 memo said, continuing a policy instituted two years earlier.
The 2024 memo also said that appointees should "avoid making public appearances in any state shortly before a primary or general election in that state, to the greatest extent practicable."
PBS News was first to report on the new guidelines.
