title: Pentagon's plan to livestream execution sparks backlash
summary: "Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do," said GOP Sen. Thom Tillis.
story: Washington — The revelation that the Pentagon plans to livestream the execution by firing squad of Nidal Hasan, the ex-Army major convicted of killing 13 people at Fort Hood in 2009, has sparked intense pushback, with one Republican senator calling it "disgusting" and critics warning it could inspire more acts of terrorism.

On Thursday, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth confirmed CBS News' reporting that the Dec. 3 execution will be livestreamed. Hegseth told Real America's Voice the execution would be public "because people need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things." Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said that Hegseth recommended, and President Trump approved, a plan to use an Army firing squad.
"Death penalty through firing squad, and he deserves it," Mr. Trump said during an unrelated White House event on Friday.
In an interview Friday night in Syracuse, New York, with WSTM-TV, President Trump said he "wasn't involved in that decision" to livestream the execution, "but I understand that decision."
"I guess they want to have it serve as an example, and I understand that very well," the president added.
Republican Sen. Thom Tillis, who is retiring, called the decision "beyond disgusting." Tillis voted to confirm Hegseth, but is now expressing his regret in doing so.

"Hasan should face the death penalty, but making his execution public and streaming it? Beyond disgusting," Tillis wrote on X. "Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do. It should not be happening in America."
Republican Rep. Austin Scott of Georgia wrote on X, "I absolutely support the sentence of death, but live-streaming executions is what jihadists do. America is better than that."
Republican Sen. John Curtis of Utah urged Hegseth to reconsider.

"Seneca warned that Rome's bloody spectacles corrupted the people who watched them," he said on X. "A civilization erodes when it cultivates an appetite for executions as a form of entertainment.  Secretary Hegseth's plan to livestream the Fort Hood execution risks feeding that appetite. The victims deserve justice administered with solemnity. Broadcasting a death diminishes us and is not an effective deterrent. I urge him to reconsider."
Democratic Sen. Chris Murphy said publicly executing someone is "medieval."

"That's disgusting. What, is he mimicking ISIS executions?" Murphy said on CNN. "I mean, I understand that in this country we have the death penalty, but public executions is medieval. It's frankly one of the things that we abhor about terrorist groups. And the fact that the United States is doing it — I just learned this, that is just absolutely extraordinary, galling. No matter whether you support or oppose the death penalty, public hangings and executions? That's what America has become?"
Ned Price, who was the State Department's spokesman during the Biden administration, said a public and livestreamed execution will create more "radicalized zealots."

"You can take it from those of us who've spent years working on terrorism: the surest way to spawn more radicalized zealots is to glorify violence, embrace a cult of death, and create a martyr for the cause," Price wrote on X. "Or take it from AQ and ISIS, whose tactics offer the closest modern-day approximation of Hegseth's proposal.  Either way, it's hard to conjure a more vivid example of his trademark performative bravado, which routinely damages America's image and, in this case, so ghoulishly leaves us more vulnerable."

Alonzo Lunsford, a former U.S. Army sergeant who was shot seven times during the Fort Hood shooting but survived, said he supports the gunman's execution by firing squad. But Lunsford said this execution is "not something you should view for entertainment purposes."
"To show the whole thing without it being censored for the general public, for me personally, I don't agree with that, but it's not about my personal belief," he told BBC Radio.
Archbishop Paul S. Coakley, president of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops, issued a statement Friday morning urging the Pentagon to reconsider.

"In no way can [Hasan's] actions be condoned but this decision is a barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered. The word of God exhorts us: 'do not repay anyone evil for evil,'" the archbishop said, citing Romans 12:17. "The public execution even of one who has done grave harm will only further undermine the moral fabric of our nation and be a blight on the conscience of its people."
Conservative talk show host Erick Erickson, who supports the death penalty, also said a public, livestreamed execution of Hasan will give him the "platform for martyrdom he wants."

"Hasan is a paraplegic, confined to a wheelchair," Erickson wrote. "The public imagery of a firing squad killing a man sitting in a chair because he cannot stand is going to undermine support for the death penalty. A society that increasingly finds ways to sympathize with the villains will do so here. This also gives Nidal Hasan the platform for martyrdom he wants. They'll be passing out the livestream video in the Middle East to inspire more terrorists to shoot up Americans to celebrate the glory of the martyrdom of Nidal Hasan."

Geoffrey Corn, a Texas Tech University law professor who served in the Army's Judge Advocate General's Corps, told CBS News that the plan to livestream the execution "raises significant moral questions, above and beyond the questions related to the death penalty generally."
"There's a certain protocol that is normally followed with executions limiting the gallery of observers, which usually includes people close to the victims and certain members of the media," he said.
Corn said "turning the execution of such a penalty into some type of public spectacle echoes of the past we seem to have put behind us."
Despite Lunsford's concerns about the livestream, the former U.S. Army sergeant said he'll be there for the execution.

"I'm going to be there [to watch in person] and before they pull the trigger, I want him to look at me in my eyes and I look at him in his eyes and I want him to know: 'Dude, you failed, I'm still here,'" he told the BBC.
The last public execution in the U.S. appeared to take place 90 years ago in 1936. That's when Rainey Bethea was hanged for rape in Kentucky. The execution reportedly drew a crowd of about 20,000.

Hegseth's announcement comes amid efforts from Democrats and Republican Rep. Thomas Massie to impeach him. A vote on his impeachment was delayed by House Speaker Mike Johnson's decision to cancel votes a day early ahead of the midterms.

Eleanor  Watson and 
                                                  
                                  Joe  Walsh
                  
        contributed to this report.

title: Vance says he wouldn't watch livestream of Fort Hood shooter's execution
summary: Vice President JD Vance cast doubt on whether the Pentagon will go ahead with livestreaming the execution of the Fort Hood shooter and said he would not tune in if it happens.
story: Washington — Vice President JD Vance on Friday cast doubt on whether the Pentagon will go ahead with livestreaming the execution of the Fort Hood shooter in December and said he would not tune in if it happens.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said Thursday that Nidal Hasan's death by firing squad would be public and available to watch. The announcement prompted intense backlash, including from several Republicans in Congress.
On a trip to Ohio, a reporter asked Vance, who is Catholic, how the plan to livestream the execution meshes with his faith.
"Well, first of all, I've seen this announcement," said Vance. "I don't know that that's actually going to happen."

Vance said Hasan committed "the worst terrorist attack on American soil outside of 9/11" and gunned down Army soldiers he was supposed to treat "at their most vulnerable." Hasan, a psychiatrist, killed 13 people and wounded more than 30 others in the attack on the Fort Hood Army base in Texas in 2009.

"So whatever the controversy is about the method of the execution, I hope that people don't forget that this is a guy who brutally murdered a lot of innocent people," Vance said. "Now that said, I mean, look, if it's ultimately livestreamed, I'm not going to be watching it."
President Trump hasn't publicly commented on the livestream aspect of the execution, although he approves of it being carried out through a firing squad.
"Death penalty through firing squad, and he deserves it," the president told a room full of guests at a White House event marking Columbus Day.

title: Judge strikes down DOJ's policy of reviewing state voter rolls
summary: A federal judge has struck down the Trump administration's plan to check state voter rolls against federal immigration databases and press states to remove voters it determines are registered illegally.
story: A federal judge has struck down the Trump administration's plan to check state voter rolls against federal immigration databases, a blow to the administration's election-related efforts in the run-up to the midterms.

In a 78-page ruling, D.C.-based U.S. District Judge Sparkle Sooknanan wrote Friday that the Justice Department "cannot run roughshod over longstanding laws that were carefully crafted to protect the rights of the American people."

The Trump administration has mounted a nationwide push to obtain complete voter rolls from every state, including sensitive information about registered voters. The Justice Department has argued the information is needed to ensure states are complying with two federal voting laws — the Help America Vote Act and the National Voter Registration Act — which aim to ensure states have programs in place for maintaining accurate voter rolls.

Eighteen states fully cooperated with the Justice Department's request for voter files, Sooknanan said. The department has brought lawsuits against most other states, and has lost almost all of the suits, according to a CBS News analysis. One state settled with the federal government.
The ruling applies to the voter files that the Justice Department has already received, as well as the files it is still litigating over.

Sooknanan rejected the Justice Department's argument that it has legal authority to demand voter lists, compare those lists against citizenship databases and urge states to remove voters who it claims are ineligible to vote. The judge also said the policy violates the Administrative Procedure Act and the Privacy Act, and said the federal databases could contain "inaccuracies."

"Today's decision does not prevent the federal government from taking lawful steps to support states' efforts to maintain accurate voter rolls. Neither does it prevent states from maintaining their own voter rolls. And to state the obvious, the Court's decision does not pave the way for ineligible voters to vote in our elections," Sooknanan wrote. "Rather, the Court vacates a policy that has removed United States citizens from the voter rolls in their home states and risks disenfranchising many more — a policy that flies in the face of duly enacted laws designed to protect Americans."

She continued: "The challenged policy represents the federal government's attempt to decide who gets to vote. But Congress has left that authority where our Constitution has always placed it: with the states."
The legal challenge against the voter roll policy was brought by advocacy group Common Cause and individual voters.
Common Cause CEO Virginia Kase Solomón called the ruling "a victory for voters and yet another loss for the Department of Justice" in a statement Friday.
A Justice Department spokesperson said the agency is reviewing the decision.

Under the Trump administration, the federal government has sought a larger-than-usual role in elections, which are typically administered by states with some regulation by Congress. President Trump argues more federal scrutiny is necessary in order to prevent noncitizens from voting and curb fraud — though most election experts say fraud and noncitizen voting are extremely rare.

The government's push to run state voter rolls through the Department of Homeland Security's Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (SAVE) database has faced court setbacks, as more than two dozen judges have denied the Justice Department's requests to compel individual states to share their voter lists.

Sooknanan also ruled in June that the Trump administration's overhauled SAVE database — which includes data from the Social Security Administration — was created unlawfully. The Supreme Court temporarily paused that ruling last month.

In practice, the impact of recent court rulings on the November midterms could be limited as federal law bars states from systematically removing ineligible voters from their voter registration lists within 90 days of an election.

Another Trump administration policy that set new rules for the U.S. Postal Service's handling of mail-in ballots was also blocked in the courts, with the Supreme Court declining the government's request to allow the rules to take effect.

title: Trump creates committee to investigate Fed's Lisa Cook
summary: President Trump established a committee to look into allegations that Fed Governor Lisa Cook made false statements on mortgage documents, the latest step in his renewed effort to fire her.
story: Washington — President Trump established a committee to look into allegations that Lisa Cook, a member of the Federal Reserve Board of Governors, made false statements on mortgage documents, the latest step in his renewed effort to fire Cook from her post with the central bank.

The president signed a memorandum, dated Wednesday, creating what he said is a "committee of inquiry" that will be made up of three members: the assistant to the president for economic policy, chair of the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission and head of the Office of Government Ethics.

After conducting its investigation into Cook, the committee will report to Mr. Trump whether there is "cause" to remove her from the Fed Board. The three-member panel will hold an in-person hearing at the White House on Nov. 5 to "consider the evidence and allegations" against Cook, according to the memorandum. The hearing will not be public, but will be transcribed, the White House said.
Cook has the opportunity to submit a "written position statement" to the committee in response to the accusations against her and can appear at the proceeding, the president's memorandum stated.

"Governor Cook may present argument, written evidence, and written witness statements regarding the evidence and allegations," it continued. "The Committee may also question Governor Cook about any representations she or her counsel make during the hearing, or it may authorize its representatives, including Department of Justice personnel, to conduct that questioning."
Abbe Lowell and Norm Eisen, Cook's lawyers, said she "welcomes the opportunity to present the facts so she can clear her name and demonstrate there is no legal basis to fire her."

"In light of the President's repeated statements that he has already decided to fire Governor Cook — regardless of the facts and evidence — we have grave doubts that this 'hearing' is a legitimate one that would conform to the law. But if it is anything close to objective, the conclusion will be that Governor Cook did not commit mortgage fraud, leaving no cause to remove her from the Federal Reserve Board," they said in a statement. "We have engaged with the White House to evaluate whether the process proposed has a possibility of being a genuine one and not simply a box checking exercise."

The president's creation of the committee to investigate the claims against Cook appears to be the latest attempt by Mr. Trump to ensure any effort to fire her can stand up to legal scrutiny. The president first attempted to oust Cook from the Fed last year after a senior member of his administration, Bill Pulte, claimed she made false statements on mortgage documents related to two properties before she joined the central bank.
Cook challenged her removal, arguing that it violated federal law, which allows a president to remove a member of the Fed's board "for cause."

The Supreme Court ruled in June that Cook could continue serving in her post while her legal challenge to her purported removal continued. In a 5-4 decision, the high court found that Mr. Trump failed to provide Cook the procedural protections she was entitled to under the law — specifically notice and the opportunity to respond to the allegations before she was fired.

"That is not to say that a Federal Reserve Governor is entitled to an audience with the President or a fullblown judicial trial," Chief Justice John Roberts wrote for the majority. "Instead, all that is required is notice 'to the officer of the charges made against him' and 'an opportunity to be heard in his defense.'"

Roberts continued: "We see no reason why that opportunity 'may not be had on written materials only,' with no oral presentation. All that is required is 'the right to support his allegations by argument however brief, and, if need be, by proof, however informal,' before a final decision is made."

Mr. Trump mounted another attempt to fire Cook after the Supreme Court ruled in her favor. In a letter to the Fed governor in August, the White House informed Cook that Mr. Trump was considering removing her because of the mortgage-fraud allegations and laid out the claims against her. The White House also set a deadline for Cook to respond.

Cook denied the accusations and argued in a response to the White House that she has "never committed mortgage fraud." Lowell, Cook's lawyer, said that attempting to remove her on the basis of the mortgage-fraud allegations would "ignore the facts and the law."

title: Trump picks "loyal" Katie Zacharia as next White House press secretary
summary: "I am confident that Katie will deliver strong results for our Country as the next White House Press Secretary," President Trump said.
story: Washington — President Trump on Friday announced conservative commentator Katie Zacharia will be the next White House press secretary, praising her "unblemished record of support."

Zacharia, a California native, briefly worked for the Department of Homeland Security as a spokesperson earlier this year, and currently works as a senior communications adviser for Truth Social, the president's social media site. She also assisted the president on the campaign trail, he said.

"She has an unblemished record of support, and has been a loyal and brilliant supporter, right from the beginning," the president wrote on Truth Social. "She is, likewise, a devoted fan and member of MAGA! I am confident that Katie will deliver strong results for our Country as the next White House Press Secretary, as she has the respect of, and will work fantastically with, the Media, the American People, and my Administration."
The president wished her luck. The New York Times was first to report that Zacharia was offered the role.

The position has been vacant since Karoline Leavitt left in late August. The White House James S. Brady Press Briefing Room hasn't hosted a briefing for the press since Sept. 3, when Vice President JD Vance addressed reporters and took questions.
In a social media post, Zacharia said "serving President Trump and the American people at this critical 250-year mark is the honor of a lifetime."

"The work ahead is to continue delivering strong results for our Country and communicating to the American people the major wins that this Administration is making every single day," she said in the post. "I look forward to working with the White House press corps, and with reporters across the country, to get that record out. Following the fabulous Karoline Leavitt is a high standard, and one worth meeting."
Zacharia, who lives in California, completed her undergraduate and law degrees at Pepperdine University in Malibu, according to her LinkedIn.

Earlier this year, Zacharia wrote an op-ed for the New York Post about her experience wearing a "Make America Great Again" hat to her local gym. She said the owner of the gym ultimately asked her to stop wearing it.
"I responded that I would never take my Trump hat off to appease the left," she wrote. "This is raw, unfiltered intolerance. Freedom of speech doesn't evaporate at the gym door."
"The First Amendment has no 'discomfort' clause," she added, although the First Amendment protects against government censorship of speech, not private businesses.

Katie Zacharia

title: Will social media platforms allow Fort Hood shooter's execution to be livestreamed?
summary: The Pentagon's decision to livestream the firing-squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan could put the spotlight on whether social media companies will allow videos on their platforms.
story: Washington — Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's revelation that the execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan will be streamed live has drawn fierce criticism and calls for him to reconsider his plan. But it has also put the spotlight on whether social media companies will allow government accounts to stream the death by firing squad on their platforms.

Hegseth has not provided additional details about the Defense Department's plans to livestream the execution of Hasan, who was convicted of killing 13 people and injuring more than 30 at Fort Hood in 2009. Hasan is set to die by firing squad at 1 p.m. on Dec. 3 at the Texas Army installation, the defense secretary said.
"We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public, because people need to understand that there's consequences for these types of things," Hegseth said.

The defense chief did not say how the execution would be streamed, and whether the Pentagon would provide that content through its social media accounts or on its website. But his comments Thursday, made to far-right political activist Jack Posobiec, provide advance warning to social media companies that the content could be posted to their platforms.

"If this were a private entity who said, 'we're going to be executing someone at this date,' I think platforms would just say, 'you can't use our platform,'" David Greene, senior counsel at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, told CBS News. "The only reason this is even a little bit more difficult of a decision for the platforms is because this is the government doing it, and there is some interest in the public understanding and being able to witness barbaric acts of its government, and there will also likely be pressure from the government to carry it."

Google, Meta, TikTok and X, which operate the nation's most popular social media platforms, all have policies governing violent or graphic content. Google, Meta and X did not respond to questions about whether they would allow the Defense Department to livestream Hasan's execution on their platforms or whether that content would violate their rules.

A spokesperson for TikTok U.S. pointed to its policy on "shocking and graphic content," which states that the platform does not allow "anything extremely gory, disturbing, or violent, especially when it could cause psychological harm."

"Some content that's less graphic or shared in the public interest may be allowed, but it may be viewable only for users 18 and older or ineligible" for its For You Feed, TikTok's policy states. That includes "graphic footage of events that would otherwise violate our rules but are in the public interest to view, such as wars and major disasters."
Meta, the parent company of Facebook and Instagram, explicitly states in its "violent and graphic content" policy that it does not allow "live-streams of capital punishments."

"We recognize that users may share content in order to shed light on or condemn acts such as human rights abuses or armed conflict," Meta's rules read. "Our policies consider when content shared in this context and allow room for discussion and awareness raising accordingly."
YouTube, operated by Google, has guidelines covering violent or graphic content, as well as harmful or dangerous content.

YouTube's harmful or dangerous content policy bars "acts performed by adults that have a risk of serious harm or death," or "content that encourages dangerous or illegal activities that risk serious physical harm or death."
The violent or graphic content policy states that YouTube does not allow "violent or gory content intended to shock or disgust viewers."

The company tells users not to post content that includes "footage or imagery showing bodily fluids, such as blood or vomit, with the intent to shock or disgust viewers" or "footage of corpses with massive injuries, such as severed limbs."
YouTube also has rules specifically governing content that involves guns and says it prohibits "live streams that show someone holding, handling, or transporting a firearm."

X, which is owned by billionaire Elon Musk, prohibits "violent media that we consider high in severity and likelihood of harm." Its policy covers "gratuitous gore" and "moment of death." Violent content is barred "within areas that are highly visible" on the platform, including live video.

The social media platform considers "gratuitous gore" to be "media of humans or animals that depicts excessively graphic or gruesome content related to death, violence or severe physical harm," including "dismembered or mutilated humans."

X says it may request the removal of "images or videos that were taken at the point of, immediately before, or after an identifiable individual's death, if we receive a request from their family or an authorized representative."

Some social media companies like Facebook and YouTube tightened their policies on harmful content in the wake of the 2019 attack at two mosques in Christchurch, New Zealand, when a gunman livestreamed the massacre. Years earlier, they scrambled to take down graphic videos of brutal executions by Islamic State militants. But social media companies have also been encouraged to ensure content showing human rights abuses or war crimes is preserved.

Greene said it would be up to the platforms to decide whether to allow content like an execution by firing squad to be streamed, even if it may violate their policies. And because the Defense Department has telegraphed its plans to show the killing, Greene said he expects people inside the companies to decide whether to allow the footage on their platforms, rather than waiting for it to be flagged by automated systems.

Executions outside of the military justice system are typically observed by members of the media, who serve as representatives of the public and provide a look into what capital punishment entails, Greene said.
But he stressed that when deciding whether to allow Hasan's execution to be streamed live, social media companies should consider the U.S. government's motives.
"This seems to be the government wanting to broadcast the execution for propaganda purposes and wanting to glorify its ability to execute people," he said.

If Hegseth follows through with his plan to livestream Hasan's execution, it would place the United States in a small group of nations that are carrying out public executions. There were at least 17 known public executions in 2025: six in Afghanistan and 11 in Iran, according to Amnesty International.

In the U.S., it appears the last public execution took place in 1936. Then, a crowd of an estimated 20,000 gathered to watch the hanging of Rainey Bethea, a Black man who confessed to the rape and murder of a 70-year-old White woman, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.

The last military execution took place in 1961, when U.S. Army Private John Bennett was hanged. Hasan's death by firing squad would be the military's first since 1945, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.

title: FBI arrests suspected member of ShinyHunters in connection with jobs site hack
summary: The FBI this week arrested another individual suspected of being connected to ShinyHunters, the cybercriminal group that hacked the bureau's job website, FBI Director Kash Patel said.
story: Washington — The FBI this week arrested another individual suspected of being connected to ShinyHunters, the cybercriminal group that hacked the bureau's job website and stole personal data about its employees, FBI Director Kash Patel said on Friday.

"This is the latest arrest this FBI has made in a matter of days involving this network, as we work non-stop to dismantle the group, pursue new leads and evidence, and act quickly," Patel said in a statement. "This arrest demonstrates the strength and reach of our efforts to protect Americans from cybercrime."

The FBI did not provide any additional details on the individual's identity or the location of the arrest, but a U.S. official and another source briefed on the matter told CBS News the suspect was detained in Pennsylvania.

A law enforcement source said the suspect is a Canadian citizen and is believed to be directly involved in the hack of the FBI's website. That source said that other suspected co-conspirators remain at large.
The sources were granted anonymity to speak about law enforcement details that have not been made public.
The New York Times reported earlier Friday that the suspect was arrested in Pennsylvania on suspicion of being involved in the theft of FBI data.
An FBI spokesperson declined to comment on the details outlined in the New York Times report.

In a statement to CBS News, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police said it "is aware of the arrest of a Canadian in the US in connection with the ShinyHunters hack. The RCMP does not comment on investigations being conducted by other countries."
CBS News has reached out to other Canadian authorities for comment.

The FBI's jobs website was hacked in September, in what some veteran agents are saying may amount to the worst breach of a federal government system since the infamous hack of the Office of Personnel Management system in 2015, when more than 22 million government records were stolen.
ShinyHunters claimed responsibility for the FBI hack, the latest in a series of high-profile data breaches committed by the notorious group.
The hackers said they stole 2 to 3 terabytes of data related to FBI workers, a feat they accomplished thanks to a new vulnerability with Oracle PeopleSoft, a human resources management program.

Earlier this week, the FBI's Cyber Division's Assistant Director Brett Leatherman announced that following a review, the bureau determined that a contractor failed to implement a security patch to the system that was targeted.
"The FBI has removed the contractor and taken all necessary steps to both mitigate any further risk and protect our workforce," Leatherman said in a statement.
Reuters was the first to report on the contractor's removal, saying the individual worked at the company Accenture.
The arrest announced on Friday is the latest in a string of arrests of suspects who are believed to be tied to ShinyHunters.
On Sunday, CBS News reported that Jordanian authorities detained Saif al-Din Khader, who uses the online moniker "Rey" and is suspected to be involved in ShinyHunters.
A second suspected member of the group, identified as 24-year-old Pepijn van der Stap, was also arrested in Amsterdam, CBS News previously reported.

However, he was taken into custody on Sept. 15, meaning he was already in custody days before ShinyHunters announced it had hacked the FBI jobs website. The intrusion was first reported on Sept. 22 by 404 Media.

Olivia  Gazis
                  
        contributed to this report.

title: U.S. sanctions ICC, vowing to dismantle it "brick by brick" without changes
summary: The U.S. imposed fresh sanctions targeting the International Criminal Court, taking action against the court itself after previously penalizing more than a dozen of its judges and prosecutors.
story: The Trump administration imposed fresh sanctions targeting the International Criminal Court on Friday, taking action against the court itself after previously penalizing more than a dozen of its judges and prosecutors.
"Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC," Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a statement announcing the measures.

The move came just hours after the Norwegian Nobel Committee announced it was awarding the Nobel Peace Prize to Navanethem "Navi" Pillay, a South African-born human rights official who served as an ICC judge from 2003 to 2008. Pillay also led a U.N. inquiry that determined last year that Israel committed genocide in Gaza. Israel strongly disputed the report's findings.

Neither the United States nor Israel is a party to the Rome Statute that established the ICC. Washington has long objected to the court's investigation of alleged war crimes by U.S. personnel in Afghanistan and its arrest warrants for Israeli leaders over alleged crimes in Gaza.
The court maintains it can prosecute crimes committed on territory under its jurisdiction, even when the accused is a national of a country that has not joined.
Rubio has previously described the ICC as a "fatally politicized supranational court" that has "maliciously abused its authority." He vowed Friday to dismantle it "brick by brick" if necessary.

Under the designation, the court's assets under U.S. jurisdiction are blocked, and U.S. companies and individuals are generally barred from doing business with the court. For now, the Treasury Department is allowing some services to continue and giving the court 180 days to maintain certain operations while its member countries address Washington's objections.

"We have structured this action to provide an opportunity for States Parties to negotiate and present a solution to address our concerns," Rubio said. "If these efforts do not bear fruit, we will continue to adjust accordingly."
The ICC condemned the designation as an attempt to interfere with its work and intimidate those who cooperate with it, calling it "an assault on the rule of law."

"The Court will continue to fully discharge its mandate, with independence and impartiality," ICC President Tomoko Akane said. The court also appealed to its 125 member states to help ensure it has adequate resources to continue operating, warning its future now depends in part on the governments that established it.
The court's member states include most U.S. allies in Europe, including every NATO member besides Turkey, as well as Canada, Japan and Australia.

The foreign ministers of Canada, Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, Japan, the Netherlands, and the U.K. said in a statement later Friday that they "regret and strongly disagree with the announcement of sanctions to be imposed upon the Court by the United States."

"[I]f put into effect, these sanctions will have a significant impact on the Court's work, its dedicated staff and their families," the countries said. "They work every day to bring those accused of the most serious international crimes to justice and to support their victims."

Pillay, the Peace Prize recipient, left the court in 2008 to become the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, and currently serves on the International Court of Justice, which is separate from the ICC.

She was also the chair of the U.N. Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory. In September 2025, the panel determined that there were "reasonable grounds" to conclude that "the Israeli authorities and Israeli security forces have committed and are continuing to commit" acts of genocide. Israel's foreign minister called the report "fake" and said it "relies entirely on Hamas falsehoods, laundered and repeated by others."
Pillay referenced the U.S. campaign against the ICC in a video following news that she had won the Peace Prize.

"We are living through an era when international law and human rights are under significant political attack," she said. "This worsening reality is particularly visible with the attacks on the International Criminal Court."
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office said the decision to award the Peace Prize to Pillay showed that the Nobel Committee "has lost its moral compass."
"It has awarded its highest honor to a bigot who built her career around inventing and propagating blood libels against the one and only Jewish state," Netanyahu's office said in a post on X.

The U.S. action against the ICC also follows a speech Rubio delivered Wednesday in Athens against the backdrop of the Acropolis, where he criticized Western governments for transferring national authority to international bureaucracies.
"[W]ith every passing year, we seemed to outsource more of our sovereignty, transferring our decisions to global bureaucracies far beyond the reach of our control," he said.

title: DOJ won't enforce parts of 1934 gun law that were gutted by court ruling
summary: The Justice Department said it will no longer enforce certain provisions of a law regulating firearms often used by mobsters, after a federal judge declared large parts of it unconstitutional.
story: Washington — The Justice Department said on Friday it will no longer enforce certain provisions of a 1934 law that was passed by Congress to regulate the types of firearms often used by mobsters, after a federal judge declared large parts of the law were unconstitutional.

The new guidelines released by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives were issued to current and future gun owners. The Justice Department determined last month it would not appeal the judge's ruling.

Under the new guidelines, the federal government will no longer require individuals to apply and receive regulatory approval before making or transferring short-barreled rifles, short-barreled shotguns, suppressors and other various types of concealable firearms.

The Justice Department also said its new legal guidance does not supersede state and local laws that restrict the sale of those categories of weapons, adding that because many state laws still require people to register those firearms, it will continue to process those applications voluntarily.

CBS News exclusively reported last month that President Trump had ordered the Justice Department not to appeal the court ruling in Texas that loosened the limits on what used to be called "gangster weapons."

The ruling impacted large parts of the National Firearms Act, which mandated that anyone wishing to sell, possess or make a firearm or device covered by the law had to submit a detailed written application to the ATF, among other requirements.
The law was aimed at addressing the most dangerous and easily concealable weapons that were often used by mobsters during the Prohibition era.

But in August, U.S. District Judge James Wesley Hendrix, a Trump appointee in the Northern District of Texas, ruled that most of the restrictions on all but two categories of specialized firearms regulated under the National Firearms Act are unconstitutional after Congress last year eliminated a $200 tax imposed on them.
"Because today's NFA does not generate any revenue from untaxed firearms, its regulatory provisions cannot be upheld under the taxing power," the judge wrote at the time.

The decision came in two consolidated cases brought against the government by 15 red states and a number of Second Amendment gun rights groups and individuals, including the Gun Owners of America and the Gun Owners Foundation.

Many lawyers within the Justice Department recommended that the decision should be appealed, saying it was already adversely impacting ongoing criminal cases and that it ran afoul of the government's duty to defend the laws passed by Congress.
Although the court's ruling blocking the ATF from enforcing large parts of the law only applied to the parties in the lawsuit, its wording had created challenges for prosecutors.
That's because the judge said his ruling would also extend to any "current or future" members of the gun groups that sued over the rules. A basic membership to the Gun Owners of America is only $25.

Given that loophole, the ATF said on Friday that going forward it will not enforce the provisions of the National Firearms Act at the heart of the lawsuit against "any person as applied to the domestic manufacturing, possession, and transfer of short-barreled rifles, short-barreled shotguns, silencers" and other applicable devices or weapons.

title: Trump promised to lower prices for Americans. Here's what the data shows.
summary: Just weeks before the midterm elections, 90% of Americans say prices in the U.S. are the main factor shaping their view of the economy. These charts show why.
story: President Trump campaigned in 2024 on promises to lower Americans' cost of living, vowing to push gasoline prices below $2 a gallon and to deliver 2% mortgage rates. Two years later, consumers face sharply higher costs for many of the necessities he pledged to make more affordable.

Less than a month before the midterm elections, the gap between Mr. Trump's promises and the financial realities facing many Americans is fueling voter frustration over the economy. Although economic growth is solid and unemployment remains low, nine in 10 Americans say prices are the most important factor shaping their views of the economy, according to a recent CBS News poll.

The financial pressures affecting Americans predate Mr. Trump's return to the White House last year. Consumers are reeling from the cumulative impact of five years of post-pandemic inflation, economists note. But his campaign promises raised hopes that he would lower consumer prices.

At the same time, some of Mr. Trump's policies have exacerbated inflation. His tariff regime contributed about 2.9 percentage points to inflation through February, according to new research from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. Without the tariffs, the price of goods would have declined, the researchers said.
Mr. Trump's decision to attack Iran in February has also led to a drawn-out conflict that has disrupted oil shipments and sharply driven up the price of oil, gas and diesel.

"It's undeniable that several of these supply shocks that the U.S. economy has been navigating through come from policy decisions made by the administration — namely, decisions to intervene in Iran and decisions to impose tariffs," Greg Daco, chief economist at investment advisory firm EY-Parthenon, told CBS News.
Inflation in September is forecast to have risen at an annual rate of 3.6%, up from 3.4% in August, according to economists polled by FactSet — well above the Federal Reserve's 2% annual target.
Ryan Bourne, an economist at the libertarian Cato Institute, said that consumers "judge the prices they're paying against the prices they paid four or five years ago, and are still shocked by it."
He added, "As a result of that, they think the economy's doing very, very badly."

The White House said that Mr. Trump's agenda "stopped Biden's inflation crisis" while creating jobs and economic growth. The administration's policies "will continue to deliver economic wins over the next two years," White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers told CBS News.

"The President has delivered tangible wins for American families: He signed the largest working-class tax cuts in history, cut the cost of prescription drugs, added more than one million private-sector jobs, locked in nearly 20 trade deals that put American workers first and sent 401(k)s to record highs," Rogers added.
The following charts show how U.S. costs have changed for expenses ranging from groceries to car insurance.
Groceries
"A vote for Trump means your groceries will be cheaper." — Mr. Trump in a campaign speech in Pittsburgh on Nov. 4, 2024.
For consumers, each visit to the supermarket is a fresh reminder of inflation's impact on food costs, which have continued to rise since Mr. Trump vowed to lower grocery prices.

The cost of food prepared at home has climbed 4% since November 2024, according to Consumer Price Index data, when Mr. Trump said a vote for him would lead to lower costs. That increase comes on top of a 23% jump in food prices during the prior four years. Because consumers tend to remember what they spent on groceries before the pandemic, they get a jolt each time they visit the supermarket, said Daco of EY-Parthenon.

"Whether it's talking about gas prices or grocery prices or restaurant prices or travel prices, everybody talks about inflation," he said. "The salience of prices is what is driving this downbeat consumer morale."

Food costs are continuing to rise due to a number of factors, ranging from the elevated price of gas and diesel, which are needed to fuel farm equipment and ship items to stores, to the Trump administration's tariffs, economists said.
Gasoline

"Energy is going to bring us back. That means we're going down and getting gasoline below $2 a gallon, bring down the price of everything from electricity rates to groceries, airfares, and housing costs."  — Mr. Trump in a speech at the Economic Club of New York on Sept. 5, 2024.

Gas prices have surged since the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran in late February. As of Oct. 9, the national average price for a gallon of gasoline was $4.37. That's up 47% from $2.98 on Feb. 27, one day before the war began, according to CBS News data. Prices at the pump are at a record high for October, according to AAA.

Diesel prices rose to a record high of $6.53 per gallon on Sept. 22 and now hover around $6.28. Diesel, which is widely used in the trucking, agriculture and construction sectors, is a factor in consumer prices for nearly every type of good, including groceries.

Gas prices tend to have an outsized impact on consumer sentiment, influencing their views on future inflation and the broader economy, according to research from the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco.
Energy and electricity

"By contrast, I'm announcing today that under my leadership, the United States will commit to the ambitious goal of slashing energy and electricity prices by half, at least half." — Mr. Trump in a campaign speech in Asheville, North Carolina, on August 14, 2024.

Consumers' energy bills have continued to increase this year. Data from the Energy Information Administration (EIA) shows that average monthly residential electricity costs rose 12.5% between December 2024 and July of this year. Electricity bills are rising as utilities spend more to upgrade the nation's aging power grid, and overall energy demand grows amid the data center buildout.

Natural gas is also more expensive. Average monthly residential prices for natural gas rose 106% between December 2024 and July 2025, according to the EIA. Energy Innovation, a nonpartisan policy and research firm, attributes the jump to geopolitical conflict, an increase in domestic exports, extreme weather linked to climate change and rising infrastructure costs.

A July report from advocacy groups The Century Foundation and Protect Borrowers found that the national average utility bill reached $280 per month in early 2026, up 12% since the end of 2024, just before Mr. Trump took office.

Many people could face even higher energy prices this winter. Americans are forecast to spend an average of $1,030 to heat their homes between mid-November and mid-March 2027, according to the National Energy Assistance Directors Association, a policy organization. Homeowners who use heating oil are projected to pay an average of $2,627 over that three-month period, up roughly 50% from last year, the group said.
Car insurance

"Car insurance is up 70% to 100%, and you can't get it. … But prices will come down. You just watch, they'll come down, and they'll come down fast." — Mr. Trump in a campaign speech in Asheville, North Carolina, on August 14, 2024.
Car insurance costs are one area where consumers are seeing some modest relief. Data shows motorists are paying 5.5% less for vehicle coverage since premiums hit a recent high in February.

Still, insurance prices have soared in recent years along with the cost of both new and used vehicles. Yelena Shulyatyeva, senior U.S. economist for The Conference Board, a nonprofit that represents businesses, attributed the recent dip in premiums to increased industry competition, rather than public policy actions.
"Some of the deceleration was a result of a pushback from consumers, rather than some legislative or other action," Shulyatyeva told CBS News.
Housing and mortgage costs

"We will drive down the rates so you will be able to pay 2% again, and we will be able to finance or refinance your homes drastically at much lower costs." — Mr. Trump at a campaign rally in Tucson, Arizona, on Sept. 12, 2024.

Mortgage rates were climbing from pandemic-era lows for several years before President Trump returned to office in January of 2025. The average rate on a conventional 30-year mortgage now stands at 7.28%, up from 7.04% when Mr. Trump took office, according to Freddie Mac.
But home loan rates have been volatile, briefly dipping below 5% in February before climbing amid surging government bond yields, rising inflation and geopolitical tensions.

Borrowing costs are just one side of the struggle: Home buyers are also contending with high prices, keeping many on the sidelines as they wait for more affordable options. The median list price for a home in August was $408,333, up 4% from $392,967 since Mr. Trump took office, according to Zillow.
The gap between the income needed to afford a home, $126,487, and the U.S. median income, $86,490, is now the widest since 2005, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta.
Credit card rates

"We're going to put a temporary cap on credit card interest rates. We're going to cap it around 10%. We can't let them make 25% and 30%." — Mr. Trump in a campaign speech in Uniondale, New York, on Sept. 18, 2024.

President Trump proposed capping credit card interest rates at 10% while campaigning, an issue he also highlighted after taking office in 2025. But while the effort drew bipartisan support, the proposal fizzled.

Currently, the average credit card rate across all commercial bank accounts is 20.94%, down from 21.58% when Mr. Trump resumed office, according to Federal Reserve data. Credit experts said the rate-cap proposal would have hindered consumers' access to credit.

"Obviously, we'd love for everyone to have low rates and be free from debt. But the unintended consequence of a 10% cap would be the loss of access to credit, because banks say they wouldn't be profitable with it capped at that low rate," Ted Rossman, principal consumer finance analyst at Money Management International, a nonprofit credit counseling firm, told CBS News.
Airfare
"We're going [to] … bring down the price of everything from electricity rates to groceries, airfares and housing costs." — Mr. Trump in a speech at the New York Economic Club on Sept. 5, 2024.

Along with promising to reduce energy prices, Mr. Trump pledged to lower airfare costs for travelers. In recent months, fares have eased slightly, although CPI data shows that they remain 17% higher than in January 2025.

The war in Iran has disrupted global oil supplies and raised jet fuel costs, which are the second- biggest expense for airlines after labor costs. Facing significantly larger fuel bills, carriers are raising prices to cover the added costs.

Jet fuel now costs $4.34 a gallon, up 85% from an average of $2.35 per gallon in January 2025, according to the Energy Information Administration. Aviation analysts also point to the May shutdown of budget carrier Spirit Airlines as another factor behind higher fares.
ACA health insurance
"I will make the ACA much, much, much better for far less money (or cost) to our greatest American citizens. …" — Mr. Trump in a Truth Social post on March 26, 2024.

Millions of Americans with an Affordable Care Act health insurance plan face sharply higher costs than a year ago. Average monthly premiums have risen to $178, or $2,136 per year, up 58% from 2025, according to a May analysis from nonprofit health group KFF.

Obamacare plan deductibles have soared from an average of $1,027 per person to $3,786, up 37% over the same period, KFF found. Prices for ACA plans spiked after Congress allowed a tax subsidy designed to lower plan costs to expire at the end of last year.
In an effort to offer relief, the Trump administration began sending $500 checks in September to nearly 1 million ACA participants in 30 states.
Prescription drugs
"When reelected as president, I will continue my efforts to protect Americans from unaffordable drug prices …" — Mr. Trump in an interview with AARP Magazine on Oct. 2, 2024.
Prescription drug prices have dropped since Mr. Trump took office in his second term, falling 3.9% after peaking in February 2025, government data show.

Mr. Trump has credited his policies lowering drug costs, with the White House stating in August that the president "has delivered" on his campaign promise. The administration cited policies such as its "most favored nation" approach, which links U.S. drug prices to those paid in other developed nations.

Experts said that while the Trump administration's policies have helped, other factors are also at play. For instance, manufacturers of GLP-1 weight-loss drugs are cutting their prices amid increased competition, while the nonpartisan Brookings Institution notes that more generic drugs are entering the marketplace, tempering healthcare costs.

title: Durbin asks watchdog to probe new FBI hiring standards on bestiality, prostitution
summary: Sen. Dick Durbin asked the DOJ's watchdog to investigate why the FBI lowered its hiring standards for candidates who may have engaged in bestiality, prostitution or employment theft.
story: Washington — The top Democrat on the Senate Judiciary Committee on Friday asked the Justice Department's internal watchdog to investigate why the FBI lowered its hiring standards for candidates who may have engaged in bestiality, prostitution or employment theft.

In a letter to Justice Department Inspector General Don Berthiaume, Illinois Sen. Dick Durbin said the lowering of the FBI's hiring standards "threaten[s] to undermine the work of the FBI and pose a grave risk to the Bureau's integrity."
CBS News first reported in August that the FBI quietly lowered its hiring standards in June, marking an abrupt shift from prior practice.
Previously, anyone who engaged in acts of bestiality, prostitution or stole from an employer was automatically precluded from working at the bureau.
Now, under the new standards, a person who engaged in acts of bestiality, animal cruelty or animal "crush" before the age of 18 can still be considered for an FBI job.
For prostitution, job applicants will not be automatically disqualified as long as they have not hired sex workers three or more times and as long as the act took place more than 10 years ago.
The new guidelines also allow the FBI to consider hiring job candidates who stole from their employers, as long as the theft took place more than three years prior.

In an extraordinary hearing last month, FBI Director Kash Patel appeared to struggle to defend the changes to the new policy, telling lawmakers that it was aimed at ensuring that sexual assault victims who were forced to have sex with animals would not be precluded from employment at the bureau.

His exchange with Republican Sen. John Kennedy of Louisiana has since become the topic of comedy shows and countless internet memes. Patel told the lawmaker that the prior hiring policy on bestiality "automatically disqualified any individual who participated on either side of it."
"Either side of what, the bestiality?" Kennedy said, later asking: "So you disqualified the animal?"

Current and former FBI agents and legal experts familiar with the bureau's hiring practices previously told CBS News they were deeply troubled by the changes, saying they were indicative of challenges the FBI may be having with recruiting new talent.

Several also said they were baffled by how the bureau was justifying the shift, noting that all applicants have an opportunity to disclose personal issues that could impact the results of their polygraph prior to taking the test, such as a history of sexual abuse.
"Director Patel's responses did little to clarify the purpose or effects of these changes," Durbin wrote in his letter to the inspector general.

"Changes of this magnitude with no discernible justification must be scrutinized. I ask that your office investigate the circumstances around the development and implementation of these policy changes," he added.

title: RFK Jr., Zeldin pressed by Democrats on possible roles in Trump pardons
summary: Democratic lawmakers are pressing HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin to explain what role they may have played in pardons granted by President Trump.
story: Washington — Democratic lawmakers are pressing Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin to explain what role they may have played in pardons granted by President Trump.

In letters sent Tuesday, the lawmakers asked Kennedy and Zeldin to answer questions by Oct. 20 so Congress can "better understand the extent to which influence and access have overridden the standard pardon review process." They were signed by Sens. Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut and Peter Welch of Vermont, as well as Reps. Dave Min of California and Mary Gay Scanlon of Pennsylvania.

Democratic lawmakers have limited options to compel answers while they are in the minority, but capturing the House or the Senate in the midterm elections would give them subpoena power to pursue a broad range of investigations into the Trump administration. The letters highlight how questions about Mr. Trump's pardons — and the cottage industry of lobbying that has sprung up around them — are expected to be a top oversight area for Democrats if they win in November.

In September, a CBS News investigation shone a light on the new pardon economy and pardon brokers, and included video of lobbyists offering to "put pressure on the president" in exchange for a hefty fee from a convicted felon.

The Democrats' letters focus on Mr. Trump's pardons for Trevor Milton, an entrepreneur convicted in 2022 of lying to investors about his electric truck company Nikola, and Troy Lake, a Colorado diesel mechanic convicted in 2024 for violating the Clean Air Act, a law designed to control air pollution.

Mr. Trump's pardon for Milton in March 2025 came after the entrepreneur and his wife donated almost $2 million to a political committee aligned with Mr. Trump's reelection, as well as $750,000 to the Make America Healthy Again Alliance PAC aligned with Kennedy's "MAHA" agenda, according to Federal Election Commission records.
The oversight letter to Kennedy cited a Reuters report in June that said Kennedy advocated for Milton's pardon to the president.

A source close to Kennedy, who was granted anonymity to speak candidly, told CBS News they have heard the secretary privately say that he will not advocate for any pardons. The Department of Health and Human Services did not immediately respond to a request for comment, nor did Milton.

In a statement after his pardon, Milton thanked Mr. Trump for granting him "this sacred pardon of innocence." He broke the news of his pardon in an email to prosecutors that they considered cocky, CBS News reported.

Lawmakers are gearing up for investigations next Congress into "everybody along the assembly line of clemency for cash," Rep. Jamie Raskin, a Maryland Democrat and ranking member of the House Judiciary Committee, said last month. Blumenthal is the ranking member of the Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, which has broad authority to probe "inefficiency, mismanagement, and corruption in government."

The congressional letter to Zeldin homed in on Mr. Trump's pardon for Lake, the diesel mechanic. Lake spent seven months in federal prison over his Clean Air Act violation. His pardon was supported by Republican Wyoming Sen. Cynthia Lummis and helped along by Wyoming political consultant and lobbyist Jeff Daugherty.
In their letter, the Democratic lawmakers cited a statement from Lake's wife that appeared to credit Zeldin with intervening to get his pardon in front of the White House.

Allies of Lake and Zeldin pushed back on any impropriety or that the EPA chief was involved in the matter. "It was a clean textbook pardon request," said Daugherty. "We followed the process. We submitted the application and there were no special favors."
A senior EPA official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to talk publicly, disputed that Zeldin advocated for the Lake pardon.
"His family reached out a few times but Zeldin did not make a recommendation or suggestion, other than just updating people internally on the facts of the case," the EPA official said.
The letters asked for any details about Kennedy and Zeldin's possible relationships with either Milton or Lake, and if the Trump administration officials advocated for any other pardons.
"Congress has a compelling interest in ensuring that the constitutional pardon power is exercised with fairness and transparency," the Democrats wrote.

title: Obama raises more than $13 million for Democrats
summary: Former President Barack Obama, who ran on "hope and change," is resurrecting his signature campaign slogan in a new series of digital ads for the Democratic National Committee that were viewed exclusively by CBS News.
story: Washington — He still calls himself the "hope guy." Former President Barack Obama, who ran on "hope and change," is resurrecting his signature campaign slogan in a new series of digital ads for the Democratic National Committee that were viewed exclusively by CBS News.

"I'll be honest with you: I never imagined some of the stuff that's been going on in our country lately," Obama said in a direct-to-camera message. "But I am energized by the millions of Americans who are taking a stand and demanding change, even when it's hard. That's what hope is all about."

During one 52-second spot, the former president never mentions President Trump by name but opines about the difficulties of the last two years and urges Democrats to "win one of the most consequential elections in our country's history."
"The most powerful office in this country has always been 'citizen,'" Obama stated. "And right now, every one of us can help turn hope into action."
The six-figure ad buy across platforms is aimed at supporting the DNC's mobilization efforts, driving voter turnout and boosting grassroots fundraising, according to a DNC official.

"Democrats are heading into November with the wind at our backs and momentum on our side, but we're not taking anything for granted," DNC Chair Ken Martin said in a statement to CBS News. "President Obama's support will motivate and mobilize voters in the home stretch and help Democrats across the country win in races up and down the ballot."

As one of the party's leading surrogates, CBS News has learned the former president has raised more than $13.6 million for Democrats through roughly half a dozen finance events and direct mail campaigns for the DNC and party committees since last year. That includes raking in more than $3.6 million this week at a fundraiser he headlined for the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee in Northern Virginia.

"There are states right now in play that I would not have imagined being in play," Obama told donors during a fireside chat Wednesday night, according to excerpts provided to CBS News. "If you had told me that the polling currently shows James Talarico ahead of Ken Paxton — now, Paxton helps. And James is an outstanding candidate. But if had you told me that he was going to be up in the polls this late, I would have said, 'eh, I don't think so.'"
"The point is, the reason I'm saying this is I don't want anyone to think this is a sure thing," he continued. "But we have a chance."

Over the past several days, Obama has made endorsements in key Senate races from Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff to Maine Democratic Senate nominee Troy Jackson. He also backed several gubernatorial candidates including Wisconsin's David Crowley, Georgia's Keisha Lance Bottoms, New Mexico's Deb Haaland and Pennsylvania's Josh Shapiro. The ads were among nearly two dozen he recently taped for Democratic candidates. In past cycles, the former president has also recorded robocalls for House candidates.

Obama is also expected to hit the campaign trail with additional activities likely to be announced in the coming days. One of those stops includes Michigan, where he will campaign with Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed on Oct. 24.

"I'm going to go to Michigan to campaign for Abdul El-Sayed," Obama said at Wednesday's fundraiser. "And people are like, 'Well, he's really left wing.' But I don't know — he's for a higher minimum wage and healthcare for all, and it doesn't seem crazy to me. You know, FDR was for that, too."

Earlier this year, Obama appeared with other candidates, shooting hoops with Josh Turek in Iowa and getting tacos in Texas with Talarico and gubernatorial nominee Gina Hinojosa. His strategy this fall is centered around where he can "move the needle" with Democrats and persuadable voters, according to his office.
That approach is on full display in his latest ad.
"Use that hope to make a difference," he said. "Get involved."

title: Guilfoyle associate says when she asked him for $100K, it was "quid pro quo"
summary: White House officials were told that text messages between Kimberly Guilfoyle and Eric Deters were real, sources told CBS News.
story: Businessman Eric Deters said he has "no doubt it was pay to play," claiming Kimberly Guilfoyle, now the U.S. ambassador to Greece and ex-fiancee of Donald Trump Jr., asked him to wire $100,000 to pay her American Express bill in exchange for her help with the Trump administration ahead of Guilfoyle's Senate confirmation hearing.

In an interview with CBS News, Deters said Guilfoyle should "lose her ambassadorship" over her alleged behavior, after texts between the two of them from last July were published in the Wall Street Journal.
"It was quid pro quo," Deters told CBS News White House correspondent Weijia Jiang Thursday.
Deters said he never gave her the money.
"Unfortunately for Kimberly Guilfoyle, at that time, at that moment in time, I didn't have $100,000 to spare to give to Kimberly Guilfoyle, or I actually would have been a dumbass enough to do it."
Deters said he made up an "excuse" that his wife wouldn't go along with it.

White House officials were told that the text messages between Guilfoyle and Deters were authentic, sources familiar with the matter told CBS News. Some Trump aides expressed displeasure about Guilfoyle's actions, they said.

The Wall Street Journal first reported this week that Guilfoyle allegedly reached out to Deters days before her congressional hearing to become a U.S. ambassador, saying she needed $100,000 to pay off her American Express credit debt in a way that wouldn't be publicly visible.

"It won't show up anywhere if you wire money to American Express that's all that will show," Guilfoyle wrote to Deters on July 3, according to screen shots of texts provided to CBS News. "I have been officially announced honey please I need you to get this done for me today," she wrote, punctuating the message with a prayer-hands emoji. Her confirmation hearing took place on July 9.
She sent him "American Express Instructions" in a PDF document.

CBS News has reviewed the texts, which were provided by Deters as part of a 292-page file that included dozens of pages of grievances against Trump world figures, communications with Guilfoyle and others, photos of Deters with Guilfoyle, President Trump, Eric Trump and Trump Jr., and a lengthy excerpt of a book Deters has written.
CBS News has reached out to spokespeople for the State Department and the White House, as well as Guilfoyle.

Deters, a longtime Trump supporter, is a retired lawyer and businessman from Kentucky who was sanctioned by the Ohio Supreme Court in 2021 for engaging in the unauthorized practice of law. He has also run unsuccessfully for Kentucky governor and for Rep. Thomas Massie's U.S. House seat.

For years, Deters has been trying to attract media attention and political support for a push to extradite orthopedic spine surgeon Dr. Abubakar Durrani. The government believes Durrani fled the country while he was awaiting trial for healthcare fraud charges. He was accused of billing Medicare, Medicaid and private insurance companies millions of dollars for unnecessary spinal surgeries that were potentially harmful to patients. Today, Deters said he feels slighted that he never received support for his push to have Durrani extradited to the U.S. from influential Trump world figures.

"I sent Susie Wiles, Don Jr. and Kimberly Guilfoyle an email, and I told them, I said, 'You got until 5 o'clock on Monday to help me out with the Durrani victims,'" he said. "They didn't respond. And I told them, 'If you don't, I'm going to go to the media and try to get the media's help because you're not helping.' So I gave them one last shot, and they ignored me."

In the text messages reviewed by CBS News, Deters, who said he also represents hundreds of Durrani's former patients, may have believed he could benefit from Durrani's extradition to the U.S. He wrote to Trump Jr. and Guilfoyle's podcast producer, Drew Lynch, and suggested, "If anyone in Don Jr or your world has an interest in listening to a pitch on how lots of money could be made for a little money in this Durrani matter let me know."
Deters, who no longer practices law, once stood to gain financially if he were able to successfully sue Durrani.

Just before he took office in 2025 and soon after Guilfoyle and Trump Jr. broke off their engagement, Mr. Trump announced he planned to nominate Guilfoyle to be U.S. ambassador to Greece. But Deters said her influence has waned since her relationship with Trump Jr. ended.
"There was no question that she would do anything for me," Deters said. "The problem was, she was on the outs of the Trump world."
Deters claimed Guilfoyle knew there was something wrong about asking for the payment.

"She knew there was something wrong about it because she kept getting mad at me," Deters said. "I mean, I'm naive, I'm putting stuff in writing, sending it to her. She's getting mad. She wants me to use Signal. I didn't know what Signal was."

In late June 2025, she texted, "Eric, I really wish you would stop papering these things. It's really dangerous and not helpful to you and not helpful to you or me while you could simply just call me on Signal." Deters had just sent her a memo to complain that she had not delivered on things that he had asked of her, including getting him booked on Tucker Carlson's podcast.

"I generously offered you $1 million dollars when Durrani settles if you got me on Tucker," he wrote. He also complained that he had prepared a "concise summary" for then-Attorney General Pam Bondi, but "I have not received nothing concrete."
Deters also sought a meeting with then-IRS Commissioner Billy Long about a tax issue, and he wanted Guilfoyle to send the lyrics to a song he had written to Kid Rock.
Deters said in the memo, "I am not naive or a sucker. I need results. No results. No need for me to pay."
He prodded her over text soon afterward: "As of this moment, I bet there have been no emails AND phone calls by you to Wells [Tucker Carlson's producer], Bondi, Long."

Guilfoyle said his accusation was "completely false" and sent as proof the PDF of a letter in which she congratulated Long on his confirmation and asked him to give his attention to Deters' tax issue.
Deters claimed he has paid Guilfoyle and members of the Trump family in the past.

"I paid her a total of $300,000," he said. "Don, Jr. $200,000 for two appearances. Eric Trump for $100,000, $125,000 for President Trump's PAC, $100,000 to go to Kentucky Derby with Trump. So, I paid a lot of money to Trump World," he said, adding that he never owed money to Guilfoyle or anyone else around Mr. Trump.

According to the documents he shared with CBS News, he says he paid Guilfoyle a total of $300,000 for appearance fees. And he said his promise of further payments to Guilfoyle and Lynch was to be for their services as consultants.
The Trump administration's response so far
In Greece, where Guilfoyle greeted his plane earlier this week, Secretary of State Marco Rubio chastised reporters for asking about the matter.

"You guys walk around thinking that because some source told you something and you reported it, it's the gospel," he said. "It's not the gospel. It's not the gospel for me. That's not the way we do things."

Rubio also declined to comment because the story had only "literally posted a few hours ago," telling reporters that "we don't conduct these things in a press conference, on a tarmac, in a foreign country." As Rubio departed Greece, Guilfoyle was present, but off to the side.
CBS News on Thursday asked Vice President JD Vance about the propriety of a government official asking someone to pay off their debt.

CBS News senior White House reporter Jennifer Jacobs asked: "Do you have any reaction to a U.S. government official, in this case a U.S. ambassador, asking someone to pay off debt in exchange to access to other government officials?"
"With that hypothetical, obviously I don't love that, but I, you know, I don't know exactly who you're talking about. I don't know the full details," Vance responded.
Deters insisted his relationship with Guilfoyle was purely political.
"Kimberly Guilfoyle and I have absolutely zero personal relationship, nada," he told CBS News.
But Deters is now determined to share his story. He said he wants to draw attention to Dr. Durrani's victims. And he wants Guilfoyle out of her post as U.S. ambassador.
"I'm a tough hombre," Deters said. "I'm going to get to take Kimberly Guilfoyle's deposition."
