title: AI leaders lobby Trump health officials in government-run chat room
summary: A Slack workspace has served as a war room for AI industry insiders and Trump administration officials to launch a rapid campaign aimed at persuading Americans to manage their healthcare and medical records on apps.
story: A cadre of elite techies, financiers, and high-level Trump administration officials have spent a year quietly charting an extraordinary and rapid campaign to persuade Americans to use apps and other artificial intelligence-powered tools to manage their healthcare and medical records.

As that campaign has unfolded, administration officials have granted tech companies an unusual opportunity to nudge the nation's health department toward a loosely regulated future for AI health apps in which the government reimburses them for services as it does medical professionals.

In February, federal health officials invited those businesses — including tech giants Microsoft, Anthropic, OpenAI, Apple, and Google — to a listening session on conversational AI products for patients, such as chatbots. Representatives from at least 35 industry organizations attended the meeting held by the Food and Drug Administration, which is responsible for regulating health apps as medical devices. Companies were prompted in advance to explain their AI products and how they access patients' sensitive medical information.

But the meeting did not appear on the FDA's public calendar or regulatory notices, nor was the public invited. Rather, the invitation for a select group to help shape federal policy governing AI in healthcare was extended in a chat room on the messaging service Slack.

"This is a great opportunity to support HHS' goals and share your state-of-the-art understanding of safe Conversational AI development and monitoring to help FDA shape future guidance," CMS senior policy adviser Morgan Taylor wrote in the Slack workspace.

The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services has not formally announced the chat room through federal regulatory channels, though CMS officials have talked about it at industry conferences. Legal experts said the chat room resembles a federal advisory panel, which would be required to operate in public view.

KFF Health News reviewed thousands of Slack messages, meeting transcripts, and video recordings that reveal how the Trump administration has granted the industry a direct line to top government officials — including former head of the Department of Government Efficiency Amy Gleason.

The conversation took place behind the scenes as federal health officials publicly worked to integrate AI and other technology into nearly every aspect of healthcare, a plan they've branded the "Health Technology Ecosystem."

"We wanted to give industry a chance to play in the sandbox of government-supported healthcare," CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz said in September at the public launch of an initiative that allows health apps to bill Medicare for AI services such as wearable device tracking. Last week, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. delivered an enthusiastic endorsement of AI in healthcare, claiming it is "much better informed than any doctor in the country."

Meanwhile, HHS staff even promised that a recently launched Medicare App Library would serve as a lucrative pipeline for those businesses to get new users. The library's webpage currently promotes only two dozen commercial apps to millions of American seniors and those with disabilities.
As Trump officials sell it, Americans will get easier access to their medical records so apps can swiftly provide health or wellness advice. In practice, however, so will the tech companies.
Doctors, meanwhile, are increasingly worried about how patients use and share their medical records with the nascent technology.

"Some of these tools just aren't ready for primetime," said John Whyte, CEO of the American Medical Association. "We don't have enough data about them. We don't understand how they work, how they're using the information. There's no liability if these tools get things wrong."
CMS officials declined to answer several questions about the Slack workspace, including about its legality.

"CMS is focused on giving Medicare beneficiaries greater access to their health information and useful digital tools while promoting an open, interoperable healthcare system," Gleason, now chief product officer for the newly created Office of Health Technology and Products at CMS, wrote in an emailed statement. "The Health Technology Ecosystem is an open, voluntary technical collaboration. CMS will continue working with patients, providers, payers, technology organizations, and other stakeholders to make health information more accessible and useful to the Americans it serves."
The FDA did not respond to a request for comment.
The conversation begins
The behind-the-scenes effort to funnel more Americans to AI-powered health apps began in August 2025 in the Slack workspace.
"Welcome all!" Gleason wrote. "Please be sure to read the Code of Conduct and see the Channel list as well to help you find channels that are relevant to you."

Gleason is best known for serving as the acting administrator of Elon Musk's Department of Government Efficiency, as it gained access to millions of Americans' sensitive personal and financial data, including at the Social Security Administration.
As her work with DOGE wound down last year, Gleason welcomed a variety of tech leaders, investors, and entrepreneurs to the chat room.

The Slack workspace's participants include representatives from major digital wellness companies like Oura Health, AI companies like Palantir, and investment outfits like 8VC, a venture capital firm associated with Kennedy's son Finn. While the Slack's member count has ballooned to 1,700 over the past year, only a handful of patient advocates, doctors, and hospital representatives are in it.
The code of conduct Gleason shared on Slack in August 2025 documented that CMS had quietly established a technology working group.

The document also set ground rules for the Slack workspace, noting that the group does not constitute an "advisory committee," nor would it be used "to obtain advice or recommendations for HHS, CMS, or any HHS/CMS officials." The code also advises that federal employees "are prohibited from endorsing any product, service, or enterprise."

Joseph Daval, a former FDA lawyer who is now a research specialist at Harvard Medical School, reviewed messages from the Slack workspace at the request of KFF Health News. He said the chat room in some ways resembles a federal advisory committee — an independent panel that can be formally stood up by an agency head, Congress, or the president to ensure agencies act in the best interest of the public rather than industry.
The law on advisory committees "was passed in part out of a concern about interest group capture, about anticompetitive capture of agency policymaking, about corruption," he said.
Daval said the chat group looks like a committee, with members interacting with one another and building consensus on preferred courses of action.
If it were a formal advisory committee, though, Daval said, it would be subject to certain "membership requirements having to do with independence and fair balance."
A "sales engine"
Over a series of video calls, CMS officials promised tech leaders participating in the Slack workspace that the agency would promote their health apps.

Jacob Shiff, the chief AI and technology officer at CMS' Innovation Center, told industry representatives in a Zoom meeting in February that he hoped the agency's work would be a "sales engine" for the health apps.

"We're going to have a directory of all the organizations," Shiff said in a video recording reviewed by KFF Health News. "The people on this call who hopefully will have amazing solutions that work will be the winners, and you have every incentive to obviously drive down your costs so you can be extremely profitable and scale. So hopefully we're selling — or enabling you guys to thrive."
A recording of the call had been publicly available through a Google Drive link but was made private the day after KFF Health News asked about comments made during the meeting.
CMS did not respond to queries about how the agency has decided which AI-powered health apps appear in the Medicare App Library or why federal employees have promised to promote the products.

Days before publicly launching the Medicare App Library, CMS officials promised AI tech leaders during an informal meeting that the new webpage would become an important distribution channel for health apps because Medicare enrollees would place trust in products listed on the CMS website.

"If medicare.gov is promoting it, for lack of a better word, then yeah, it would be an app that I would trust and explore," CMS' Taylor said during the April 7 meeting, channeling enrollees, according to a transcript of the call.

The Medicare App Library's webpage encourages older and disabled Americans to manage health conditions such as obesity, cancer, or diabetes using two dozen AI-driven apps developed by some of the world's largest corporations, including Microsoft and Google. Many of the apps promise in their product descriptions to give insight, perform analyses, or develop plans that will help patients lose weight or manage diabetes.

CMS officials have suggested to tech representatives during at least two meetings this year that those apps will be prioritized for a new agency program that reimburses companies for AI chatbot advice or wearable device tracking, according to video recordings.
CMS has not publicly divulged all the criteria it uses to decide which apps are listed in its library, but the webpage promotes apps still in their infancy.

Among them is Slothwise, a health app launched this year from a San Francisco apartment by a young, self-described biotech entrepreneur and triple citizen of Russia, Israel, and the U.S. The app says it "knows your whole health" by analyzing medical records and tracking health data for $9.99 a month. It has been reviewed on the Apple and Google app stores only a handful of times.
"I trusted slothwise with my health info because it was endorsed by medicare," one reviewer wrote in a Google review in August. "Connecting info was smooth and I learned a lot about my health."

In a statement, Slothwise CEO Sofia Sigal-Passeck did not answer questions about the size and medical expertise of her current team, nor about the availability of a doctor to consult with patients who use the app. The app, she said, is only "informational" at this time.

"I've spent years building at the intersection of AI and complex biological data," Sigal-Passeck wrote in an email. "A small team is not the same thing as an inexperienced team. Slothwise is built by physicians, PhD researchers and engineers."
"No regulation, no rulemaking"
What's often less clear — and buried deep in lengthy privacy policies — is that these apps are tapping into the intimate details of patients' medical records to fuel their AI-driven analyses.

Tech vendors have lobbied the government to treat these apps, once they are vetted and authorized by a third-party company, like a patient requesting records. That position gives apps sweeping access to pull sensitive health data from the national network through which providers electronically exchange medical records, called the Trusted Exchange Framework and Common Agreement, or TEFCA.

A small but influential group of those tech company executives directly made the case to federal health officials during a formal meeting in May, arguing that when health apps request medical records they should be treated as if they are standing "in the shoes" of a patient.

On Slack, tech vendors have lobbied for a "frictionless pathway" for verified users, after they've consented once, that allows the app to gain limitless access to patients' medical records from the TEFCA network.

Ryan Howells, a healthcare management consultant who lobbies for a Washington, D.C.-based digital health tech organization called the CARIN Alliance, has spearheaded an effort for patients — vis-à-vis apps — to more easily access medical records. He has regularly noted in Slack that health apps accessing TEFCA must be vetted by a third-party organization — one of which he sits on the board of — and agree to a code of conduct, developed by the alliance he lobbies for.

"What more can you do to have trust in these apps?" he wrote in a March Slack message, responding to concerns about how much patient consent is needed for apps to access medical records on the network.
Kristen Valdes, the CEO of b.well, a company that also connects apps to the TEFCA network, made a similar argument.
"My opinion is that we need to stop protecting patients from themselves," she wrote in the same message thread. "Full stop."

Howells did not respond to an emailed list of questions from KFF Health News. In an interview, Valdes told KFF Health News that her comment reflected her frustration at the "paternalism" of the healthcare system, which she said has historically made it difficult for patients to access their records. Although, she said, "there are going to be good and bad apps."
Other tech leaders worried in Slack about the approach.
One startup founder cautioned the group to think about the pitfalls of giving health apps broad leeway to pull medical records.

"We might all be good, honest actors here but security & privacy systems have to be designed around the presence of malicious actors – especially if we want this system to scale up to thousands of apps," wrote Jason Kulatunga, who runs Fasten Health, a medical records management platform.

Gleason, the CMS official, has publicly championed the vision shared by Howells and Valdes. In her speeches, she frequently urges doctors to accept patient medical records directly from apps and calls on them to "Kill the Clipboard," also the title of a 2025 white paper co-authored by Howells that urges doctors' offices to abandon paper records.

Last month, Gleason spoke to a crowd gathered at a swanky hotel in Washington for an event hosted by the MAHA Institute, a think tank that supports Secretary Kennedy's agenda. She laid out her work with tech companies over the past year as she discussed the Trump administration's efforts to make medical records more digitally accessible.
As she told it, more Americans can now download an app and access their medical records.
"Once you've verified your identity you can just click a simple button and say, I'd like my medical records into whatever app I choose," Gleason said.
She continued: "That was all done just — no regulation, no rulemaking — just by challenging industry to work together."

KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF — the independent source for health policy research, polling, and journalism.

title: Google unveils Gemini AI agent to handle workplace tasks
summary: The Gemini agent can write and run code, integrate into apps like Gmail, and help workers knock out everyday workplace tasks, Google said.
story: Google on Thursday unveiled a new AI agent tailored for workplace tasks, positioning it to compete with other technology giants racing to offer their own virtual office assistants.

Called Gemini, the AI is a "universal agent" that can write and run code, create images and media and integrate with Google products like Gmail, Docs, Drive and Sheets, as well as third-party apps like Slack and Microsoft 365, Google said in its statement.
Thomas Kurian, the CEO of Google Cloud, shared the new product during a keynote address at Gemini at Work 2026 on Thursday, an annual event where Google showcases its suite of AI technology.

Google said the agent can seamlessly integrate into people's workflow, acting like a co-worker that can carry out tasks autonomously. Workers can delegate tasks to the agent, and it will return a finished product, Kurian said in the company's blog post.

"Gemini can function as your personal assistant or as a team member, where it works on behalf of a group of people, like a project manager within a team, or on behalf of a specific role in an organization, like an analyst in your finance department," he wrote.

To execute on certain tasks, Gemini can create its own "sub-agents," which Google described as "temporary, job-specific agents, each with their own identity," that can work together to accomplish goals over several days.
The AI agent, which runs in the Cloud, is designed to build memory and skills based on the tasks it's assigned and the questions users ask it.
"You never have to re-brief it or wonder which machine you told it to do something on," Kurian wrote in the blog post.

Gemini joins a growing field of AI agents marketed for personal and workplace use. In September, Meta introduced Muse, a personal AI assistant that has been downloaded millions of times. OpenAI followed suit late last month with the introduction of "Dots", an "AI helper" available to ChatGPT users with Pro and Business Premium accounts.

title: Musk's data centers push out family that's owned land for generations
summary: A plant in Southaven, Mississippi, that powers Elon Musk's SpaceXAI data centers in the area has sparked backlash from residents concerned about noise and air pollution.
story: On a 2-acre property in Mississippi, 52-year-old Krystal Polk's family lived off the land for generations, raising chickens and pigs, growing onions and herbs and trading their peaches for pears.
The land, on the border with Tennessee in the city of Southaven, was her family's survival, Polk said. "We lived a very simplistic life," she told CBS News.

While life there may have been simple in Polk's view, the circumstances surrounding her home rarely ever were. Her family acquired the property "before people of color were allowed to have land," she said, and it's been passed down for four generations. When Polk's parents first moved in, they discovered "KKK" scrawled at the bottom of the hill of their property, she said.

Holding on to the land was made more difficult a year ago when a noisy neighbor appeared across the street — a power plant so loud, it drove the family away. Since then, the land has sat mostly empty, occupied only by an unrelenting hum.

The plant, which is powering Elon Musk's SpaceXAI data centers in the Memphis area, has sparked backlash from Southaven residents concerned about noise and air pollution. A petition by the resident-run Safe and Sound Coalition calling to shut down the power plant has over 1,400 signatures.
Polk said she remembers when she could hear the birds chirping at her family home. Now, she said the plant's "constant roaring" lingers in her ears even after she leaves.
"It's like you're in the middle of the airport where the planes are taking off, but they never take off," she said.

SpaceXAI, formerly known as xAI, recently said in a July press release that it is investing millions of dollars in sound walls and silencers with "advanced quieting technologies" around the plant. Southaven residents have told CBS News that one sound wall installed so far has provided little reprieve from the noise.
"We gathered there"

Over the course of two years, Musk has expanded his footprint in the Memphis region starting with the construction of his Colossus 1 data center just north of Southaven in 2024. By January 2026, two more data centers were announced. This July, Musk quietly confirmed the construction of another local data center, "Minihard," in a reply to a post on his platform X.

Musk's SpaceXAI projects will total more than $20 billion in investments to Southaven, which Mississippi Gov. Tate Reeves said in a press release will "bring amazing opportunities to its residents for generations."
But for Polk, the development has meant a new kind of strain on her family.
"We don't know the future," she said. "So we're not sure what to invest into it."

Polk moved away from the family home after getting married, and for years, it bounced between relatives. It was where Polk churned her own ice cream as a child, held her rehearsal dinner when she got married and hosted the holidays each year.
"We gathered there and we thanked God for what we had," she said. "It was always a celebration."

She planned to return as a retiree and eventually pass the property down to her children. But now, those plans have been put on hold. Apart from the "24/7" noise, Polk said she and her family have asthma and are concerned about fumes from the gas turbines at the plant.

"I'm afraid that we will be the ones that everyone looks back on and says, 'Hey, remember they tried to tell us that these things were hazardous to our health and causing harm,'" Polk said. "I'm afraid that we're going to be those casualties."

The National Association for the Advancement of Colored People and other groups sued xAI and its subsidiary MZX Tech in April, alleging that the plant "emits significant amounts of harmful pollutants."

In June, SpaceXAI filed a motion to dismiss the case, and the Department of Justice also moved to intervene and dismiss the case. The Justice Department said in a statement that the matter "concerns national security and Mississippi's lawful action regarding permitting" and that the NAACP's lawsuit "could hinder the War Department's use of AI for national defense."
CBS News reached out to SpaceXAI multiple times for comment and has not heard back.

The company has entered into an agreement with the Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality that includes removing the 69 temporary turbines at the plant and replacing them with 41 permanent turbines over the course of a year.

But a study conducted by EmPower Analytics Group found that the plan to install dozens of gas turbines would increase air pollution in the area and would be concentrated in communities that are disproportionately Black. The study was commissioned by the Southern Environmental Law Center, which is co-counsel for the plaintiffs in the NAACP's lawsuit against xAI and MZX Tech.

The Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality said in a statement that it doesn't comment on "third-party reports or matters involved in pending litigation" and that it "remains committed to carrying out its responsibility to protect public health and the environment through implementation and enforcement of applicable state and federal environmental laws and regulations."
MDEQ said that as part of the permitting process, MZX Tech was required to demonstrate that the proposed facility would not violate air quality standards.

Still, residents are not convinced. Shannon Samsa, a 27-year-old physician assistant living in Southaven, is concerned about the plant's impact on her community's health. She's become an outspoken advocate against the plant, speaking up at city meetings and leading the Safe and Sound Coalition as its director.
"It's not just my neighbors, it's not just my family and friends, it's my future patients," she said. "It's also a huge healthcare issue."
Priceless property
As SpaceXAI extends its reach in the region, the future of Polk's property hangs in the balance. Some companies have expressed interest in purchasing it.

Polk said she was approached by real estate firm Cushman & Wakefield Commercial Advisors with an offer. After multiple "nos" over the course of weeks, she said she eventually filed a Better Business Bureau complaint, accusing the company of harassment and manipulation.
In the complaint, reviewed by CBS News, Polk alleged the firm tried to coerce her into agreeing to services.

Cushman & Wakefield Commercial Advisors, in response to the complaint, said it was exploring the potential acquisition of Polk's land on behalf of a client, who was not identified. The firm confirmed it made multiple attempts to contact Polk "by phone, text and written correspondence," but denied engaging in "harassment, pressure tactics, or inappropriate conduct."
Polk said the company has not reached out since she filed the complaint. She declined to disclose the firm's offer, but said that "it was not worth anything."
Selling the land is complicated — keeping it was her father's dying wish, Polk said.
"He asked me to please keep it as much as I could within reason," she said. "I'm not sure if you could offer a value."

title: Mayor to homeowner losing sleep over data center plant: "Consider selling"
summary: Noise from a Mississippi plant powering Elon Musk's xAI data centers in the area is causing migraines, ringing ears and sleepless nights, residents say.
story: It was 4 a.m. on a Sunday and 46-year-old Jason Haley was once again wide awake.

The suburban silence that Haley had grown used to in his two decades as a resident of Southaven, Mississippi, had, for the last few months, been replaced by a constant whirring, like an airplane hovering over his home, he said.

The noise keeping Haley awake was coming from a plant powering Elon Musk's xAI data centers in the area, according to a lawsuit filed in June against the company and its subsidiary, MZX Tech. Haley and two other Southaven residents, who live within a mile of the plant, allege in the suit that "near-constant" noise and vibrations are causing negative physical and psychological health effects.

The filing comes amid growing resistance toward data center development, with the majority of Americans opposing local construction of a data center, according to a Gallup poll published earlier this year.

Similar disputes are playing out across the country, like in Mount Pleasant, Wisconsin, where a lawsuit this month filed by residents alleges a data center emits "unreasonable and excessive noise" onto residents' properties and in Lowell, Massachusetts, where noise from a data center's cooling center "disrupts neighbors' sleep," according to an April suit.

There are more than 4,000 data centers in the U.S., according to a recent United Nations report. To power the data centers, developers are building their own plants, sometimes with little warning to residents like Haley.

Haley reached out to Southaven Mayor Darren Musselwhite about the noise in emails he shared with CBS News. In one last November, he urged Musselwhite to drive through the neighborhood "and take a listen to the constant high pitch noises."
"I am aware of the noise and working on a solution with xAI officials," Musselwhite had responded to Haley an hour later. "It is a problem," he said in another email later in the day.
But soon, another sleepless night rolled around and Haley was emailing the mayor again.

"Anyone else I can reach out to?" Haley wrote to Musselwhite. "It's almost 4 am and I can hear it from my bed. The high pitch and roaring combined is full force at this time. My ears are ringing. I can't live in this. How was this ever approved?"
"I don't care that this is Elon's project"

Just north of Southaven, which sits on the Mississippi-Tennessee border, xAI's data center Colossus went online in Memphis in September 2024. The company dubbed it "the world's largest AI supercomputer."
By late July 2025, Musk was announcing that another data center, Colossus 2, was set to begin operation in the area within weeks.

Days later, an announcement popped into the Facebook feeds of Southaven residents: An energy facility that had been dormant for decades will be revived to support xAI's expanding data center operations in the area, Musselwhite said.
The post was met by a flood of comments, with some lauding the development and others expressing concern about the plant's impact on the environment and strain on local resources.
Meanwhile, Haley started hearing sounds.
"My first thought was somebody's got a leaf blower going all the time," he said.

By December, the noise had become a fixture. He started getting headaches, stopped getting sleep and slipped into feelings of hopelessness and depression. The noise was inescapable, he said, and despite his best efforts to drown it out (sleeping with earplugs, getting a box fan for white noise), it continued to drone on.

So Haley began speaking up — at city government meetings, on Facebook and through TikTok, where he posts videos of himself measuring the noise with a sound meter. He later became involved in a grassroots coalition called Safe and Sound, drawing awareness to concerns surrounding xAI's undertakings in the region.
The "activist" label is one he's reluctantly accepted.

"I've never been into any kind of activism, never really kept up with politics a whole lot," he said. "I'm just a guy that has a problem with this noise, and started speaking out and trying to raise awareness."

When he emailed Musselwhite about the noise again in December, his message came with a disclosure: "I am not a republican or democrat, I don't care that this is Elon's project. I didn't know whose it was when I started complaining about the noise that started in August."
Musselwhite responded a few days later.

"As I mentioned to you in the public meeting, you seem to be a reasonable person," he said. "I will give you some unsolicited advice from an older man, be careful with whom you associate so you don't damage your credibility."

By January, xAI was expanding its footprint with a third data center in Southaven, MACROHARDDR. As residents like Haley continued pushing back online and in city meetings, Musselwhite had a new message.

Southaven, he said in a Facebook post, was "under attack by all who choose to oppose Elon Musk because of his high-profile political stances." He warned residents to "beware of the smokescreen of radical politics."
In his emails to Haley, Musselwhite continued to acknowledge the noise as a problem.
"The noise issue is one of my highest priorities and I have been in detailed discussions with xAI and many independent professionals to resolve this," he wrote in March.
But in the same email, he offered Haley more advice: "I know they want houses for employees, so you may want to consider selling your home."
CBS News made multiple attempts to speak with Musselwhite and did not receive a reply.
Migraines, ringing ears and sleepless nights
Moving isn't Haley's preference, but he said he is in the financial position to do so if he chooses.
That's not the case for everyone.
A little over a decade ago, 31-year-old Taylor Logsdon bought a home for her growing family in Southaven and began building her life around it.
"We loved it here," she said. "It was peaceful, it was quiet, didn't have to worry about nothing."

But that was before the noise, so loud, she said, that it sometimes shakes her home. Logsdon, who is also involved in the Safe and Sound coalition and is suing xAI with Haley and one other Southaven resident, said she has experienced migraines and anxiety as a result of the noise.
She said she has persistent ringing in her ears and so do her children. A full night of sleep has become rare for the family.
"I would move tomorrow if I could," she said, adding that she needs to save money before she can afford to move.
Her children, all under the age of 13, are having trouble staying awake at school.
"One of them is extra angry all the time — never, never has been that way, but he's just irritable like all the time," she said. "I feel like I'm snappier too."
xAI spent millions of dollars trying to mitigate the sound with a sound wall, a berm and evergreen trees, Musselwhite said in a February Facebook post.
"It still hasn't helped. It hasn't even put a dent in it," Logsdon said.
People living in areas where there is "constant humming or buzzing" report headaches, stress and sleep disturbance, said Dr. Samoon Ahmad, a clinical professor of psychiatry at New York University.

A 2023 study found that environmental noise exposure can lead to adverse associations for cardiovascular disease and mortality, diabetes, hearing impairment, neurological disorders and adverse reproductive outcomes.
"People think of annoyance as an abstract term," Ahmad said. "It's not an abstract term because it has real physiological ramifications."

The World Health Organization recommends less than 40 decibels of annual average nighttime noise outside of bedrooms to prevent adverse health effects. Haley has recorded noise levels over 60 decibels as late as 10:15 p.m. from his Southaven backyard.
Musk's Memphis
Even before Logsdon and Haley decided to take action against xAI, Musk's growing presence in the Memphis area garnered attention from advocacy groups over health and environmental concerns.

The National Association for the Advancement of Colored People filed a lawsuit in April against xAI claiming the Southaven plant emits "significant" amounts of harmful pollutants from its 27 gas turbines, which has since increased to 59, according to a court filing reviewed by CBS News. The NAACP has also filed an appeal to challenge the Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality's decision to issue an air permit allowing the Southaven plant to operate 41 permanent methane gas turbines. A study found their operation would increase air pollution in an area already grappling with a disproportionate number of asthma-related emergency room visits. The study was commissioned by the Southern Environmental Law Center, which is co-counsel for the plaintiffs.
CBS News has reached out to xAI for comment.

Musk's investment in the latest Southaven data center brings his company's contribution to the area to $20 billion, according to the office of Mississippi Gov. Tate Reeves. The governor called it "the largest economic development project in Mississippi's history."

Musk's financial footprint has also extended beyond the data centers — MZX Tech donated over $1.3 million to the Southaven Police Department in February, according to the donation agreement obtained by CBS News, and has offered half-priced Starlink for those in the Memphis region.
But Logsdon says the cost to her and her family's health has her wondering why it feels like her city is willing to "hurt the few to get the benefits."
"We were not a failure town before," Logsdon said. "It's not like our economics were terrible here."
Southaven had a median household income of over $70,000 in 2024, according to the U.S. Census Bureau — $20,000 more than the state average.
Logsdon, currently a stay-at-home mom, will be searching for work this fall so she and her husband can start saving up to move away from the plant. For now, her goal is a full night's sleep.
"I hope that my family can go back to having our normal," she said. "Being able to sleep at night, being able to enjoy my backyard, being able to go swimming."

title: Detecting deepfakes, in a world where even reality is suspect
summary: Hany Farid, a leading expert on deepfakes and digital manipulation, estimates that half of the content widely viewed on the Internet is fake. What does this mean for our ability to detect images generated or hallucinated by artificial intelligence?
story: Last February, a Tomahawk cruise missile struck an Iranian elementary school, killing more than 150 people, most of them children. President Trump initially suggested that it could have been somebody else's Tomahawk: "Whether it's Iran or somebody else, the fact that a Tomahawk – a Tomahawk is very generic, it's sold to other countries, but that's being investigated right now," he said.

When Iran put out video as evidence that it was a U.S. missile, Hany Farid, one of the world's foremost experts on deepfakes, was contacted by several media outlets to determine if it was real or fake.

A professor at Dartmouth College, Farid is also co-founder of GetReal Security, a cyber security firm. "What was difficult about this case was you had very little to work on," he said. "We had a very grainy, shaky video. The missile is extremely small. And we had to reason about the physical plausibility of that missile striking the ground."

But he also had certain aspects that he could study scientifically, involving the speed of sound, the speed of light, and the size of the missile: "And those three things were enough for us to say that this is physically plausible," he said. "And this is the important part: all evidence led us to the belief that the video was authentic, and there's been no refuting of that."
But that's the world we live in: Reality itself, so perfectly mimicked by artificial intelligence, that even reality is suspect.

Farid said, "Here's the thing that makes me a little crazy, as a scientist in particular: I don't think you should be able to go into a court of law and say, 'Here is some evidence that is damning enough to put this person to death,' and then the judge says, 'Well, how do you know it's real?' And I say, 'Well, because the computer told me so.' This is not an answer

"And if I can't explain to you, to a judge, and to a jury, what is happening here – because the lighting, because the shadows, because the geometry, whatever it is – that's what we need to be able to do."
A case in point: Alex Pretti, who was killed by an ICE agent in Minnesota. If you remember the scene last January 24, it was chaotic. Several ICE agents with guns surrounded Pretti.

Farid showed us a blurry photo of Pretti that was taken from the original video. "Somebody took this and 'enhanced' it," he said. According to Farid, the crispness of this "enhanced" image makes the scene feel "more real, but what it also did is when it enhanced it, it seems to have put a gun in [Pretti's] hand. If you go back to this video, the camera's panning a little bit and what's happening is, there's a shadow behind his hand on the street. And what the AI did is that it hallucinated this."

Farid says artificial intelligence has learned, "When you see photos like this with three men with guns, everybody's got a gun." And now, when you do Google searches for events like Pretti's killing, it shows the "enhanced" image.

By Farid's estimate, half of the content that's widely viewed on the Internet is fake, basically a toss of the coin. Much of it has its own sneering label: "AI slop." Footage of airplanes skidding on the tarmac, toddlers dancing a two-step, Elvis. "AI slop is a broad term that defines people generating content using AI just to grab eyeballs, video after video after video driving engagement," Farid said.

For the most part, Farid limits his examinations to the really serious stuff, the deepfakes. Even so, he's inundated. He said, "We're seeing deepfakes being weaponized in many, many different ways, from the creation of child sexual abuse material, to non-consensual intimate imagery, to full-blown state-sponsored disinformation campaigns, to what the North Koreans have done, [which] is to have their IT workers interview for jobs remotely. And they conceal their accent using AI. They can conceal their identity using a deepfake, where they change their identity from eyebrow to chin, cheek to cheek, in real time over a video call. They can conceal their geolocation. And they interview for jobs. I will tell you, just about every single Fortune 500 company has hired one or more of these, whether they know it or not.

"And now, the question you want to ask yourself is, what's next? Well, so one CEO said, 'Okay. No more virtual interviews. No more remote work.' That's insane. … We're gonna start flying people across the country? That can't be the answer. I mean it's exhausting. Let's be honest. I mean, if we're always looking at our shoulder over every email, every text message, every voicemail, every phone call, every video call? It's exhausting. I'm exhausted, and I do this for a living."

Asked if he has nightmares over deepfakes, Farid replied, "I look at content all day long. And usually the things I look at are not pleasant. I'm looking at bad things that involve horrific crimes, and when you view these things over and over and over again, they sit with you and you can't get them out of your head.

'And number two is, I don't want to be wrong. And five years ago I felt a lot more confident about our ability to distinguish real from fake. It's gotten harder. And then I worry more. I feel like the ground is constantly shifting," he said.

It builds – the stress, the pressure. After seven years on the West Coast, Farid returned to Dartmouth College, where he had previously spent 20 years on faculty. His wife, Emily Cooper, is also a professor there. The two of them bought a rural property in neighboring Vermont, where Farid mows acres of meadows, and cuts enough wood to feed their stoves through the winter. It's enough mowing and cutting to rinse some of those disturbing images away. It's isolated – there's no mail delivery, no garbage pickup –  but it's peaceful.

Certain work-related issues linger. Social media? Farid loathes it: "You can look at social media, at online platforms and say there is measurable harm coming to young kids, to adults, to seniors, across the boards. And I think we have been so mesmerized by these products which are, by design, meant to be addictive.

"I think we did an experiment on an entire generation of these young kids coming up, putting these devices in their hands. And now we've woken up and we're like, 'Oh, my God. This is terrible.' This generation right now has lower learning outcomes than any generation in history. Go to Palo Alto at the fanciest private schools where all the tech billionaires send their kids. There's no devices in those classrooms. They know."
That $17 billion settlement that Meta reached a few weeks back includes some safeguards, like a two-hour time limit for users under the age of 18. Farid thinks that's a start, but not nearly enough.
"The darkest vision I have is that everybody lives in their own information ecosystem, and nobody knows how to talk to each other anymore," he said.

On platforms where algorithms prefer fake to real content, Farid thinks all of us should stay off social media, or at the very least take those apps off our phones, to resist the temptation. As for those websites that promise to detect AI fakes, he says it's not that simple: "Here's what I think is next (and by saying next, I mean in the coming year), which is most of the deepfakes that we are seeing today have a human somewhere in the process. Somebody's hands are on the keyboard. There's still a human in the loop. But what's gonna start happening is AI agents are gonna start creating their own fakes."

And what is an AI agent? "An agent just has more autonomy, and what we have started to see is when you give it a problem to solve, it will find creative ways to do it, including creating a fake identity to interact with a human to get a human to do something and then it will lie about it," he said.

AI agents have been in the news recently for going rogue in testing trials, intensifying the global debate over AI safety and the very course of humanity. These are issues Hany Farid grapples with every day.

"I think there is a near-future where people will have an AI agent that they grow up with," he said, "and it will know them better than anybody else who knows them. And I think that thing can live on forever.

"My wife and I have been talking about this," he said. "She's younger than I am. We've been talking about, should we be incorporating into an AI agent my voice, my likeness, how I think, how I talk, the type of questions I ask her in the morning, how I respond to her when she's sad, how I respond to her when she's happy? Do I think AI can mimic that to near-perfection? Yes."

Asked if – should Farid be hit by a truck – an AI agent of him might be an adequate replica of him for his wife, Farid said, "I think, for my generation, the answer is probably no. But the next generation, the generation after that, that will think about these things differently? I don't know."

title: At least 4 dead as Isaias brings threat of floods across the Southeast
summary: More than 700,000 customers are without power after Isaias made landfall as a hurricane on the northern Gulf Coast.
story: What we know as Isaias moves across the Southeast:

Isaias, the first hurricane of the 2026 Atlantic season, made landfall in the northern Gulf Coast near Destin, Florida, on Friday night as a Category 2 storm, but within hours had weakened to a post-tropical cyclone.At least four people have died due to the storm — two in Alabama and two in Florida. Two died as a result of trees falling on their homes, officials said.The weakening storm is still forecast to bring powerful winds, flash flooding and storm surges to a large swath of the Southeast through the weekend. It is expected to dissipate on Sunday.Tens of thousands of people have evacuated the region, officials said, and more than 700,000 customers are without power across the region.

Isaias, the first hurricane of the 2026 Atlantic season, made landfall in the northern Gulf Coast near Destin, Florida, on Friday night as a Category 2 storm, but within hours had weakened to a post-tropical cyclone.
At least four people have died due to the storm — two in Alabama and two in Florida. Two died as a result of trees falling on their homes, officials said.
The weakening storm is still forecast to bring powerful winds, flash flooding and storm surges to a large swath of the Southeast through the weekend. It is expected to dissipate on Sunday.
Tens of thousands of people have evacuated the region, officials said, and more than 700,000 customers are without power across the region.

title: Vehicle driven by ICE agents in Texas hits and injures man, sheriff says
summary: The Harris County Sheriff's Office said in a statement that the incident appears to have occurred during an ICE enforcement action.
story: A vehicle driven by Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents hit and injured a man in the greater Houston area on Saturday, the Harris County Sheriff's Office said.
"The incident appears to have occurred while ICE authorities were conducting an enforcement action in the area," the sheriff's office said in a statement.
During a press conference, Major McConnell of the Harris County Sheriff's special investigation bureau said the sheriff's office was called to the scene around 7:20 a.m.
ICE agents were headed south in pursuit of a wanted suspect, McConnell said, and the suspect drove west in an eastbound lane. The suspect bailed out of his vehicle and went on foot, he said.
The driver and passenger fled and ICE agents attempted to capture them both, he said. While trying to capture the passenger, the ICE agent hit him with his vehicle.
The victim was taken to a local hospital. McConnell said it appears the man has a broken leg, but no further details were given on the man's condition.
McConnell said the victim is a 48-year-old male and is currently in the custody of ICE at the hospital.
CBS News reached out to the U.S. Department of Homeland Security for more information.

title: Christa Pike released from hospital following botched execution, lawyers say
summary: Christa Pike survived despite being given two doses of a lethal injection.
story: Christa Pike, the woman whose execution by lethal injection was botched last month in Tennessee, has been released from the hospital and is now back in prison, according to her lawyers.
She has been transferred back to Deborah K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center in Nashville, where she had been held before her planned execution on Sept. 30.

"Christa Pike was discharged from a local hospital and is now at Deborah K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center where she has been housed for more than 30 years," her attorneys, Stephen Ferrell, Luke Ihnen, Randy Spivey and Kelly Gleason, said in a statement Saturday. "She is grateful to the first responders and her medical team for their care in these extraordinary circumstances. She is continuing to receive medical care at the prison, and we will continue to track her recovery."

Pike, 50, was given two doses of a lethal injection drug, but her legal team confirmed shortly after the failed procedure that, in an unprecedented turn, she was alive and had been hospitalized. One witness, a media attendee, noted she could be heard loudly snoring about one hour after the procedure had started. She was then taken by ambulance to an area hospital.
Her legal team said on Tuesday that she had regained consciousness and was speaking from her hospital bed.

On Wednesday, Pike began "taking limited steps" with help, according to her team. And on Thursday, her attorneys detailed more progress, saying in a statement that she was walking "with some assistance" and her arms were "healing and regaining movement and strength." They also said that her "lungs are clear, and she has started to eat a regular diet."
Pike is the only person known to have survived an execution attempt in the U.S., according to the Death Penalty Information Center.

Pike was convicted in 1995 of the brutal murder of her classmate, 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer. Court filings show that Pike, then 18, tortured and killed Slemmer, slashing her with a meat cleaver and box cutter for up to an hour in a wooded part of the University of Tennessee campus, with help from her boyfriend and a friend.
Pike's execution was allowed to move forward after the Supreme Court denied a last-minute effort to halt it. She was set to be the first woman executed in the state since 1820.
It's still unclear what will happen with Pike moving forward.

Pike's attorneys attended an emergency hearing in Davidson County court on Wednesday, during which they requested and were granted a decision saying Tennessee's correctional department must preserve records and other evidence of her failed lethal injection.

Her legal team has renewed its calls for Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee to commute Pike's death sentence, pushing him to change the sentence to life in prison without parole so the state can't attempt to execute Pike a second time. This is the usual course of action after an inmate survives botched execution proceedings, her attorneys said.
However, while others have survived botched procedures before, Pike is the only known inmate in the United States' modern death penalty era to remain alive after actually receiving lethal chemicals.
"The state has made no promises that Ms. Pike will not be subject to a future execution," Ihnen, one of Pike's attorneys, said in court on Wednesday.

title: Pope says death penalty "inadmissible" amid U.S. plans to livestream execution
summary: The firing squad execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, convicted of a 2009 shooting at Fort Hood, will be livestreamed, the U.S. Defense Department said.
story: Pope Leo XIV declared that capital punishment is "inadmissible" as the United States plans to livestream an execution by firing squad.

The American pope, in a post on X marking the World Day Against the Death Penalty, quoted the revised Catholic teaching on capital punishment ushered in by his predecessor, Pope Francis. The Catholic teaching states that capital punishment attacks the inherent dignity of a human being.

"The common good can be safeguarded and the requirements of justice can be met without recourse to capital punishment," read the post under Leo's official handle, @Pontifex. "Effective systems of detention have been developed that protect citizens while at the same time do not completely deprive those who are guilty of the possibility of redemption."

The U.S. Defense Department announced Thursday that the firing squad execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, convicted of a 2009 shooting at the Fort Hood military base, will be livestreamed. Hasan, scheduled to be executed at Fort Hood on Dec. 3, was convicted of killing 13 people and wounding 32 others. It would be the first U.S. military execution since 1961.
The decision to livestream the execution has drawn fierce criticism.

Leo's post didn't refer specifically to the planned execution in the U.S. or the botched lethal injection of Christa Pike in Tennessee late last month which has revived debate over the death penalty in the United States. However, it is common for the pope's official social media accounts to post messages marking such commemorations like the World Day Against the Death Penalty.
However, Leo's post came just hours after his top deputy, Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Vatican secretary of state, said explicitly that the planned U.S. public execution was "unacceptable."

Speaking specifically about the United States, Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Vatican secretary of state, said the planned livestreamed execution was "truly incomprehensible" and "unacceptable to turn death into a spectacle."

"The Church's position is one of total opposition to the death penalty; it is incompatible with human dignity and serves as no deterrent… ," Parolin said in comments carried by Vatican News. "It is truly incomprehensible that anyone would want to use this system today — I don't know for what purpose. It is certainly unacceptable to turn death into a spectacle; even if the person is guilty, of course, there are other methods."
The head of the U.S. bishops conference, Archbishop Paul Coakley, expressed "shock" and "great sorrow" at the Pentagon's plans.

"In no way can Hasan's actions be condoned but this decision is a barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered," he said in a statement Friday. "The public execution even of one who has done grave harm will only further undermine the moral fabric of our nation and be a blight on the conscience of its people."
On Friday, President Trump said he approves of Hasan's execution by firing squad.

"He will be killed. He will be, through firing squad," Mr. Trump told reporters before flying to Syracuse, New York, for a political event. "I really don't care how he goes, as long as he goes. And I think the death penalty is a very worthy way of going for him."
Mr. Trump did not appear to answer when asked whether it was appropriate to livestream the event or whether he was going to watch the execution.

Vice President JD Vance, who is a Catholic convert, appeared to cast doubt on Friday about the livestream, telling reporters he wouldn't watch it and, "I don't know that that's actually going to happen."

title: Blanche, other DOJ appointees can take part in campaigns, memo says
summary: The Justice Department has loosened the guidelines for the attorney general and other senior ​political appointees, allowing them to participate in political activities.
story: The Justice Department has loosened the guidelines for the attorney general and other senior political appointees, allowing them to participate in political activities.

A memo sent this week by Assistant Attorney General Jolene Ann Laurie relaxes ethics restrictions on Senate-confirmed presidential appointees such that they can speak at rallies, canvass for votes and even serve as delegates or officers of a national political party as long as those activities are conducted in their personal capacities.
The guidance applies to the attorney general, the deputy attorney general, assistant attorneys general, the FBI director, U.S. attorneys and others.
Former Attorney General Pam Bondi had loosened the regulations somewhat during her tenure by allowing political appointees to attend rallies and fundraisers. The new memo goes a step further.

It specifically states that presidentially appointed, Senate-confirmed Justice Department employees are exempt from the more stringent guidelines imposed on some other DOJ employees, such as administrative law judges and those in the Criminal Division.

Attorney General Todd Blanche addressed the Republican midterm convention in September and attended a rally for a North Carolina Republican Senate candidate, drawing criticism that he violated long-standing Justice Department norms intended to keep politics independent from the law.
"I am not in any way violating any rule or law," Blanche said about his appearances at these events, adding they were done in his personal capacity.
These moves come after the Biden-era Justice Department clamped down on appointees' political activities.
"Non-career appointees may not attend any partisan political events, even in their personal capacities," a 2024 memo said, continuing a policy instituted two years earlier.
The 2024 memo also said that appointees should "avoid making public appearances in any state shortly before a primary or general election in that state, to the greatest extent practicable."
PBS News was first to report on the new guidelines.

title: Hurricane Isaias makes landfall on Gulf Coast
summary: Hurricane Isaias, the first Atlantic hurricane of 2026, made landfall near Destin, Florida, on the northern Gulf Coast.
story: Update: Isaias is continuing north across the Southeastern U.S. after being downgrade from a hurricane to a post-tropical cyclone. See the latest here, and our earlier story is below.

Hurricane Isaias, the first of the 2026 Atlantic season, made landfall Friday night along the northern Gulf Coast, bringing drenching rains, powerful winds and the risk of life-threatening flash flooding and storm surges to a large swath of the Southeast.

The center of Isaias made landfall near Destin, Florida, at around 8 p.m. Eastern Time, according to the Miami-based National Hurricane Center. It made landfall as a Category 2 storm, but quickly weakened into a Category 1.
President Trump late Friday night told reporters that White House officials were tracking the hurricane "very closely."

Isaias had earlier in the day briefly strengthened into a Category 3 storm, which is defined as a major hurricane. Tens of thousands of people have evacuated the region, officials said. More than 697,000 customers were without power across Florida, Alabama, and Georgia, according to utility tracker PowerOutage.us.
Maps show hurricane's path
Isaias had maximum sustained winds of 90 miles per hour as of Friday night, according to forecasters, and life-threatening storm surge was likely along the Florida Panhandle and Alabama coasts.

The core of Isaias, pronounced "ees-ah-EE-ahs," was about 45 miles northeast of Pensacola, Florida, heading north at 20 mph late Friday night, the NHC said. Hurricane-force winds extended outward up to 35 miles from the storm's center, and tropical storm-force winds extended outward up to 160 miles.

The hurricane center warned "dangerous and damaging hurricane force-winds" were expected across the Florida Panhandle, southern Alabama and southern Mississippi, where residents who had not evacuated were advised to have a safe room to ride out the storm and prepare for the possibility of long-term power outages.
The center of the storm was forecast to move across Alabama and into the Tennessee Valley on Saturday and Sunday.

It was expected to weaken to a post-tropical storm Saturday as it moves inland, but will still produce gusty winds. The central U.S. Gulf Coast and much of the Southeast is likely to see heavy rainfall through the weekend, with flash flooding possible.
Watches and warnings in effect

A hurricane warning is in effect from the Mississippi/Alabama border to the Bay/Gulf County Line in Florida. A tropical storm warning was in place from east of the Bay/Gulf County Line to the Aucilla River in Florida.
A storm surge warning was in place from Dauphin Island, Alabama, to the mouth of the Suwannee River in Florida.

The combination of a dangerous storm surge and the tide will cause normally dry areas near the coast to be flooded, forecasters warned, with heights of up to 9 feet from the Alabama-Florida border to Grayton Beach, Florida. Other parts of the Florida Panhandle could see storm surge up to 6 feet.
Hurricane-force winds are expected to spread inland as far as 100 miles from the coast into southern Alabama, forecasters said.

A wind gust of 112 mph was measured at Santa Rosa Sound, Florida, according to the hurricane center. Other areas of the Southeast that were also expected to see "damaging wind gusts" included northern Georgia, the southern Appalachians and southern Middle Tennessee.
The hurricane center forecasts 4 to 8 inches of rain and as much as 15 inches in some places along the coast, from southern Alabama to the Florida Panhandle, Florida's Big Bend and southwest Georgia.
Two to 5 inches of rain are expected across much of the rest of the Southeast, with up to 10 inches possible, especially across the southern Appalachians and coastal Carolinas.

There is also a risk of tornadoes spinning off from the storm beginning Friday and continuing through Saturday, forecasters said. The tornado threat on Saturday will extend to areas of Georgia and the Carolinas.
Florida, Georgia and Alabama declare states of emergency

"Folks who are in the path of this storm should know, this is not a random tropical system," Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said in a news conference Friday. "It's a major hurricane. And it's going to potentially do a lot of damage."

Evacuations were ordered in parts of Florida's Okaloosa and Walton counties, which are both in the Panhandle. Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey has told tourists and visitors in the state's coastal areas to leave immediately.

Ivey's evacuation order "requires all non-residents, tourists and visitors in Baldwin County south of the Gulf Intracoastal Waterway, including Gulf Shores and Orange Beach, and on Dauphin Island in Mobile County, to evacuate immediately," a news release said.

DeSantis declared a state of emergency for more than two dozen counties in Florida, and Ivey issued a state of emergency for 40 counties in Alabama. Government buildings closed in nine Alabama counties on Friday, Ivey announced. Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp also declared a state of emergency.
The Trump administration approved federal emergency declarations for Florida and Alabama.

In Orange Beach, Alabama, streets and beaches were empty during what was supposed to be a busy weekend for tourists. The gridlock on area roadways caused by fleeing residents over the past 48 hours was gone, and the evacuation window had closed, officials said, because winds were too strong.
The few residents left were trying to make the best of it. Christi Woods manages a wine store in Orange Beach, one of the only businesses that was still open Friday.
"We do take precautions, I mean, we're kind of in the flood zone," Woods said.

Three shelters were open as of Friday morning at schools in Mobile County, Alabama. At least four churches in Dothan, Alabama, are being offered as shelters Friday, and they're also providing snacks and drinks.
Dauphin Island Mayor Jeff Collier told CBS News his biggest concern for the coastal Alabama community is whether its residents and visitors would heed official warnings.

"Because what inevitably happens is people hear the warnings, but they don't actually take any action until it's much too late," Collier said. "And oftentimes if it's really bad, first responders can't get out to people until things calm down a bit."

DeSantis warned Friday of significant storm surge and likely wind damage that could put "a lot of people's lives in jeopardy if they haven't heeded evacuation orders." He said storm surge "does the most significant damage from these storms."

"Everywhere from Pensacola all the way into the Big Bend section of north Florida, you could see storm surge. So please take caution of that," he said, adding: "And we always say you hide from the wind, but you run from the water. When the water's rising and things are happening, it's a very, very difficult conundrum — and you do not want to be caught in that."
The U.S. Coast Guard also said it was preparing for Friday's landfall and urged seafarers near the Gulf to stay informed and remain vigilant leading up to the hurricane's approach.
The latest for a first hurricane since 1905

Isaias' progression into a hurricane on Wednesday, Oct. 7, marked the latest date in 121 years for the Atlantic season's first hurricane to develop, just missing a record set on Oct. 8, 1905, according to National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration data.
The season, which has been unusually quiet in the Atlantic this year, runs from June 1 through Nov. 30.

An Atlantic hurricane season typically produces, on average, 14 named storms, seven hurricanes and three major hurricanes, according to the hurricane center, which used climate data collected between 1991 and 2020 to calculate those figures. A season's first named storm normally forms in mid- to late June, while the first hurricane tends to form in early to mid-August, and the first major hurricane often comes in late August or early September.

Forecasters predicted there would be less Atlantic storm activity than usual this year, but so far it has been even quieter than anticipated. Meteorologists say that's largely due to the onset of a strong El Niño over the summer, which typically correlates with cooler water temperatures and greater fluctuations in wind patterns over the Atlantic, conditions that dampen the growth of tropical systems. The Pacific, meanwhile, has seen an unusually active series of hurricanes.

title: Pentagon's plan to livestream execution sparks backlash
summary: "Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do," said GOP Sen. Thom Tillis.
story: Washington — The revelation that the Pentagon plans to livestream the execution by firing squad of Nidal Hasan, the ex-Army major convicted of killing 13 people at Fort Hood in 2009, has sparked intense pushback, with one Republican senator calling it "disgusting" and critics warning it could inspire more acts of terrorism.

On Thursday, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth confirmed CBS News' reporting that the Dec. 3 execution will be livestreamed. Hegseth told Real America's Voice the execution would be public "because people need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things." Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said that Hegseth recommended, and President Trump approved, a plan to use an Army firing squad.
"Death penalty through firing squad, and he deserves it," Mr. Trump said during an unrelated White House event on Friday.
In an interview Friday night in Syracuse, New York, with WSTM-TV, President Trump said he "wasn't involved in that decision" to livestream the execution, "but I understand that decision."
"I guess they want to have it serve as an example, and I understand that very well," the president added.
Republican Sen. Thom Tillis, who is retiring, called the decision "beyond disgusting." Tillis voted to confirm Hegseth, but is now expressing his regret in doing so.

"Hasan should face the death penalty, but making his execution public and streaming it? Beyond disgusting," Tillis wrote on X. "Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do. It should not be happening in America."
Republican Rep. Austin Scott of Georgia wrote on X, "I absolutely support the sentence of death, but live-streaming executions is what jihadists do. America is better than that."
Republican Sen. John Curtis of Utah urged Hegseth to reconsider.

"Seneca warned that Rome's bloody spectacles corrupted the people who watched them," he said on X. "A civilization erodes when it cultivates an appetite for executions as a form of entertainment.  Secretary Hegseth's plan to livestream the Fort Hood execution risks feeding that appetite. The victims deserve justice administered with solemnity. Broadcasting a death diminishes us and is not an effective deterrent. I urge him to reconsider."
Democratic Sen. Chris Murphy said publicly executing someone is "medieval."

"That's disgusting. What, is he mimicking ISIS executions?" Murphy said on CNN. "I mean, I understand that in this country we have the death penalty, but public executions is medieval. It's frankly one of the things that we abhor about terrorist groups. And the fact that the United States is doing it — I just learned this, that is just absolutely extraordinary, galling. No matter whether you support or oppose the death penalty, public hangings and executions? That's what America has become?"
Ned Price, who was the State Department's spokesman during the Biden administration, said a public and livestreamed execution will create more "radicalized zealots."

"You can take it from those of us who've spent years working on terrorism: the surest way to spawn more radicalized zealots is to glorify violence, embrace a cult of death, and create a martyr for the cause," Price wrote on X. "Or take it from AQ and ISIS, whose tactics offer the closest modern-day approximation of Hegseth's proposal.  Either way, it's hard to conjure a more vivid example of his trademark performative bravado, which routinely damages America's image and, in this case, so ghoulishly leaves us more vulnerable."

Alonzo Lunsford, a former U.S. Army sergeant who was shot seven times during the Fort Hood shooting but survived, said he supports the gunman's execution by firing squad. But Lunsford said this execution is "not something you should view for entertainment purposes."
"To show the whole thing without it being censored for the general public, for me personally, I don't agree with that, but it's not about my personal belief," he told BBC Radio.
Archbishop Paul S. Coakley, president of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops, issued a statement Friday morning urging the Pentagon to reconsider.

"In no way can [Hasan's] actions be condoned but this decision is a barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered. The word of God exhorts us: 'do not repay anyone evil for evil,'" the archbishop said, citing Romans 12:17. "The public execution even of one who has done grave harm will only further undermine the moral fabric of our nation and be a blight on the conscience of its people."
Conservative talk show host Erick Erickson, who supports the death penalty, also said a public, livestreamed execution of Hasan will give him the "platform for martyrdom he wants."

"Hasan is a paraplegic, confined to a wheelchair," Erickson wrote. "The public imagery of a firing squad killing a man sitting in a chair because he cannot stand is going to undermine support for the death penalty. A society that increasingly finds ways to sympathize with the villains will do so here. This also gives Nidal Hasan the platform for martyrdom he wants. They'll be passing out the livestream video in the Middle East to inspire more terrorists to shoot up Americans to celebrate the glory of the martyrdom of Nidal Hasan."

Geoffrey Corn, a Texas Tech University law professor who served in the Army's Judge Advocate General's Corps, told CBS News that the plan to livestream the execution "raises significant moral questions, above and beyond the questions related to the death penalty generally."
"There's a certain protocol that is normally followed with executions limiting the gallery of observers, which usually includes people close to the victims and certain members of the media," he said.
Corn said "turning the execution of such a penalty into some type of public spectacle echoes of the past we seem to have put behind us."
Despite Lunsford's concerns about the livestream, the former U.S. Army sergeant said he'll be there for the execution.

"I'm going to be there [to watch in person] and before they pull the trigger, I want him to look at me in my eyes and I look at him in his eyes and I want him to know: 'Dude, you failed, I'm still here,'" he told the BBC.
The last public execution in the U.S. appeared to take place 90 years ago in 1936. That's when Rainey Bethea was hanged for rape in Kentucky. The execution reportedly drew a crowd of about 20,000.

Hegseth's announcement comes amid efforts from Democrats and Republican Rep. Thomas Massie to impeach him. A vote on his impeachment was delayed by House Speaker Mike Johnson's decision to cancel votes a day early ahead of the midterms.

Eleanor  Watson and 
                                                  
                                  Joe  Walsh
                  
        contributed to this report.

title: When 2 dogs went missing in a car crash, a volunteer spent weeks searching
summary: Christine Quaiff has found dozens of dogs over the last few years. She's part of a growing national network of lost pet recovery specialists who offer this service, often for free.
story: Christine Quaiff is a hunter of sorts, often going deep into the woods around Richmond, Virginia, to track and trap family members.
"When someone loses their dog, that's their child," Quaiff told CBS News.
Quaiff has found dozens of lost dogs over the last few years. She's part of a growing national network of lost pet recovery specialists who offer this service, often for free.
"It's about being kind to other people and doing what you wish people would do for you," Quaiff said.
Her most recent case was a desperate search for two Goldendoodles, Bailee and Tobey, who belonged to 66-year-old Annie Olup.
Olup lost her husband in August 2024, and caring for those dogs had become her purpose.
"I thought, I'm going to go back to this house and it's just going to feel so empty," Olup said of her husband's death.
In September, Olup got in a car accident. She was driving in heavy rain when she hit a guardrail, flipped her car and almost died. Her dogs were also in the car. They survived but went missing.
"Dogs typically are going to just run away as quick as possible from the commotion and look for quietness," Quaiff said.

Quaiff used drones and trail cameras to narrow the search. Then she set traps, changed the food twice a day and agreed to stay on the case indefinitely. This was all in addition to her day job as a senior technical account manager in software development.
Quaiff was constantly checking cameras and even sleeping in her car in the search area.
"The joy of seeing them be reunited is ultimately what makes us keep going," Quaiff said.
In the end, it took 10 days for Quaiff to find Tobey and 16 days to find Bailee.

And it took no time at all for the tears to flow once Olup saw her babies were back. The three are now home together again thanks to a stranger who believes it takes a village to raise a child — even the furry ones.

title: 3 men found guilty in murders of American, Australian surfers in Mexico
summary: A local judge has found three men guilty of murdering two Australian brothers and their American friend in Baja California, Mexico, in April 2024.
story: A local judge on Friday found three men guilty of the murders of two Australian brothers and their American friend in April 2024 in the Mexican state of Baja California.

The trial for the triple homicide that shocked Mexico and drew international attention concluded Friday after Judge Raúl Hernández in the coastal city of Ensenada ruled that Jesús Gerardo García, alias "El Kekas," Irineo Francisco "N" and Ángel Jesús "N" were responsible for the murders of Australians Callum and Jake Robinson and American Carter Redd Rhoad.
The defendants, who had been in custody for more than two years, were also found guilty of armed robbery and armed carjacking.

Debra Robinson, the brothers' mother, told the courtroom the murders of her sons had taken "the future we had imagined with them," CBS News' partner network BBC News reported. Debra Robinson and her husband, Martin Robinson, were at the court in the coastal town of Ensenada throughout the trial.
"It's hard for a parent to lose a son, and we lost two sons," Martin Robinson said, BBC reported.

The three friends traveled to Baja California in April 2024 to surf, but shortly after arriving in the town of Punta San Jose, about 50 miles from Ensenada, they were reported missing. Their bodies were found on May 3 in a well.
García, identified as the perpetrator of the murders, was arrested in May 2024 in connection to the case, along with his ex-partner Ary Gisell Silva Raya, Irineo Francisco "N" and Ángel Jesús "N."

During the monthlong trial, chilling details of the brutal crime were revealed. Silva Raya testified last month during a hearing that García confessed to her that he arrived at the tent where the foreigners were staying with a 9 mm pistol.
Upon seeing him, they began throwing their belongings to prevent him from attacking them, and one of them begged for his life, which the assailant ignored, she said.

The state prosecutor's office reported that Silva Raya arrived in Punta San Jose on April 27, 2024, where she met the three foreigners and "instigated one of her companions to rob them," which was carried out the following day.

The woman, who was found in possession of one of the victims' cellphones, was sentenced in November 2025 to 20 years in prison after pleading guilty to "aggravated robbery with violence" and "vehicle theft with violence" in an expedited proceeding. However, García and his two accomplices decided to go to trial.
The judge will announce the final sentence on Oct. 16. The Baja California State Attorney General's Office requested for each defendant the "exemplary sentence" of 210 years in prison.
