title: U.S. sanctions ICC, vowing to dismantle it "brick by brick" without changes
summary: The U.S. imposed fresh sanctions targeting the International Criminal Court, taking action against the court itself after previously penalizing more than a dozen of its judges and prosecutors.
story: The Trump administration imposed fresh sanctions targeting the International Criminal Court on Friday, taking action against the court itself after previously penalizing more than a dozen of its judges and prosecutors.
"Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC," Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a statement announcing the measures.

The move came just hours after the Norwegian Nobel Committee announced it was awarding the Nobel Peace Prize to Navanethem "Navi" Pillay, a South African-born human rights official who served as an ICC judge from 2003 to 2008. Pillay also led a U.N. inquiry that determined last year that Israel committed genocide in Gaza. Israel strongly disputed the report's findings.

Neither the United States nor Israel is a party to the Rome Statute that established the ICC. Washington has long objected to the court's investigation of alleged war crimes by U.S. personnel in Afghanistan and its arrest warrants for Israeli leaders over alleged crimes in Gaza.
The court maintains it can prosecute crimes committed on territory under its jurisdiction, even when the accused is a national of a country that has not joined.
Rubio has previously described the ICC as a "fatally politicized supranational court" that has "maliciously abused its authority." He vowed Friday to dismantle it "brick by brick" if necessary.

Under the designation, the court's assets under U.S. jurisdiction are blocked, and U.S. companies and individuals are generally barred from doing business with the court. For now, the Treasury Department is allowing some services to continue and giving the court 180 days to maintain certain operations while its member countries address Washington's objections.

"We have structured this action to provide an opportunity for States Parties to negotiate and present a solution to address our concerns," Rubio said. "If these efforts do not bear fruit, we will continue to adjust accordingly."
The ICC condemned the designation as an attempt to interfere with its work and intimidate those who cooperate with it, calling it "an assault on the rule of law."

"The Court will continue to fully discharge its mandate, with independence and impartiality," ICC President Tomoko Akane said. The court also appealed to its 125 member states to help ensure it has adequate resources to continue operating, warning its future now depends in part on the governments that established it.
The court's member states include most U.S. allies in Europe, including every NATO member besides Turkey, as well as Canada, Japan and Australia.

The foreign ministers of Canada, Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, Japan, the Netherlands, and the U.K. said in a statement later Friday that they "regret and strongly disagree with the announcement of sanctions to be imposed upon the Court by the United States."

"[I]f put into effect, these sanctions will have a significant impact on the Court's work, its dedicated staff and their families," the countries said. "They work every day to bring those accused of the most serious international crimes to justice and to support their victims."

Pillay, the Peace Prize recipient, left the court in 2008 to become the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, and currently serves on the International Court of Justice, which is separate from the ICC.

She was also the chair of the U.N. Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory. In September 2025, the panel determined that there were "reasonable grounds" to conclude that "the Israeli authorities and Israeli security forces have committed and are continuing to commit" acts of genocide. Israel's foreign minister called the report "fake" and said it "relies entirely on Hamas falsehoods, laundered and repeated by others."
Pillay referenced the U.S. campaign against the ICC in a video following news that she had won the Peace Prize.

"We are living through an era when international law and human rights are under significant political attack," she said. "This worsening reality is particularly visible with the attacks on the International Criminal Court."
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office said the decision to award the Peace Prize to Pillay showed that the Nobel Committee "has lost its moral compass."
"It has awarded its highest honor to a bigot who built her career around inventing and propagating blood libels against the one and only Jewish state," Netanyahu's office said in a post on X.

The U.S. action against the ICC also follows a speech Rubio delivered Wednesday in Athens against the backdrop of the Acropolis, where he criticized Western governments for transferring national authority to international bureaucracies.
"[W]ith every passing year, we seemed to outsource more of our sovereignty, transferring our decisions to global bureaucracies far beyond the reach of our control," he said.

title: Thieves steal 30,000 bottles of Italian wines in $5.8M heist
summary: The theft targeted the Marchesi Antinori winery near Cortona, in the province of Arezzo, the company said.
story: Thieves stole about 30,000 bottles of some of Italy's most prized wines worth an estimated $5.8 million from a winery in Tuscany, in what the producer described Friday as the country's largest wine theft on record.

The theft targeted Marchesi Antinori's facility near Cortona, in the province of Arezzo, where a group of at least seven thieves on Saturday night made off with bottles of some of Italy's most sought-after wines.

Chief Executive Renzo Cotarella said the thieves disabled the winery's alarm system and surveillance cameras before entering with two large trucks. Using the company's forklifts, they loaded the vehicles with wine and fled during the night.

"It is certainly a very well-prepared gang," Cotarella said, adding that it may be the same group that has targeted other Italian wineries in recent months. "A theft of this size and value has never occurred in Italy."
Wine Spectator reported that in July, 3,300 bottles were stolen from the renowned Italian producer Castello Banfi.
Cotarella received the 2026 Winemakers' Winemaker Award from the Institute of Masters of Wine, and the winery is well known for producing Italy's most renowned vintages.

Thieves made off with wines, including bottles of Solaia, Tignanello and Guado al Tasso. The theft was discovered Monday, but the company made it public on Friday to avoid interfering with the investigation.

The stolen bottles were all from the 2023 vintage and are typically sold at a retail price of between 150 euros (approximately $168) and 500 euros each ($560). They included about 10,000 bottles of Solaia, one of Antinori's flagship wines, from what Cotarella described as an exceptional year.
The company, founded in 1385 and run by the Antinori family for 26 generations, said it was alerting customers worldwide to be wary of offers outside official sales channels.
"We are informing our clients around the world and asking them to pay attention to any offers outside the official channels," Cotarella said.

Authorities are investigating how the stolen wine may be sold. Police and Carabinieri officers are examining surveillance footage and other evidence. Cotarella said he remained confident investigators could trace the shipment, noting that two truckloads of wine would be difficult to move without attracting attention.

The theft eclipses previous high-profile wine robberies in Italy. In 2017, thieves stole about 2,000 bottles of rare wines valued at 750,000 euros — about $840,045 — from a warehouse near the Adriatic resort town of Cervia.

title: Only 2 other countries hold public executions as U.S. plans first in 90 years
summary: The execution of Nidal Hasan, convicted in the 2009 killings of 13 people at Fort Hood, will be livestreamed, the Defense Department said.
story: When Nidal Hasan is put to death by firing squad during a public livestream, he will become the first person to be publicly executed in the United States in nearly a century.

The Defense Department announced Thursday the execution of Hasan, the ex-Army major who was convicted in the 2009 killings of 13 people at Fort Hood, will be livestreamed on Dec. 3. Hasan is paralyzed from the waist down and confined to a wheelchair after being shot in the back by police who responded to the mass shooting.

"He's gonna get a firing squad of soldiers, as it should be," Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told Jack Posobiec on Real America's Voice. "We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public — because people need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things."
The decision has generated widespread, bipartisan criticism.
The list of countries that still carry out public executions, whether on video or in a public place, is very short and almost entirely countries accused of human rights violations.

Afghanistan and Iran are the only two known countries to execute anyone publicly in 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025, according to Amnesty International. Yemen publicly executed multiple people in 2021, according to the group.

"Hasan should face the death penalty, but making his execution public and streaming it? Beyond disgusting," Republican Sen. Thom Tillis wrote on X. "Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do. It should not be happening in America."
History of public executions in U.S.
Two public executions in the mid-1930s are considered to be the last public uses of the death penalty in the United States.

The last large-scale example of a public execution in the United States was Rainey Bethea in 1936. The crowd on hand to watch the hanging was estimated at 20,000 people, according to a local newspaper at the time.

Bethea was accused of raping and murdering a 70-year-old woman in her home in Owensboro, Kentucky, in June 1936. He accidentally left his recognizable prison ring at the scene, and confessed to the crime several times, though he did recant during a failed appeal.
He was never convicted of murder, only rape, which still carried the death penalty. Bethea, who was 26 years old, was hanged on Aug. 14, 1936.

A year later, Roscoe "Red" Jackson was executed in Galena, Missouri, also by hanging. He was convicted of killing a traveling salesman and stealing his car after being picked up by the victim as a hitchhiker.
The crowd for Jackson's execution was much smaller, since it was not held in the public streets of the city like Bethea's hanging.

"Just how many were inside is not known, though it is thought the space would accommodate at least 400 people," wrote the authors of an article on the execution from the local Stone County News-Oracle.

"Executions shouldn't be public spectacle," Human Rights Watch interim U.S. Program Director Michael Bochenek told CBS News in a statement. "The death penalty is a relic of an inhumane past and should be abolished once and for all."
Public executions in Iran

Iran, which the United States has accused of gross human rights violations, is one of the most prolific users of public executions in the world currently. The U.S. and Iran are also locked in a war, and President Trump has routinely cited Iran's executions of protesters as a reason the regime deserved to be deposed.
At least 24 people were publicly executed in Iran from 2022 to 2025, according to Amnesty International.

Fifty-nine people were executed this year in Iran between March 18 and Aug. 31, including dozens who took part in anti-government protests earlier this year, according to Human Rights Watch. Five of those executions have been public, the organization said.
While not capital punishment, thousands of protesters were also killed by government troops opening fire on those demonstrations.
In late February, eight days before launching strikes against Iran, Mr. Trump said he had threatened military action against Iran if they publicly executed hundreds of people.

"They were going to hang 837 people, and I gave them the word, if you hang one person, even one person, that you're going to be hit right then and there," Mr. Trump said. "I wasn't waiting two weeks and negotiating. And they gave up the hanging. They didn't hang 837, supposedly they didn't hang anybody."
Public executions in Afghanistan
Afghanistan has publicly executed at least 12 people since 2022, according to Amnesty International, though its reports note there were possibly more.

Public executions in Afghanistan have spiked since the Taliban swept back into power in August 2021. Executions have even been carried out in front of thousands of onlookers in sports stadiums, including one in November 2024 that earned worldwide condemnation.

"I condemn today's horrific public execution," Richard Bennett, who monitors human rights violations in Afghanistan for the United Nations, said in a statement at the time. "These atrocious punishments are clear violations of human rights and must be immediately halted."
Another person, reportedly convicted of murder, was publicly executed in a sports stadium in October 2025, according to the U.N.
The Taliban regularly carried out public executions during their first period of rule in the 1990s, until the U.S. invasion in 2001 forced them out of power.
Public executions elsewhere in the world
North Korea is also believed to carry out public executions, though reporting is difficult from the extremely isolated country.

In February, Amnesty International put out a report that included interviews with North Korean defectors who said they had been forced to watch public executions as a way of warning them against committing similar supposed crimes — sometimes for as little as watching foreign television programs.

"Authorities told everyone to go, and tens of thousands of people from Sinuiju city gathered to watch," one female defector interviewed by the human rights group said. "They execute people to brainwash and educate us."

Saudi Arabia, which was widely criticized for its public executions for decades, has apparently ended its use entirely in recent years. The infamous Deera Square, where many beheadings took place in the capital, Riyadh, has not hosted an execution since 2019, according to Reuters.

The death penalty is still used frequently in Saudi Arabia, even if not public. There were a record 347 people executed in 2025, according to the European Saudi Organisation for Human Rights. The year prior 345 people were executed. By comparison, 47 people were executed in the United States last year.

The Iran-backed Houthi militant group, which controls large areas of western Yemen, also sometimes carries out public executions. Though not recognized as the controlling government, they do hold enormous power in the country. Nine people were executed at once in public in 2021 for the killing of a Houthi general, according to the Geneva International Centre for Justice.

"International human rights bodies have long found public executions as incompatible with the prohibition on cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment," Justin Mazzola, deputy director of research at Amnesty International USA, said in a statement to CBS News. "The claim that the death penalty serves as a greater deterrent is simply unfounded: there is no evidence that it has a unique deterrent effect. The death penalty does not make us safer."
"Livestreaming the taking of a life by firing squad would only compound the cruelty of the death penalty and perpetuate the cycle of violence that the authorities purportedly seek to end," he added.

title: Nobel Peace Prize awarded to former ICC judge Navi Pillay
summary: Nobel Peace Prize 2026 was awarded to Navanethem "Navi" Pillay, a former judge on the International Criminal Court, drawing a quick, angry rebuke from Israel.
story: The Nobel Peace Prize for 2026 was awarded Friday to Navanethem "Navi" Pillay, a South African-born former judge with the International Criminal Court who went on to become the United Nations human rights chief and is still serving with the U.N.'s other judicial body, the International Court of Justice. She also led a U.N. inquiry last year that accused Israel of genocide in the Gaza Strip, and Israel was quick to condemn her receiving the honor on Friday.

The Nobel Committee said it was honoring Pillay "for her efforts to promote peace and international law," and that awarding the prize to someone with her body of work on international justice was a message to those seeking to undermine international law institutions.

The South African-born former United Nations human rights chief, who is 85, was recognized for her efforts to promote peace and international law, said Jørgen Watne Frydnes, chair of the Norwegian Nobel Committee.
"This is definitely a message to those who are undermining the international system and institutions," Frydnes said.

"The system of international law is under tremendous pressure and its institutions are under attack," he said, noting what the committee saw as a shift "towards power politics at the expense of legal frameworks and global respect for law and justice."

The International Criminal Court (ICC) has come under fire from Israel and the Trump administration in recent years, with the U.S. imposing sanctions against the U.N. court last year after it issued an arrest warrant in 2024 for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. President Trump accused the court of "illegitimate and baseless actions targeting America and our close ally Israel."
The ICC condemned the U.S. sanctions against its staff and said they were intended to "harm (the Court's) independent and impartial judicial work."

Pillay served as an ICC judge from 2003 until 2008, when she resigned to take on the role of United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights. She was the chair of the U.N. Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory that said last year it had concluded Israel's actions in Gaza amounted to genocide. Israel dismissed the report as "scandalous."

Pillay is currently serving as an ad hoc judge for the International Court of Justice (ICJ), which is separate to the ICC, in the case of Gambia v. Myanmar, in which Myanmar's ruling military junta stands accused of genocide over its treatment of the nation's Rohingya Muslim minority in the western state of Rakhine.

Frydnes said the committee wasn't immediately able to reach Pillay Friday to tell her she had been awarded the prize, adding from the podium that if she was watching and saw a call coming in from a Norwegian phone number, to "please pick up."

She soon appeared in a video posted on social media by the head of Amnesty International, being applauded by well-wishers at the Palace of Justice in Nuremberg, Germany, where Nazi leaders were put on trial for their crimes against humanity after World War II.

"Perhaps it was meant to be that I was in this historic courtroom... when the announcement was made and I was informed of the award," Pillay said. "We are living through an era when international law and human rights are under significant political attack ... This worsening reality is particularly visible with the attacks on the International Criminal Court."

"If you clap a little bit louder I may share this prize with Trump," she quipped, drawing laughs from the crowd. She said that when she was informed that she had been awarded the prize, she first thought "it must be a joke," and that as a "lawyer and a judge, I still want to verify this thing."

She noted that she was lauded by the Nobel committee for her courage, which she questioned, saying: "You can imagine how surprised I was. Why would you need courage to speak the truth? You interpret the law, you look at all the facts, so it's an impartial decision you make."
Israel condemns Pillay's honor, U.S. further sanctions ICC

The Israeli Foreign Ministry blasted the Nobel committee for awarding the prize to Pillay on Friday, saying in a statement posted online that "if there were an award for lies, hatred, and blood libels, Navi Pillay wouldn't just be a contender. She'd be a frontrunner. Her role in the relentless, politically motivated demonization of Israel and promotion of the genoLIE speaks volumes."
It condemned the committee for awarding her as "the grotesque weaponization of an award to legitimize anti-Israel hatred and prejudice."

A separate statement posted on the X account of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the Nobel committee had "lost its moral compass. It has awarded its highest honor to a bigot who built her career around inventing and propagating blood libels against the one and only Jewish state."

The Trump administration, hours later, announced further sanctions against the ICC. Secretary of State Marco Rubio called the ICC a "threat to U.S. sovereignty" and said the new measures were deemed necessary to ensure the court, which the U.S. has never been a state party to, can never prosecute a U.S. national.

He said the new sanctions would "ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate," adding: "We expect our allies, many of whom are part of the ICC and that rely on American servicemembers for their defense, to rein in the court. If they do not, the United States will continue its campaign to dismantle the ICC, brick by brick, until Americans are threatened no longer."

The ICC has never prosecuted or indicted a U.S. national, but it has investigated the actions of U.S. forces abroad, in countries where it does have jurisdiction, including Afghanistan, and it could theoretically seek to prosecute Americans.

According to Human Rights Watch, there are "limited situations in which the ICC has jurisdiction over the nationals of countries, such as the U.S., that have not joined the Rome Statute. This includes when a citizen of a non-member country commits war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide on the territory of an ICC member country. That's why U.S. citizens may be subject to the court's jurisdiction as it investigates alleged grave crimes that took place in Afghanistan."
Nobel prize history

Last year, Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado won the Nobel Peace Prize for her struggle to achieve a democratic transition in the South American nation, winning recognition as a woman "who keeps the flame of democracy burning amid a growing darkness."

Machado gave President Trump, who has long said he deserves the prize, her Nobel medal shortly after the United States ousted then-President Nicolás Maduro. But it was largely a symbolic gesture: The Nobel Committee has said the honor itself cannot be transferred.

Nominations can be made by a select group of people and organizations, including heads of state or politicians serving at a national level, university professors, directors of foreign policy institutes, past Nobel Prize recipients and members of the Norwegian Nobel Committee itself.

Four of this year's Nobels were announced earlier this week. The Nobel for medicine went to three scientists whose work led to a tool that uses light to help unravel how the brain works. The physics award recognized a scientist's efforts to demystify a rare group of neutrinos. The chemistry prize recognized two scientists for untangling mysterious mirror images in molecules, a discovery that has been used to develop countless drugs.
Canadian poet, essayist and translator Anne Carson won the literature prize Thursday for "bold and inventive" works that fuse the classical and the modern and blur the boundaries of poetry and prose.
The Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences will be announced Monday.
The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million).
Education activist Malala Yousafzai is the youngest Nobel Peace Prize laureate; she won at 17 in 2014.

The United States is the most-credited country, with 24 awards naming U.S. institutions or individuals, ahead of the United Kingdom (13) and Switzerland (11). No laureate listed as American has won since then-President Barack Obama was awarded in 2009.

The prize has gone unawarded on 19 occasions, most of them during the world wars. In 1948, the year Mahatma Gandhi was assassinated, no prize was awarded; he had been nominated 12 times and never won.
In 1939, a Swedish member of parliament nominated Adolf Hitler, then withdrew the nomination, saying it was never meant seriously.

title: 2 Renoir paintings stolen from French museum recovered, mayor says
summary: Two paintings by the French impressionist master Renoir stolen a month ago from a museum dedicated to the artist have been recovered, according to the local mayor.
story: Nice, France — Two paintings by French master Pierre-Auguste Renoir have been recovered a month after they were stolen from a museum in southern France, the town's mayor said Friday.
In September, thieves broke into the museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer and managed to escape with two works by the French impressionist painter, abandoning two others as they fled.
"These two paintings are not simply works of art. They are part of our city's history," said Bryan Masson, the mayor of Cagnes-sur-Mer. "Knowing they have been recovered is an immense relief."
There has not yet been any statement from the police.

The suspects cut through a fence to enter the museum's tree-lined grounds, smashed a window to get inside, and used an electric saw to cut through the frame mountings, Masson said at the time of the robbery in early September.
A source close to the probe told AFP earlier this week that police had arrested five people as part of the investigation.
The Renoir Museum lies a half-hour drive from the southern city of Nice, in Renoir's last home before he died aged 78 in 1919.
The heist was the latest in a string of such robberies in France including the daylight theft last year of crown jewelry valued at around $100 million from the Louvre in Paris.

title: USS Lincoln docks in San Diego, returning home for first time in 321 days
summary: The USS Abraham Lincoln and its more than 4,500 sailors returned home to San Diego on Thursday for the first time in 321 days.
story: The USS Abraham Lincoln and its more than 4,500 sailors and Marines returned home to San Diego on Thursday for the first time in 321 days, a jubilant homecoming after a long deployment that included months in the Middle East.

Hundreds of family members and friends waited for hours in the sun to greet their loved ones. As the ship pulled into the harbor, a roar of cheers erupted from a pier. Sailors stood at attention on the deck for the aircraft carrier's long approach, and after they were released, smiles and waves broke out as sailors took out their phones to call people on the pier.
In one such reunion, McKenzie Adkins held her 10-week-old son Declan as she waved to her husband, Alexander, on the ship's deck, before the new father met his son for the first time.

The Lincoln carrier strike group had been deployed for more than 10 months, including more than 250 uninterrupted days at sea this year. Much of that time was spent in the Middle East, where the aircraft carrier and its escort ships supported the U.S. war with Iran. It left the region in late August and began sailing back toward its home port of San Diego, stopping in Thailand and Guam. The Japan-based USS George Washington, another U.S. aircraft carrier, arrived in August in the Middle East to replace the Lincoln.

During the Lincoln's record-long time at sea, the Navy drew scrutiny for conditions aboard the ship. Reports circulated of supply shortages and faulty plumbing, and families of crew members raised concerns about deteriorating mental health conditions.

Congressional Democrats expressed outrage and pressed the Navy for more information about reports of shortages and mental health issues on the Lincoln. The Pentagon has defended conditions on the ship.

title: FlyDubai co-pilot bashed women in thousands of "manosphere" X posts
summary: Social media posts show the FlyDubai co-pilot accused of a hijack attempt spent a year bashing women with "manosphere" rhetoric.
story: The FlyDubai co-pilot whose alleged violent attempt to crash a flight to Israel last week and kill everyone onboard has a history of writing and sharing misogynistic remarks on social media using the rhetoric of the so-called manosphere, CBS News has found.

Many posts written and shared by Hamam al Hamami on an X account that has since been deleted used derogatory language about women espoused by misogynistic online influencers. Some of his posts included violent rhetoric. In one, he threatened to "stamp on your head, wipe the floor with you, make you an example to others, and then release you." It is not clear if he was speaking about one person in particular, or referring to women in general.

Multiple sources familiar with the investigation into the alleged hijacking attempt told CBS News last week that al Hamami is an Omani national and was the co-pilot who attacked the plane's captain with a cockpit emergency ax as it approached Israel on Sept. 27. Passengers and crew managed to subdue him, according to their own accounts, and an off-duty flight crew on the jet made a safe emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.

An Israeli security official told CBS News authorities were investigating the possibility the incident could have been an attempted Sept. 11-style terror attack. President Trump suggested a couple of days after the incident that the co-pilot could have links to Iran, "based on what I'm hearing."

The co-pilot's posts on X, which were made between November 2021 and late October 2022, paint a picture of a man who, at least during that period, had a very skewed view of women and a low opinion of men who, in his words, "grovel" to them.

"No matter how much you grovel or 'lick their feet,' you can forget about ever being with them; you chose the cheap, easy route to approach the opposite sex instead of elevating your own value as a man," he said in one post, which CBS News found an archived version of online. The posts were written in Arabic.
The Financial Times reported Wednesday that it discovered some 3,000 misogynistic messages posted or shared by al Hamami as part of an investigation, including him calling women "rotten meat."
According to the FT, he also lauded flying as "the safest means of public transport."
CBS News has not independently reviewed all of the posts cited by the FT.

Al Hamami's posts mingled the rhetoric of extremist interpretations of Islam with that of the manosphere movement. The only woman he spoke of positively was his mother, whom he credited with raising him and his siblings "on religion, morals, and virtue."

In one archived post seen by CBS News, al Hamami uses the manosphere term "simp" to describe a man "who hangs around feminist circles, licking women's feet in hopes of gaining their approval and getting closer to them. Typically, only a low-value male resorts to this behavior, turning to foot-licking as the easiest way to ingratiate himself with women. Does this mean I have to lick women's feet? The only woman whose feet I would kiss is my mother. As for the 'simp,' he has no dignity; he licks the feet of any woman — worthy or unworthy — just in hopes of getting close to one of them."
Al Hamami said in January 2022, that he was hoping to get married and move out of his parents' home as he neared the age of 25, but that he would only consider a woman who met very specific criteria.

He turned to a Muslim dating website in the hope of finding a woman between 18 and 23, according to the FT, and said he was seeking a "religious Saudi from a tribal background" who was willing to wear a face cover, not seek work outside the home, and to live abroad.
His failed search led him to conclude, according to the X posts viewed by FT, that most women "care primarily about money" and are "skilled at pretense."

The posts seen by the British newspaper included more aggressive language, including the assertion that a woman's "only obligation is to lift her legs," and that women who seek a divorce deserve "a good thrashing."

Israeli investigators believe the co-pilot acted as a lone wolf in the alleged hijacking attempt at the end of last month, people familiar with the matter told CBS News. He is in the United Arab Emirates, where he is undergoing interrogation by Israeli and UAE authorities.

Speaking to Fox News last week, Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu said Israel knew the co-pilot "underwent Islamist radical indoctrination," based on "personal information" gathered during questioning. He did not offer any further information on the alleged indoctrination, but added to Fox that the attacker was "suicidal," and that after he was subdued by other crew members and passengers, he shouted: "Kill me, kill me!"

Al Hamami worked for a short time for Oman Air, where he entered new pilot training. Surveillance by the Omani government discovered that he was visiting radical websites, the sources said. Oman Air then transferred him to an office job.
One source told CBS News that he resigned from his job at Oman Air after being placed on desk duty, and then left the airline around 2024.

At one point, sources said, al Hamami posted a video of planes belonging to Israeli flag carrier El Al airlines in Dubai with a photo at the end of the clip showing Ayman al-Zawahiri, the al Qaeda leader believed to have helped plan the Sept. 11 terror attacks on the U.S., who was killed in a U.S. drone strike in 2022.
Al Hamami moved to Dubai, and FlyDubai hired him without vetting him with the Omani government, the sources told CBS News.

It remains unclear how, despite his history of espousing both Islamic radicalism and misogyny — and questions over whether he should have been cleared to fly to Israel at all as an Omani national —  he managed to become a pilot flying dozens of people to and from Tel Aviv.

title: Russian guided missile kills 30 on packed Ukrainian city buses
summary: Russian missiles have hit an apartment building and civilian buses, killing more than 50 people in two days, as the Kremlin says there's "no clear path" to peace.
story: At least 30 people were killed Thursday when a Russian guided bomb slammed into a street near two packed city buses in Kramatorsk, eastern Ukraine, according to officials. At least 18 more people were wounded in the attack, the Donetsk region's governor said.

"There is no doubt that Russia is cynically targeting civilians," Oleksandr Honcharenko, head of the Kramatorsk military administration, said in a statement, adding that rescue efforts were hampered by Russia launching further attacks with small drones.
Video shared online by Ukraine's Ministry of Internal Affairs showed bodies on the debris-strewn road near the charred, twisted metal shells of destroyed vehicles.
According to the ministry, three more people were killed by Russian shelling in neighboring villages, where emergency services pulled one body from a collapsed house.

It was the second consecutive day of heavy attacks by Russia. On Wednesday morning, a missile hit a five-story apartment building in the northern city of Pryluky, killing at least 22 people. Rescue workers said at least 50 more people were wounded in the strike.

"Russia comes to the Ukrainian land with death. It hits our cities, kills our people and multiplies its crimes every day," Donetsk Gov. Vadym Filashkin said after the Thursday attack in Kramatorsk, accusing Russia of deliberately trying to "kill as many people as possible."
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Thursday in Moscow that he didn't see a "clear path" to any peaceful resolution to the war, which was sparked by Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.

Last week, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told the Reuters news agency his country would double down on attacking Russian oil refineries in response to what he said were expanding Russian tactics aimed at forcing people to abandon Kyiv and other major cities by increasingly targeting civilian infrastructure. Zelenskyy stressed that Ukraine would not target Russian civilians.

"We saw documents and we know that they allow them [Russian forces] to attack infrastructure, logistics, and especially to attack in the cities, in the villages, everywhere, roads, schools, hospitals," said Zelenskyy, "to pressure people to leave the capital, leave different cities. This is the goal of the operation."

Russia has always denied targeting civilians, despite regular attacks on residential buildings throughout the war. But the foreign ministry in Moscow, in a recent statement, urged foreign nationals and diplomatic personnel to leave the Ukrainian capital, warning of "systematic and sustained strikes against military targets in Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities."

The Ukrainian military said later Thursday that it had hit Russia's largest oil refinery, 1,550 miles from the country's shared border in Siberia. The sprawling facility in Omsk, operated by state company Gazpromneft, was last attacked in July, according to Reuters.
Ukraine's military did not provide details about the strike but said the refinery was supplying fuel to Russia's forces.

Another Ukrainian strike hit a data center belonging to Russian technology and AI company Yandex on Thursday, which said it was working to restore equipment at the facility after a fire that forced it to suspend operations at the site. The impact brought some of the tech giant's cloud services down.

Visiting Pryluky in northern Ukraine on Thursday morning, Zelenskyy reiterated his request for the U.S. to increase pressure on Russia, adding that Ukrainian negotiators would visit the U.S. for discussions on Friday and Saturday.

title: U.K., Israel both claim a moral win with apparent truce in diplomatic feud
summary: Israel had threatened to close the U.K.'s century-and-a-half-old Jerusalem consulate over new British sanctions, but they found a way to avoid "blowing the whole relationship up."
story: London and Tel Aviv — The U.K. and Israel appeared Thursday to have narrowly avoided a major diplomatic confrontation, reaching a compromise to allow Britain's nearly 200-year-old consulate in east Jerusalem to remain open, but under a new name and with a significantly reduced staff.
Israel had threatened to shut the facility down completely in a dispute over British sanctions barring the import of goods from Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.

The agreement — which has been framed very differently by London and Tel Aviv — may prevent the tension between the two longstanding allies from escalating, but it has highlighted how strained ties have become between Israel and several European governments over Israel's ongoing actions in the Palestinian territories.
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said talks with the U.K. had taken place "with the aim of preventing further deterioration in relations," following weeks of escalating tension.

The dispute began in September when London announced sanctions — along with 11 other Western nations —   targeting Israeli settlements in the West Bank. The measures include a ban on goods produced in the settlements and sanctions against companies and individuals involved in facilitating settlement expansion.
British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband described the measures as the "beginning of a new approach" to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict.

Israel retaliated by giving Britain 30 days to close its east Jerusalem consulate. The facility has been operating since 1839, when Jerusalem was still part of the Ottoman Empire, predating the founding of Israel by more than a century. The consulate has historically operated independently of the U.K. Embassy in Tel Aviv, as Britain's principal diplomatic link with Palestinian officials in east Jerusalem, the West Bank and the Gaza Strip.
On Thursday, both governments sought to claim the diplomatic high ground.
Saar, in his statement, presented the agreement as a demonstration of Israel's willingness to respond to measures taken against it.

"It is not possible to act against Israel without Israel taking appropriate measures in response," he wrote. "We did not want to reach this point, but the actions of the UK Labour Government brought us here."
Saar insisted Israel had followed through on its September vow to retaliate for the sanctions, including by lifting the U.K. consulate's previous diplomatic status.
Under the new arrangement, Britain's consul general and 19 diplomats will leave Israel, while no more than seven diplomats will remain at the renamed mission, according to Saar.

Israeli officials have not said explicitly whether the remaining diplomats at the mission would retain their accreditation and diplomatic immunity, but Britain's top diplomat Miliband said in his statement that, "without an understanding, we would not have the necessary assurances for the security and protections of our staff and premises," indicating that those protections were likely part of the negotiations.

Miliband also said in his statement that the U.K. did "not accept that the Government of Israel has the legal right to close the British Consulate General in Jerusalem," reaffirming Britain's longstanding position that "East Jerusalem is occupied territory."

Miliband said the newly renamed U.K. Mission would remain independent and operational, continuing to work with Palestinians. He also pledged to rebuild Britain's diplomatic presence in the coming months and ruled out any retaliatory measures —   as long as "credible" discussions with Israel continue.

Both sides appeared to have moderated their responses because their bilateral security and business ties are too important to risk, Israeli political scientist Jonathan Rynhold told CBS News on Thursday.

The U.K. is an important economic market, and it punches above its weight diplomatically on the global stage, said Rynhold, a senior researcher with the Begin-Sadat Center at Israel's Bar Ilan University.
"They found something to do without blowing the whole relationship up," Rynhold said of the compromise.

Israel regards Jerusalem as its capital, while Britain and much of the international community do not recognize Israeli sovereignty over east Jerusalem, which Israel captured from Jordan in the 1967 Six-Day War and subsequently annexed.
The dispute comes amid a broader deterioration in Israel's relations with several European governments.

Spain has withdrawn its ambassador from Israel and imposed an embargo on arms sales to the Jewish state, while France formally recognized Palestinian statehood last year, drawing rebukes from the U.S. and Israel. Israel has also clashed with Ireland and Norway over their recognition of a state of Palestine.

The other nations that joined the U.K. in September in announcing sanctions or plans to impose sanctions targeting West Bank settlements were Canada, Denmark, Finland, France, Iceland, Ireland, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Spain, Sweden.

title: Nicolas Maduro, wife face torture charge in new U.S. indictment
summary: The couple were already facing charges of narco-terrorism conspiracy; cocaine importation conspiracy; and possession of machine guns and destructive devices.
story: Deposed Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro   and his wife, Cilia Flores, are now facing an additional charge of conspiracy to commit torture as federal prosecutors filed a superseding indictment in the Southern District of New York on Thursday.

"As alleged in the indictment, the Maduro regime subjected over a dozen American citizens to torture while held in custody of the Venezuelan government — including drugs, electrocution, sexual assault, and more," FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement on social media. "They will now answer for their crimes."

The couple were already facing a slew of charges, including narco-terrorism conspiracy; cocaine importation conspiracy; possession of machine guns and destructive devices; and conspiracy to possess machine guns and destructive devices.

The 30-page superseding indictment accuses the couple of overseeing a system of political repression that relied on Venezuela's military, intelligence agencies and security forces to torture their opponents, silence dissidents and maintain power.

"To undermine Venezuelan democracy and entrench themselves in power, these same leaders presided over a system of repression that relied on violence against political opposition, arbitrary detention, and the torture of detainees, including United States citizens," prosecutors wrote. "That torture included electric shock, asphyxiation, rape, forced nudity, prolonged isolation, starvation, punishment cells, and psychological torture, such as threats to harm and kill victims' families, including children."

Maduro and Flores were indicted by a federal grand jury in January on charges stemming from what prosecutors said was his role in a scheme to import "thousands of tons" of cocaine into the United States and enrich themselves, their family and senior members of the Venezuelan government.
The U.S. military took the couple into custody in an overnight operation and brought them to the U.S. to face the charges. They have pleaded not guilty to the initial charges.

Prosecutors allege Maduro ordered political opponents detained and tortured, received regular updates on interrogations and instructed officials to intensify abuse. During one briefing about a defiant prisoner, Maduro allegedly told officials to "squeeze them harder."

During political unrest in 2014, Maduro allegedly proposed abducting five to seven military officers suspected of disloyalty and extracting information through torture. According to the indictment, Flores agreed with the proposal.

The indictment also includes cases involving U.S. citizens subjected to electric shocks, drowning, severe beatings and other abuse while detained in Venezuela. One American arrested in 2022 was allegedly given injections that caused seizures.

A U.S. citizen detained in 2023 was severely beaten and tortured by Venezuelan intelligence officers, prosecutors said. One officer allegedly told the prisoner he had been kept alive because his U.S. citizenship made him useful in a potential prisoner exchange.
At a bail hearing for Flores on Thursday, her lawyer asked for the arraignment on the new charge to be delayed since they just received the indictment that morning, which was allowed by the judge.

Flores' lawyer argued she should be allowed release on bail with strict conditions due to health concerns related to her heart. The judge denied bail for Flores, noting she had access to "considerable funds" and calling the charges "serious allegations."
The case against the couple was brought in the Southern District of New York, where Maduro and 14 others were first indicted in March 2020, during the first Trump administration.

title: Bear kills man, seriously injures woman in their home in Mongolia
summary: The woman, who fled after sustaining injuries and sought help from neighbors, is being treated in a hospital, officials said.
story: A bear killed a man and seriously maimed a woman in their home in the outskirts of Mongolia's capital, authorities said Thursday, warning that sightings of the animals have skyrocketed across the country this year.

The man in his 40s and the woman in her 50s were attacked on Wednesday night in the Bayanzurkh district on the outskirts of Ulaanbaatar, the city's environment department chief Munkhbayar M told a news briefing.
The woman fled after sustaining injuries and sought help from neighbors, and she is being treated in a hospital, he said.
A team of 35 rangers is trying to locate and kill the bear.

Bear sightings have risen in Mongolia, with 24 confirmed sightings in Ulaanbaatar so far this year, compared with just two in 2018 and one in 2019, Munkhbayar said. Across Mongolia, 754 bear sightings have been reported in 11 provinces and the capital in 2026. Of those, 80% involved cubs or female bears accompanied by cubs.

Investigations are underway to determine what has caused the rise in sightings. Authorities have issued bear-hunting permits across eight provinces and are seeking to procure tranquilizer dart guns to support rangers in rural areas.

A bear that was hunted and examined in the eastern province of Khentii was found to have no food in its stomach, Baljinnyam N, an official at the Environment and Climate Change Ministry, told reporters.
As a result, authorities banned in September the harvesting of nuts and berries from mountainous areas for this year, he said.
Bear attacks increasing in parts of Asia
A spike in human-bear encounters has been reported in other parts of Asia recently.

In September, prosecutors said at least six people had been killed in bear attacks in Russia's vast Siberian region of Krasnoyarsk over a one-month period, and an official in a neighboring region reported bears had put one town "under siege."
Prosecutors said they opened a probe into criminal negligence, accusing local officials of failing to control bear numbers.
Russia's brown bear population has more than doubled since 1990, from around 130,000 to almost 308,000 in 2026, according to Russia's natural resources ministry.

Meanwhile, Japan has also recorded a sharp rise in bear sightings and attacks on humans in recent years, including in the outskirts of towns and cities. A record 13 people were killed by bears in Japan last year, and there has been a jump in encounters as the animals emerge hungry from hibernation.
The animals have been seen on airport runways, walking on golf courses, roaming near schools and causing panic in supermarkets and hot spring resorts almost on a daily basis.
The problem was so bad that last year, the U.S. State Department warned Americans in Japan to be alert for bears.
The causes are complex and include variations in food available — something potentially linked to climate change — as well as rural depopulation, experts say.

title: Trump aide's daughter pictured with pro-Russia politician
summary: Katie Wiles is a partner at the political lobbying firm Continental Strategy. A spokesperson for the firm acknowledged to CBS News that Wiles had taken the trip to Republika Srpska but on business for another firm's client.
story: An image circulated on social media and verified by CBS News shows Katie Wiles, the daughter of White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, recently traveled to Republika Srpska, the Bosnian-controlled territory led by pro-Russian Serb strongman Milorad Dodik.

The photo raises further questions about possible White House links to the pro-Russian politician. President Trump on Wednesday distanced himself from two top political advisers after the New York Times reported they had traveled to Republika Srpska last week to assist Dodik's pro-Russia party in Bosnian elections.

The image, shared online by conservative Albanian American activist Evi Kokalari, shows Wiles holding a rifle and standing next to a man CBS News has identified as Željko Budimir, the interior minister of the semi-autonomous Republika Srpska administration. In a post on X, Kokalari claimed the image was taken in August. CBS News Confirmed has verified the image is of Wiles and that it was taken in Republika Srpska. The image appears to be a screenshot of a story from Wiles' personal Instagram account, with a caption "mostly work + some serious fun!"

CBS News confirmed the veracity of the images through satellite imagery and previous social media posts from the shooting range where the image was captured. The position of the sun in the image also indicates that it was taken in the summer.
The RIS shooting range is located in northern Republika Srpska and is frequented by Budimir, the interior minister, according to Bosnian media reports.
Katie Wiles is a partner at Continental Strategy, a large political lobbying firm based in Washington, D.C., according to its website.
A spokesperson for the firm acknowledged to CBS News Thursday that Wiles had taken the trip in mid-August but on business for another client of Continental Strategy.

"Katie Wiles visited the country in mid-August for two days with a U.S.-based company who was invited to do a feasibility study in the region," the spokesperson said. "Wiles provides strategic communications support to this US company and has done so for over two years. Wiles has not spoken with any United States Government official regarding Srpska."
CBS News has asked Continental Strategy for the name of the company.
U.S. foreign agent registration filings [FARA] reviewed by CBS News show that Continental Strategy registered to lobby on behalf of Republika Srpska in early 2026.
"Susie does not discuss work matters with her daughters," a White House official told CBS News Thursday.

Another FARA filing from the same firm this year lists the signature of Alejandro Garcia, a former deputy political director for Mr. Trump's presidential campaign, as a consultant for Republika Srpska. Garcia is also a partner at Continental Strategy.
The lobbying firm's spokesperson told CBS News that Garcia attended Bosnia's election day on Oct. 4 "but no other member of the team was present."

"Garcia is the sole person who has interacted with the United States government regarding Srpska, and his contacts have all been meticulously tracked to be reported in accordance with FARA requirements," the spokesperson said.

White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles met with Željka Cvijanović, a close ally of Milorad Dodik, last month, and a White House official told CBS News that meeting was arranged by Garcia, not by Katie Wiles.

On Tuesday, the New York Times reported that James Blair and Chris LaCivita, two key GOP strategists in the Republicans' midterm election efforts, spent some of last week in the small, self-governing territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina to help Dodik's party with its own campaigning.  Katie Wiles has no such involvement with Mr. Trump's political operation.

Under the control of Dodik's party, Republika Srpska has forged close ties with President Vladimir Putin's government in Russia, while also spending heavily on U.S.-based lobbying firms to court associates of Mr. Trump, according to FARA filings reviewed by CBS News.

Serbian secessionist leader Dodik, who until recently served as the president of Republika Srpska, has long been accused of undermining the U.S.-brokered Dayton Accords, which ended the bloody sectarian violence between Bosnia, Croatia and Serbia in the 1990s. A Sarajevo court last year convicted Dodik of failing to comply with the terms of Bosnia's 1995 peace accords. He was then removed as president and banned from holding political office by Bosnia's electoral authorities.
In a Truth Social post Wednesday, Mr. Trump said he did not "have any idea" who LaCivita and Blair had been working for and he pledged, "if there's a conflict, I will terminate them, immediately!"
Later Wednesday, Mr. Trump appeared to slightly soften his language.

"They don't have a conflict, because they're independent people. You know, they don't work for me," Mr. Trump said, addressing reporters in the Oval Office. "They are consultants and I assume they have a lot of clients. I don't know who their clients are. If I thought they had a conflict here, I would terminate them."

As CBS News reported this week, the involvement of a U.S. firm linked to associates of Mr. Trump in an energy project in Bosnia and Herzegovina worth more than $1.5 billion has raised questions about the White House's relationship with Dodik.

Last month, House Democrats published a report accusing the Trump administration of lifting sanctions against Dodik in an effort to enrich and empower allies of Mr. Trump, and of undermining longstanding U.S. foreign policy interests in the region in the process.

The central allegation is that AAFS Infrastructure & Energy, a company incorporated in the U.S. last year and headed by Mr. Trump's former personal attorney Jesse Binnall and Joseph Flynn, the brother of Trump ally Gen. Michael Flynn, secured the contract to build a key gas pipeline between Bosnia and Croatia after the sanctions were lifted against Dodik, who had previously opposed the development.

FARA filings cited in the report and reviewed by CBS News show that Michael Flynn, Mr. Trump's former national security adviser, worked as a paid lobbyist for Republika Srpska in October 2025, the month during which the sanctions against Dodik were lifted.

Within six months of the sanctions being lifted, Dodik's party, which has veto power in Bosnia's legislature, dropped its opposition and the Bosnian parliament passed legislation naming AAFS as the lead developer on the billion-dollar project.
The White House declined to comment on the pipeline project last week, but an administration official said the sanctions against Dodik were lifted to prevent instability in the Balkans.

"This is yet another example of President Trump's pragmatic, farseeing foreign policy that has prevented disasters on perennial issues that his predecessors so often stumbled into," a White House official told CBS News on Friday, without elaborating on the type of disasters the Trump administration was preventing.

title: Newly obtained footage shows Iran attack on major U.S. post in Kuwait
summary: CBS News obtained new video from a person on the ground showing an Iranian attack on a U.S. base at the beginning of the war.
story: Washington — New videos obtained exclusively by CBS News show Iranian attacks on a major U.S. military base in Kuwait as the war with Iran kicked off seven months ago. American forces faced ballistic missiles, drones and what witnesses described as Iranian F-5 fighter jets.

The footage obtained by CBS News was recorded by a person stationed on the ground at Camp Buehring, and captures the moments of impact and their explosive aftermath. Damage to buildings and military equipment can also be seen in the videos.

The attacks on Camp Buehring offer a window into the strain Iranian attacks placed on American forces during the opening days of the war. CBS News has learned that soldiers defending the base ran critically low on .50-caliber ammunition as some soldiers were repositioned into the Udari Desert in Kuwait. Two soldiers were injured by lightning there in late April, according to U.S. officials with knowledge of the matter.
Contacted by CBS News, U.S. Central Command, the primary unit which oversees American military operations across the Middle East, declined to comment.
The Pentagon did not comment, but pointed back to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's comments on March 4 regarding the removal of U.S. troops from bases and the employment of defensive measures.

"As we built up offensive combat power, we moved the vast majority of American troops — over 90% of Americans that were on our bases — what we say off the X, out of the range of Iranian fire," Hegseth told reporters in March.
Camp Buehring, or CBKU, sits about 25 miles from the Iraqi border and has for more than two decades served as a major staging ground for American forces deploying across the Middle East.
CBS News authenticated the videos using metadata embedded in the files and compared the footage to other photographs showing damage to the base.

Ahead of the war, sources said most of the roughly 7,000 troops there were moved elsewhere — as were the majority of U.S. forces in Kuwait — as a part of the Pentagon's "get off the X" plan, military shorthand for moving away from a position vulnerable to attack.

Once the war started, Iranian attacks, some originating from Iraq, repeatedly threatened the installation. Missiles and drones forced soldiers into bunkers. Three U.S. service members told CBS News that Iranian F-5 fighter jets were also used during the attacks, a detail first reported in April by NBC News.
"They ran so close to us I could see their helmets," the eyewitness described. "They came in, they hit us, and then took off."

While most of the U.S. service members were moved off of Camp Buehring, a tranche of more than 100 soldiers stayed behind. The service members feared the isolated base was ill-equipped to handle a mass-casualty event if the attacks continued.

"They hit us bad," the source told CBS News on condition of anonymity because of the military's strict media restrictions. "It was horrible. There were a lot of brave guys who stayed to fight there — and people at home don't know what happened. We had to abandon the base."

A senior Army official working in logistics, managing operations from another post in Kuwait, confirmed to CBS News there were concerns about the availability of .50 caliber ammunition and other "exquisite" munitions like Patriot missile batteries.

The decision ultimately was to leave. Service members packed up, loading their vehicles with whatever equipment they could and drove at night deep into the Kuwaiti desert. Their remote locations would emerge as forward operating bases, or "FOBs," where the soldiers would remain indefinitely.

No one was killed by enemy fire at Camp Buehring or at the FOBs, but several were injured, including two soldiers who were struck by lightning in desert sandstorms. One soldier suffered burns after the direct strike while the other suffered a ruptured eardrum, according to U.S. officials with knowledge of the matter.

Before the lightning strike, Army leaders had been trying to move the troops out of the area, but were not able to do so quickly enough. In May, the soldiers left the FOBs for Camp Arifjan, and then relocated to other positions both in and out of the Middle East.
"CBKU got demolished," the source added. "They need to do an investigation. How come no one came to reinforce us?"

The Defense Department's inspector general last month released a report on the war with Iran that revealed "equipment losses" worth up to $3.7 billion — including nearly 60 aircraft. On Monday, the Congressional Research Service, which provides nonpartisan analysis to members of Congress, reported that 81 fixed or rotary-wing aircraft including drone assets had been lost or damaged by Iran since February, according to news reports and statements from the Defense Department.

In a first-of-its-kind mandatory report to Congress, the inspector general added that U.S. Central Command had reported Iranian strikes at U.S. bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, UAE, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman and Jordan.

Although strikes were mentioned in the report, pictures and videos of any impact zones have been extremely limited. Beyond Camp Buehring, CBS News earlier obtained exclusive photos of damage at Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia and Camp Arifjan in Kuwait.
CBS News has also reported extensively on the deadliest attack of the war against U.S. troops at the Port of Shuaiba, which killed six American service members.

title: Amelia Earhart investigators to study mysterious object in Pacific
summary: Investigators have begun an expedition to study a mysterious "visual anomaly" that they say may be Amelia Earhart's long-lost plane.
story: A team searching for Amelia Earhart's lost plane has begun its expedition to the Pacific, where it plans to study a mysterious object that researchers say may be her aircraft.

The item, known as the Taraia Object, has been visible in photos dating back to 1938, the year after Earhart and navigator Fred Noonan disappeared over the Pacific Ocean during Earhart's attempt to become the first female pilot to circle the world. Earhart, Noonan and their Electra 10E plane were never found.

Researchers identified the "visual anomaly" in a lagoon on Nikumaroro, a small island in Kiribati about halfway between Australia and Hawaii. The island is about 400 miles southeast of Howland Island, where Earhart and Noonan were planning to travel.

Now, a team of researchers from Purdue University and the Oregon-based Archaeological Legacy Institute are traveling to Nikumaroro to examine the object. The research team previously said in a news release that there is "very strong" evidence that the object is Earhart's lost plane.

The team previously said they will take photos and videos of the lagoon and Taraia Object. Then, they will use magnetometers and sonar devices to scan the area before dredging the item from the water so researchers can attempt to identify it. The process will be documented by the Archealogy Channel, with short vlogs on their streaming platform, Heritage Broadcasting Service.

Richard Pettigrew, from the Archaeological Legacy Institute, said that he believes Earhart and Noonan landed on Nikumororo and camped there. He believes they survived on the island for some time, citing 1930s relics and human skeletal remains that were found there but lost over the decades.

"We owe it to Amelia's legacy at Purdue to follow the evidence," Steve Schultz, a senior vice president at Purdue University and field assistant on the expedition, told CBS News. Earhart lectured at the school before embarking on her final flight. Some of her belongings remain on display in the university's archives.

Some experts are skeptical. Ric Gillespie, the executive director of the International Group for Historic Aircraft Recovery, told NBC News in 2025 that he does not think the Taraia Object is related to the Earhart expedition.
"We've looked there in that spot, and there's nothing there," he said.

For nearly a century, researchers have tried to find Earhart's missing plane, believing it will help them answer the question of what happened to the famed aviator. In 2024, another expedition team captured a sonar image that seemed to resemble a plane resting at the bottom of the sea. But the object was later determined to be a rock formation.

Wendy Rover of The Ninety Nines, an international organization for women pilots that Earhart helped establish, said she hopes the mystery of what happened to Earhart can someday be solved. Rover told CBS News that when she is flying and looking for safe places to land, she imagines Earhart doing the same while over the Pacific.
"Amelia Earhart was out there. She was going through that exact same thing," Rover said. "So yeah - what happened? What did happen? I would love to know."

title: Country star Drew Baldridge lifts curtain on Jelly Roll's 'wild' entourage, Luke Bryan's 'country boy' life
summary: Drew Baldridge reveals why Jelly Roll's backstage scene is wildly unpredictable and how Luke Bryan's dove-hunting trips show his country roots.
story: Drew Baldridge tells Fox News Digital about Jelly Roll's massive backstage entourage.
Country music superstars may share the spotlight, but their lives behind the scenes can look very different.

Drew Baldridge, who recently released his album, "FARM FAITH FAMILY," got a front-row seat to both worlds — from Luke Bryan's down-home lifestyle to Jelly Roll's jam-packed backstage scene, where the next unexpected guest could be just around the corner.

title: Michael Douglas' wildest Hollywood confessions: From A-list actress bite to Julia Roberts clash
summary: Michael Douglas alleges a confrontation with Julia Roberts, secret affairs and a cocaine-fueled evening with O.J. Simpson in his new memoir.
story: In his memoir, "One Helluva Ride," the actor admitted he had an affair with his "Basic Instinct" co-star, Jeanne Tripplehorn. (This video contains AI-assisted content.)
Michael Douglas is pulling back the curtain on the most explosive moments of his life, both in front of the camera and behind the scenes.

In his memoir, "One Helluva Ride," the actor-producer also opens up about secret affairs, heavy cocaine and alcohol use, a "rehab or divorce" ultimatum from his first wife, Diandra, and the painful family struggles that followed him from childhood into fatherhood.

Douglas details his volatile relationship with his late father, Kirk Douglas, his son Cameron’s addiction and imprisonment, and the stage IV cancer diagnosis that forced him to confront his own mortality.
Michael Douglas's memoir, "One Helluva Ride," was released on Oct. 6.  (Getty Images)
Here are the top ten bombshells:
MICHAEL DOUGLAS CONFIRMS SECRET AFFAIR WITH KATHLEEN TURNER ON 'ROMANCING THE STONE' SET
An A-list actress bit him during casting dinner
Debra Winger allegedly bit Michael Douglas in the 1980s. (Getty Images)
In the book, Douglas recalled that he and the filmmakers were trying to convince Debra Winger to star as Joan Wilder in "Romancing the Stone," but the meeting took an odd turn.

"We took Debra to dinner and, once again, it was an epic meal. Any time you have dinner with Jack or Danny, it’s a riot. … But the real goal of the dinner was to get Debra on board to make Romancing the Stone, and no matter how hard we tried, she would not give us an answer, one way or the other. We were stuck in limbo."
MICHAEL DOUGLAS ADMITS HE ALMOST LEFT HIS WIFE FOR HIS 'BASIC INSTINCT' CO-STAR AFTER AFFAIR

"Stories had filtered back that Debra was delivering an incredible performance in Terms of Endearment, but also that she was difficult during shooting and had huge, blow-out fights with Shirley MacLaine," he wrote.

"We all left the restaurant and were walking down the street when, the way somebody might punch you in the arm as you part company, Debra leaned over and bit me. I mean, she really bit me. Jesus, I had a whole set of teeth marks dug into my arm. We still had no answer from her, but that bite sealed the deal for me. No, thank you!"
MICHAEL DOUGLAS REVEALS HE MADE FIVE PHONE CALLS TO FIVE WOMEN THE DAY HE CHOSE CATHERINE ZETA-JONES
Douglas said he later reenacted the moment for Fox executives, telling them, "She bit me. Hard. Look at the teeth marks in my arm."
Although the studio pushed back because Winger was a major star, Douglas held his ground. Winger ultimately did not join the project, and Kathleen Turner was cast in the role.
Fox News Digital has reached out to reps for Winger for comment.
Douglas confronted Julia Roberts over his teenage son
Michael Douglas said he once snapped at Julia Roberts while drunk.  (Getty Images)
Douglas experienced another tense moment involving Julia Roberts at a Golden Globes party.

Douglas was at the event with his son Cameron, who was about 13 at the time. In the book, Douglas alleges that Roberts had her arm around Cameron and was "kind of nuzzling him." Douglas, who admits he was drunk, claims Cameron looked stunned.

"I told her, ‘Take your hands off my son and take that Golden Globe and stick it where the sun don’t shine,’" he writes.
Douglas later apologized to Roberts and her then-boyfriend, Kiefer Sutherland.
BRAD PITT ADMITS HE BEGAN DRINKING AGAIN AFTER YEARS OF SOBRIETY
"I sent Julia roses with an apology for my behavior, and then back in the production office, I apologized to her and Kiefer in person," he wrote.
Fox News Digital has reached out to reps for Roberts for comment.
Douglas reveals secret affair with Lee Purcell
Lee Purcell and Michael Douglas had a secret affair in the 1970s. (Getty Images)
While filming "Adam at 6 A.M." early in his career, Douglas says he and his married co-star Lee Purcell became lovers.

"As filming progressed, my relationship with Lee changed and we became lovers," he writes. "Our intimate relationship was complicated by the fact that she was married, and we had to keep it a secret from the cast, crew, the people in the town we were filming in, and of course her husband. It was a passionate affair that lasted through filming."

Purcell told Fox News Digital, "This story came as a complete surprise to me. I have fond memories of Michael and our time together. However, our recall appears to differ. First, I remember the process of searching for his character of Adam after having already been hired by Steve McQueen for the role of Jerri Jo. Secondly, we had a strictly professional relationship during filming, the personal one came much later."

Years later, while making "Romancing the Stone," Douglas also admits he had an affair with screenwriter Diane Thomas, who wrote the film. He says he and his first wife, Diandra, were both involved in extramarital relationships as their marriage deteriorated.
Diandra gave him a ‘rehab or divorce’ ultimatum
In the midst of his substance abuse and infidelity, Douglas said his first marriage to Diandra Luker eventually came to a head at the Beverly Wilshire Hotel.
After Diandra initially declined to stay with him at the hotel, Douglas called a woman he had been seeing. The woman came to his room, where they had drinks.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Douglas says Diandra unexpectedly returned, obtained a key from the front desk and walked in on them.
Michael Douglas and Diandra Luker married in 1977. (Ron Galella Collection via Getty Images)
"She gave me an ultimatum: ‘Rehab or divorce,’" he writes.

"The indiscretion, the drugs, the booze. I was in a constant state of temporary pleasure or temporary escape," he writes. "In my heart, I knew that I was heading down a very bad road at a very high speed, but I was trying my best to compartmentalize…"
Douglas entered the Sierra Tucson rehabilitation clinic in Arizona in 1992 to receive treatment for alcohol and substance abuse.
PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE
Douglas denies being a sex addict
Douglas says his rehab stay was later exploited by a tabloid.

He claims two fellow patients sold information about the program to a publication and then left treatment. According to Douglas, the story transformed his treatment for alcohol and drug abuse into a sensational headline portraying him as a sex addict.

"The story that was printed was utter bulls—," Douglas writes. "I had made mistakes, had moments I wasn’t proud of, made choices I wouldn’t have if I wasn’t high, but I was never a f---ing sex addict."
Douglas says the story damaged his reputation and continued to follow him in interviews for decades.
Douglas recalls partying with O.J. Simpson
Michael Douglas claims he once partied with O.J. Simpson. (Getty Images)
Douglas also writes about an encounter with O.J. Simpson and Rolling Stone co-founder Jann Wenner.

Douglas says he and Wenner encountered Simpson at a "Saturday Night Live" after-party. Wenner invited Simpson back to his apartment, where Simpson allegedly pulled out a rolled dollar bill and offered them cocaine.
"Jann and I were looking at each other — Are we really doing this with O.J. Simpson?" Douglas writes.
He also claims cocaine was readily available throughout Hollywood. Douglas says that at one major talent agency, a valet could allegedly replace a $100 bill left in a car with a packet of cocaine.
Fox News Digital has reached out to Wenner for comment.
Douglas describes a private evening with Princess Diana
Diana, Princess of Wales, talks to American actor Michael Douglas at the London premiere of the film "Wall Street" on April 28, 1988. British actor Terence Stamp is in the center. (Getty Images)
Douglas writes that he spent a private evening with Princess Diana at a London screening of "Wall Street."
He says they sat beside each other during the film, with their hands occasionally touching on the shared armrest. Afterward, they spent time together at a private dinner away from the cameras.
"The truth was simple: she was in an unhappy marriage and wanted a different life," he writes.
He does not claim they had a romantic relationship, but describes their time together as "very special."
He recalls growing up afraid of Kirk Douglas
Actor Kirk Douglas and actor Michael Douglas in 2011.  (Getty Images)
Douglas describes his father, Hollywood icon Kirk Douglas, as a powerful, but volatile presence.
"Kirk Douglas was my father, a flawed man with a ferocious temper and a burning ambition," he writes.
Douglas says his father’s behavior left him and his brother Joel frightened. He recalls Kirk saying, "I yell and scream because I care," while Douglas writes that Joel endured more of the abuse.
Douglas’ cancer was misdiagnosed for nine months
Douglas says doctors initially treated his persistent throat pain as an infection and prescribed multiple rounds of antibiotics.
A Canadian specialist eventually discovered a subtle swelling at the back of his tongue. A biopsy revealed squamous cell carcinoma.
"It’s stage IV cancer," the doctor told him, according to Douglas, who says the tumor was the size of a walnut.

Douglas writes that three doctors had missed the cancer and that he had been given the wrong diagnosis for nine months. He feared surgery would require removing part of his tongue and jaw, potentially ending his acting career.
His doctors publicly referred to the disease as throat cancer rather than tongue cancer because they feared reports about possible disfigurement would become sensationalized.
Douglas once tried to kidnap Cameron and force him into rehab
Douglas also describes the darkest years of his son Cameron’s addiction.
"When he was really strung out in New York, I decided I was going to kidnap him and force him into rehab," he writes.

Douglas said that Cameron was addicted to cocaine and heroin, dealt methamphetamine and carried a Glock for protection. During one incident, Cameron flashed the weapon at a drugstore and was nearly shot by police.

Cameron Douglas and Michael Douglas attend the 2024 Vanity Fair Oscar Party at the Wallis Annenberg Center for the Performing Arts on March 10, 2024, in Beverly Hills, Calif. (Variety via Getty Images)
At one point, Douglas says he arranged for two large men to help abduct Cameron and force him into rehab.
"When we came back, I asked to hold the leash. Cam figured it out. He looked at me, like, ‘Dad, how could you?’ Like I had broken his heart. Again."
Cameron realized what was happening and resisted, so Douglas threw the plan out of the window.

Cameron later served seven years in prison after a federal drug case. Douglas writes that his son’s heroin relapse behind bars led a judge to add four and a half years to his sentence, and Cameron also spent two years in solitary confinement.
