story: John Cena avoided questions from the media after his WrestleMania 41 win, decrying them as ‘clickbait.’
John Cena’s Hollywood career nearly ended before it ever truly got off the ground.

The WWE legend admitted he was "ran out of the movie business" because he simply didn’t care enough about acting, revealing that his heart remained in the wrestling ring as he struggled to embrace the slower pace of life on a film set.

Cena reflected on the rocky start to a Hollywood career that would eventually include roles in "The Suicide Squad," the "Fast & Furious" franchise and "Peacemaker" during an appearance on the "Today" show.
SYLVESTER STALLONE'S ADVICE TO THOSE WHO ARE STRUGGLING 50 YEARS AFTER 'ROCKY' CHANGED HIS LIFE
John Cena admitted Hollywood once "ran" him out of the movie business after he struggled to embrace acting while his heart remained in professional wrestling. (Theo Wargo/Getty Images)
"It’s been a long journey," he explained. "I think that’s the important one. People think things happen overnight. Those early projects – truth be told – I didn’t have my heart into."
For Cena, his priorities were elsewhere.

"As a young 20-something, God, traveling the world, being out in front of tens of thousands of people every night going nuts and then doing it night after night. That’s where I wanted to be, and that’s where I felt comfortable and fluent," he said, referencing his successful career in the WWE.
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE
John Cena eventually found success with roles in "The Suicide Squad," the "Fast & Furious" franchise and "Peacemaker" after developing a new passion for acting. (Michael Buckner/Getty Images)
Cena described working on a film set as "super patient" and "super slow."
"I just didn’t have the wisdom for the process," he claimed.
But Hollywood apparently had little patience for Cena’s lack of enthusiasm.
"I got ran out of the movie business for not caring and that’s justifiably so," he added. "If you don’t care about something, give somebody the opportunity that does."

Cena began his acting career with roles in movies such as "The Marine" and "12 Rounds." However, Cena didn't see success until the 2010s with roles in "Trainwreck," "Blockers" and "The Suicide Squad."
He's said his role as Peacemaker in the DC Extended Universe changed his life. The 2021 movie has since been turned into a TV series.

John Cena credited self-reflection and personal growth for helping him earn a second chance in Hollywood before officially retiring from WWE in 2025. (Gabe Ginsberg/WireImage)

Cena also joined the "Fast and Furious" franchise in 2021, playing Vin Diesel's character's brother in "Fast 9: The Fast Saga" and "Fast X." The actor later made a cameo in "Barbie" in 2023 and starred in the Hulu original movies "Vacation Friends" plus "Vacation Friends 2."
But after years of finding his footing in Hollywood, Cena said his attitude toward acting couldn't be more different today.

"I’m now super passionate about what I do, and that’s everything from filming to sitting here talking about this movie with you guys. And I’m so lucky to be given a second chance," he said. "And that took 20 years to craft."

The "Today" hosts also highlighted Cena’s self-awareness as he reflected on how much he has changed over the years.

"Man, I think there’s nothing wrong with taking inventory of yourself, looking in the mirror, loving yourself for your strengths and your flaws and trying to work to be better than you were yesterday," he said.
Cena began his WWE career in 2002 on "Smackdown!" as "The Prototype," eventually transforming into his rapper persona, the "Doctor of Thuganomics."
Throughout his career, Cena has won a record-breaking 17 WWE world championships. He officially retired in 2025.

title: Zachary Levi says Texas gives him the ‘freedom’ he couldn’t find in California
summary: Zachary Levi says he traded California for Texas "freedom" and values that are "more aligned with mine." The actor is starring in the new Western remake "Angel and the Badman."
story: "Angel and the Badman" star Zachary Levi explains why he believes Texas’ values align more closely with his own after leaving California behind.
Zachary Levi believes Texas offered him the kind of freedom and shared values that he no longer felt he had in his home state of California.
In 2017, the 45-year-old actor, who is starring in the new Western movie "Angel and the Badman," left Los Angeles behind and moved to a ranch outside Austin.

During a recent interview with Fox News Digital alongside his "Angel and the Badman" co-stars, Neal McDonough and Meg Fraser, as well as the film's director, Julio Quintana, Levi reflected on trading the Golden State for the Lone Star State, noting that the "great state of Texas" is a "much easier place to live than a lot of the other places that I have lived."
'FRIDAY NIGHT LIGHTS' STAR ADRIANNE PALICKI SAYS TEXAS GAVE HER SOMETHING HOLLYWOOD COULDN'T
Zachary Levi shared that he found the freedom to "live the life that I'm meant to go live" in Texas after leaving California. (Getty Images)
"I love California. It's a beautiful state," he said. "Unfortunately, I think it's got a lot of issues and I don't see those going anywhere."

"Whereas in Texas, I think that their values are more aligned with mine," he continued. "I appreciate that I don't have to pay state income tax and there's liberty. There's the liberty to go do what I want to go do, which is, like, go buy a bunch of land and build a movie studio."
NEWSOM SAYS FILM TAX INCENTIVES ARE BRINGING HOLLYWOOD HOME BUT INDUSTRY EXPERTS WARN IT MAY BE 'TOO LATE'

"You can be a crazy person and go do that," Levi added. "If Walt Disney tried to go build Disneyland in California today, I don't think it would ever get done, you know, so it gives me the freedom to go live the life that I believe that I'm meant to go live."

Levi is currently building Wyldwood Studios, a $100 million film and lifestyle campus on his 75-acre property in Bastrop County outside Austin. Designed as a hybrid production hub and creative retreat, the multiphase project pairs soundstages and production offices with housing and wellness spaces. Wyldwood is expected to open its first two soundstages in 2027.
WATCH: ZACHARY LEVI SAYS TEXAS GAVE HIM THE FREEDOM HE COULDN'T FIND IN CALIFORNIA
The "Chuck" alum previously told Fox News Digital that the inspiration to build Wyldwood was rooted in his longstanding desire to rethink how the entertainment industry operates from the inside out.

"Ever since I started working in Hollywood and I saw how broken it all was, I felt very compelled by God to go build a better Hollywood — like a new United Artists kind of studio — where it's owned and operated by the artists, where we can cut out all the middlemen, where we all can do really well, build a community," Levi said.

"And then not just a place to work," he continued. "People can live there, and kids can go to school there. And we have an organic farm, and, like, all of the things that I think everybody really wants these days."
Levi is starring in the Western remake "Angel and the Badman." (Angel Studios )

Levi's latest project, "Angel and the Badman," which was produced by Angel Studios, is a remake of the classic 1947 Western of the same name that starred John Wayne, Gail Russell, Harry Carey and Bruce Cabot.

The official plot synopsis for the remake reads, "When feared outlaw Quirt Evans staggers onto a rancher's land with a bullet in his back, he expects a quick death, not mercy. But Penny, the rancher's daughter, offers him a chance at something he’s never had: a life beyond violence. However, the past doesn’t forgive. With the marshal closing in and an outlaw gang ready to burn the ranch to the ground, Quirt must decide what kind of man he’ll be when the world demands blood."

Levi stepped into Wayne's original role as Quirt Evans (the Badman) while Fraser plays Penny (the Angel) and McDonough portrays the marshal. "Angel and the Badman" also stars Tommy Lee Jones as the outlaw gang leader Laredo.
WATCH: NEAL MCDONOUGH SAYS YOUNG PEOPLE NEED TO SEE ‘THE BAD GUY GETS WHAT HE DESERVES’
While speaking with Fox News Digital, McDonough explained how he believes "Angel and the Badman" conveys an important message for the young people of today.

"I think nowadays — with the temptation of social media and what we look at and what we hear and what we listen to — who do we look up to as heroes anymore?" he said. "Especially for the younger generation, it's really hard for them."

"The younger generation who don't really know Westerns so well, to go to a film like ‘Angel and the Badman,’ you see, ‘OK, the bad guy gets what he deserves in the end,’" McDonough continued. "Where in modern day, the bad guy sometimes gets to go scot-free and that's tough to really learn from as a kid. What do you learn from that as a young adult?"

"So films like this are important because it tells us, you should be trying to do the right thing," he added. "You should redeem yourself and not do the dumb things that you used to do. Try to be a better person, try to give glory to Him, try and do the right thing for your family. I love doing films like these because they do exactly that, and thank goodness for Angel Studios."
Neal McDonough is pictured in a scene from "Angel and the Badman." (Angel Studios )
Quintana said he believed that the story’s redemptive themes feel especially relevant in a social media era when public mistakes can quickly become permanent scandals.

"In modern culture, in some ways, we actually have the inverse situation where it seems like we're always — you make one public mistake, and it's like your life is ruined," he said. "Our media outlets thrive on downfall and self-destruction and things like that. And I think this is a good reminder that actually what's really inspiring is people making mistakes and ultimately making the sacrifices to make amends and try to claw their way back up and try to be better, because we don't really see the redemptive side of a public downfall. Nowadays, we only see the dark side."
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

McDonough shared that he personally resonates with redemptive storytelling after his past struggles with substance abuse issues. During a 2025 interview with Fox News Digital, the "Band of Brothers" star explained that he gave up alcohol in 2016 after realizing he had to make his life about serving God, "rather than serving me." He also credited his wife of over 22 years, Ruvé, with giving him the motivation he needed to quit drinking as he recalled, "She grabbed me and says, it's us or the bottle, you choose," and he "never looked back."
Reflecting on "Angel and the Badman's" message of redemption, McDonough admitted, "I think that we all do things that we are not proud of at times."
WATCH: ‘ANGEL AND THE BADMAN’ STAR ZACHARY LEVI SAYS REDEMPTION STORIES APPLY TO EVERYONE

"We all make mistakes," he continued. "None of us are perfect. We all sin, we all do dumb things, but every once in a while, you get called out and something might happen to make you think, ‘Hmm, maybe I should be a better dad. Maybe I should be a better husband. Maybe I should be better coworker. I need to stop doing that thing.’"

"Years ago, I stopped drinking because it took me off my game, and it just wasn't keeping me focused to do His work," McDonough remembered. "And ever since then, I focused so hard on doing His work and giving glory to Him and everything that I do. So we all have to overcome these things and that's redemption. And ‘Angel and the Badman,’ boy, you know, Quirt Evans has to go through that."

"It's that redemptive quality that Westerns have more than any other films," he added. "They keep it simple. There's a good guy, there's a bad guy. Good guy's gonna win, but he has to overcome something because the bad guy couldn't. And that's what we did in ‘Angel and the Badman.’"

Neal McDonough, Zachary Levi, Meg Fraser and Julio Quintana attend the "Angel and the Badman" world premiere on Oct. 1, 2026, in Santa Fe, New Mexico. (Sam Wasson/Getty Images for Angel Studios)
Levi told Fox News Digital that he also believed that the movie's message was universal.

"I love a good redemption story," he said. "It's one of the most classic stories that you can tell, and if you can tell it within a classic genre like a Western that has a little bit of all of these subcategories of action-adventure and romance and drama and comedy and heart and charm and all of those things woven into one beautifully shot and directed story — then you get to tell a story that I believe applies to everyone."

"Because everyone knows deep down inside of them, they either have been redeemed or are in need of redemption," Levi continued. "It's a human story. It's a human story. So those are the ones that I like to tell the most."

title: James Bond legend Roger Moore's son calls out TikTok culture, Hollywood's recycled comic book movies
summary: Geoffrey Moore stars in spy thriller "Knightfall" and shares why Hollywood needs stronger stories over big-budget spectacle and recycled comics.
story: Former Bond girl Alison Papworth shares why she wants the next 007 to stay true to the books as speculation swirls over the role.
Forget bigger explosions — Geoffrey Moore says Hollywood needs better stories.

The son of the late James Bond legend Roger Moore told Fox News Digital that today’s films have become too reliant on recycled comic book material and big-budget spectacle, while originality and meaningful dialogue have taken a back seat.

"I think that today, it's too much TikTok," the actor told Fox News Digital. "A person will have a conversation with you, and it's the conversation that he read or heard on TikTok, as opposed to actually having read Hemingway and knows what he's talking about."
GABRIEL BASSO SAYS SOCIAL MEDIA HAS TURNED PEOPLE INTO VOYEURS OBSESSED WITH STRANGERS' LIVES: 'IT'S WEIRD'
Geoffrey Moore, son of late James Bond icon Roger Moore, is starring in the British spy film "Knightfall." (Saban Films)

"I think it's important that the art of storytelling maintains the culture," Moore said. "There's just too many studio executive heads deciding what's right, as opposed to what people want to hear or people should hear and see."

Moore stars in the British spy thriller "Knightfall," which has its share of guns and fight scenes. However, he said the film doesn't rely on over-the-top action to keep audiences hooked and instead leans on a strong storyline and sharp dialogue.
Geoffrey Moore told Fox News Digital that today's Hollywood films are too lengthy and rely heavily on comic book franchises. (Saban Films)
"I would like to see more culture in films, as opposed to the regurgitation of these comics," Moore said.
WATCH: BOND GIRL ALISON PAPWORTH REVEALS HER HOPE FOR THE NEXT 007

"And everything's so negative. Oh, my goodness. It's like, you need to have a certain budget with helicopters flying upside down. But the storyline has to be strong. Good dialogue, good storywriting are key. You don't have to have constant action to keep the person's attention going. You also need action in the storyline, in the words."
Moore also believes "Knightfall" has something else working in its favor in the social media era: It doesn't overstay its welcome.
Geoffrey Moore attends the London premiere of "Knightfall" at Cine Lumiere in London, England, on Sept. 13, 2026. (Alan Chapman/Dave Benett/WireImage)
The actor said the film was deliberately kept short, acknowledging that today's audiences may not have the patience to sit through a lengthy saga.

"Knightfall" tells the tale of Charles Knight, a former spy catcher who must work with his estranged daughter to avert a homeland security bloodbath and survive a terrifying home invasion. Geoffrey Moore plays Hugh. (Saban Films)

"You can't sit through a three-hour movie," he argued. "You can imagine today, it's just everyone on the treadmill. You need that right amount of length before someone starts asking, 'When is it over?' That's the direction I would take with today's films."
For Moore, "Knightfall" also marks a full-circle moment.
Roger Moore's 4-year-old son Geoffrey watches from the edge of the set on Aug. 11, 1970. (Getty Images)

The actor grew up immersed in the entertainment business as the son of one of Hollywood's most famous spies. Now, decades later, he's stepping in front of the camera as a spy himself at roughly the same age his father was when he made his final James Bond film.
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE
Geoffrey Moore told Fox News Digital he was eager to help boost the British film industry with his new movie. (Saban Films)

"I have not been an actor all my life, even though I did start as a child actor," Moore said. "My second womb was the soundstage. But just because you're related to someone in the entertainment industry, it doesn't make me a part of the entertainment industry or even an actor. But this time, it just felt right. It wasn't forced. And also, it's never too late. I mean, yes, go figure, it's a spy film, but there's a twist. And really, it's never too late."

Moore was six years old when his father filmed his 007 debut, "Live and Let Die," which was released in 1973. The Telegraph reported that Moore was present for all of his father's Bond films and the famous stunts that came with them. Once the director yelled "cut," the patriarch would look at his son and ask if he wanted to get ice cream.
British actor Roger Moore walks through London Airport with his son Geoffrey, 6, and daughter Deborah, 8, on Aug. 2, 1972, before leaving for a short holiday in Rome, Italy. (Getty Images)

"Look, I've been on enough film sets to know how laborious it can be," Moore said. "It's a demanding schedule and you mustn't break your ankle. But I've never had a big role where I'm doing a lot of running around. I have to say on some mornings when I wake up, if you've ever been horseback riding, you recognize muscles you never knew you had. I'm doing all of this running around and going, 'Oh my goodness, I thought I was fit!'"
Geoffrey Moore, 60, is marking his first acting role in 33 years with "Knightfall," The Telegraph reported. (Saban Films)

"I was never like, 'I'm looking for a job in front of the camera,'" Moore continued. "It just felt right. And I was intrigued. It's an independent British film and very few films aren't dictated by executive heads. This isn't a regurgitation of another franchise where they're spending lots of money. Here, the conditions were harsh. It was physically demanding. Rewrites are happening on the day. It was back to back."
"The food was good, considering this wasn't a multimillion production," he said. "And if the money is good, that'll get your attention."
Geoffrey Moore attends the Rosewood Munich grand opening on Oct. 25, 2023, in Munich, Germany. (Getty Images for Rosewood Munich)
Moore said the key to making it in the movie-making business is simple: don't take yourself too seriously.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Geoffrey Moore attended the "Spectre" premiere after party at the British Museum on Oct. 26, 2015. (GC Images)

"If an actor shows up on the set and doesn't understand the importance of the production, what each person does, then they're in the wrong business," he said. "It's a team effort. Everyone is as important. You're nothing without the guy who knows how to keep you in focus. If you make something look good, it's usually not that easy. And to be a film star, you have to be a good actor. There's no such thing as an ignorant person who can act."
Despite following in his father's footsteps by playing a spy, Moore isn't campaigning to become the next James Bond.
English actor Roger Moore poses for a portrait in London, England, on July 20, 1979. Moore portrayed James Bond in the Bond series. (Getty Images)

"I think the next James Bond should be someone who can carry the decade, a reflection of the times," Moore said. "When it comes to who's the next Bond, it's really who depicts the times, who is relevant to today, whether it be a tall person, a short person, someone who doesn't know how to tie a tie or who doesn't know how to read because he's on TikTok the whole time. Who knows who they'll choose."
Geoffrey Moore told Fox News Digital he's not looking to follow in his father's footsteps and play 007. (Saban Films)

"I think they know what they'll be doing. They're not just handing it over to Amazon, that was basically a delivery service, and now they're in the film business. Who they ultimately choose is someone relevant to the times. And I think that's the key to Bond."

Amazon MGM Studios gained creative control of the James Bond franchise in 2025 after forming a joint venture with longtime Bond producers Michael G. Wilson and Barbara Broccoli. The transaction closed March 24, 2025, with Amazon MGM Studios, Wilson and Broccoli remaining co-owners of the franchise.
Geoffrey Moore looks at a double-breasted mohair dinner suit believed to have been made for Sir Roger Moore in "The Spy Who Loved Me" in 1977. (PA Images via Getty Images)
Several actors have been linked to the role, including Paul Mescal, Jacob Elordi, Jack O'Connell, Jack Lowden and Callum Turner.
PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE
Sir Roger Moore, who starred as James Bond, died on May 23, 2017, at the age of 89. (Keith Hamshere/Getty Images)

The next installment will be the 26th film in the official Bond series, which began with "Dr. No" in 1962. Denis Villeneuve is set to direct, with "Peaky Blinders" creator Steven Knight writing the screenplay.
As Moore looks ahead to making more films, there's one piece of advice from his late father, who died in 2017 at age 89, that he hasn't forgotten.
"Make sure you get paid," he joked.

"Knightfall" is available now. (Saban Films)
"Knightfall" is available on digital and on demand.

title: Glen Powell wants no part of political fights that divide people
summary: Glen Powell says political discourse is "the worst version of a conversation" and reveals how movies remain his preferred way to express himself.
story: "Twisters" actor Glen Powell joined Luke Combs on stage for musician's traditional beer swigging contest.
Glen Powell wants nothing to do with Hollywood's political firestorms.
The "Top Gun: Maverick" star opened up about his decision to stay out of politics and why he believes the growing divide has made it nearly impossible to have a healthy conversation.

"Over time, I realized that politics divide people," Powell told Esquire. "People trying to prove their point – for me, it’s the worst version of a conversation. I genuinely do not like the discourse. It’s not as healthy as it once was."
DWAYNE 'THE ROCK' JOHNSON REJECTS HOLLYWOOD’S POLITICAL OBSESSION, BLASTS CELEBRITY ATTACK CULTURE
Glen Powell refused to wade into politics in an interview with Esquire. (Michael Tran/AFP via Getty Images)
For Powell, engaging in politics is "not presently possible."
"I applaud people for jumping into those things and fighting for what they believe in," he added. "If I were a political person, I would be talking about it. For me, my calling is elsewhere."
Powell's reluctance to wade into politics dates back to his upbringing.

Despite his mother's work in the Reagan administration at the U.S. Treasury Department, the actor said politics and current events weren't regular topics of conversation around the family dinner table.
He echoed the sentiment in a previous interview with The Guardian.
"I’m not a political person," he said in October 2025. "I like things that bring people together."
DOLLY PARTON REFUSED TO PICK POLITICAL SIDES FOR DECADES: ‘I’M NOT IN POLITICS, I’M AN ENTERTAINER’
Glen Powell had his breakthrough moment with his role in "Top Gun: Maverick" alongside Tom Cruise. (Chung Sung-Jun/Getty Images for Paramount Pictures)

With politics increasingly dividing audiences, even Hollywood's biggest stars are finding it harder to appeal to everyone. Powell weighed in on whether entertainment can still bring Americans together and if action movies are one of the last remaining escapes from the political divide.

"That’s a good point. There’s a universal language of action, which is also why those movies translate so well internationally," he added. "'Running Man' is about something universal – what you would be willing to do for the people you love? But also how people can feel powerless in the face of a world that feels more and more unequal, more unfair."
"So, you’re not going to see me talk politics. But movies – that’s how I express myself," he added. "Movies are a conversation; politics always felt to me like two people trying to prove a point."
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE
Glen Powell has previously said he likes to express himself through movies. (Gilbert Flores/Variety via Getty Images)
Powell has become one of Hollywood's most recognizable leading men, thanks to standout performances in "Top Gun: Maverick," "Anyone But You" and "Twisters."
Yet his stardom didn't light overnight.
He once had a casting director tell him he'd be lucky to "play a dead body" on CSI as he struggled for a decade to get his foot in the door.

"There was a point where I realized that acting is not a meritocracy," he said during an appearance on "CBS Mornings." And just because you exist on a longer timeline doesn't mean it's going to work out. Right? There's a lot of other bigger forces at play."
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Glen Powell starred in "How to Make a Killing." (Ilze Kitshof/A24)

"The fact that all of those sort of detours along the way about learning how to sort of develop and raise money and write – all these things are now kind of leading me to a place where all of those weapons are at my disposal," he added.

The Hollywood heartthrob kept his hot streak alive in 2026, starring alongside Margaret Qualley in the dark comedy thriller "How to Make a Killing" before lending his voice to Fox McCloud in "The Super Mario Galaxy Movie."

title: Natalie Wood's daughter confronts very painful way she learned Hollywood icon had died at 11
summary: Natasha Gregson Wagner describes the childhood sleepover that shattered her world when she learned Natalie Wood had died off Catalina Island.
story: When Robert Wagner turned 90 years old, we took a look back at the acclaimed actor's iconic career. The star turned 96 on Feb. 10, 2026.
Natasha Gregson Wagner was just 11 years old when an ordinary childhood sleepover turned into a moment that shattered her world.
While staying at a friend's house, she heard the devastating news on the radio: her mother, Hollywood actress Natalie Wood, was dead.

"As a child, I always knew my mom was home because her Jungle Gardenia scent arrived before she did," Gregson Wagner, now 56, wrote on the website for her fragrance brand, L'Amour Mere. "After she died, I spent hours lying in her bed or sitting in her closet among her clothes. If I could somehow keep her fragrance alive, perhaps she would not be entirely gone."
CHARLIZE THERON RECOUNTS THE NIGHT HER MOTHER FATALLY SHOT HER FATHER WHEN SHE WAS 15 YEARS OLD

Natalie Wood’s (left) daughter, Natasha Gregson Wagner (right), recently opened up about losing the Hollywood icon at just 11 years old and carrying on her mother’s legacy. Gregson Wagner celebrated her birthday on Sept. 29, 2026. (Jack Mitchell/Getty Images; Casey Flanigan/IndieWire/Penske Media via Getty Images)

In the immediate aftermath of Wood's death, Gregson Wagner said the two father figures in her life — her biological father, British film producer Richard Gregson, and her stepfather, actor Robert Wagner — came together to support her.

"Luckily, I had these two men, Daddy Gregson and Daddy Wagner, who came together and rose to the occasion and completely put me first," Gregson Wagner told the Daily Mail. "They got me into therapy right away, and I had that same amazing therapist here in Beverly Hills until my 20s."

Wood, who was nominated for three Oscars and starred in "West Side Story" and "Rebel Without a Cause," was on the family's yacht with Wagner, actor Christopher Walken and captain Dennis Davern during Thanksgiving weekend in 1981. Her body was found floating in the water off Southern California's Catalina Island. She was 43.
WATCH: ROBERT WAGNER'S MOST MEMORABLE ROLES, FROM ‘HART TO HART’ TO ‘AUSTIN POWERS’

Investigators initially ruled Wood's death an accidental drowning but reopened the case in 2011 to determine whether Wagner or anyone else played a role after the yacht's captain said he heard the couple arguing the night of her disappearance, The Associated Press reported. The Los Angeles County coroner's office amended Wood's death certificate in 2012, changing the cause of death to "drowning and other undetermined factors."

In 2018, Los Angeles County sheriff's investigators described Wagner as "a person of interest" in Wood's death. In 2022, the department said it had exhausted all leads in the case, and Wagner was no longer considered a person of interest. Wagner has long denied having any involvement in his wife's death.

The boat Splendour, owned by Robert Wagner, is docked off Two Harbors, Catalina Island, Calif., on Nov. 30, 1981, the day after Natalie Wood's body was discovered in the waters off Two Harbors. (Getty Images)
Gregson Wagner said that while she was growing up, her two fathers were determined to give her a normal upbringing away from the glaring media spotlight.
From left: Natasha Gregson Wagner, Robert Wagner and Katie Wagner attend "An Evening with Actor Robert Wagner" on Oct. 2, 2008, in Santa Monica, California. (Michael Bezjian/WireImage/Getty Images)

"I had to do my laundry," she told the outlet. "We had dinner on the table at six o'clock. I learned how to cook in their kitchen. I learned how to do laundry. I learned how to take a bath with a hot tap and a cold tap, putting it in a pot and pouring it on my head and all these things."
Gregson Wagner also told the outlet she avoided the drugs and alcohol that have troubled some children of famous parents.
American actress Natalie Wood holds her baby daughter, Natasha Gregson Wagner, in 1970. (Getty Images)

"I've definitely felt pressure in my life," Gregson Wagner said. "I know what's right, I know what's wrong. I'm not saying I haven't had very, very painful things in my life.... But in the home, it was all very safe and secure and warm. So, I got lucky in that way."
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Natasha Gregson Wagner launched a fragrance in honor of her mother. (Penske Media via Getty Images)
Still, Gregson Wagner said she continues to feel the impact of losing her mother.

"When I was younger, I would get stopped on the street by people who would say things like: 'You look so much like this actress, you've probably never heard of her, but her name was Natalie Wood,'" Gregson Wagner recalled. "Most of the time I wouldn't admit I was her daughter, and just say: 'Oh, I hear that a lot!'"
Natalie Wood, star of the musical film "West Side Story," in January 1961. (Getty Images)

"We looked so much alike and had so much in common. Where did the mother end and the child begin? We were so completely connected — and she was so sharp and perceptive — that I sometimes believed she could see right into my mind."
Natasha Gregson Wagner participated in the HBO documentary "Natalie Wood: What Remains Behind." (Penske Media via Getty Images)

Gregson Wagner has been married to "7th Heaven" alum Barry Watson, 52, since 2014. They share a daughter, Clover. Gregson Wagner also launched the fragrance brand L'Amour Mere, which she says was inspired by her mother and their connection through scent.
Gregson Wagner has previously spoken about her mother's legacy.
Actress Natalie Wood and groom Richard Gregson pose in front of Holy Virgin March Church after their Russian Orthodox wedding. (Bettmann Archive)
In 2020, Gregson Wagner appeared in the HBO documentary "Natalie Wood: What Remains Behind," which featured interviews with Wood's family, close friends and confidants.
Robert Wagner and his wife Natalie Wood, circa 1972. (Silver Screen Collection/Getty Images)
Wagner, now 96, also appeared in the documentary and discussed his relationship with Wood and her death.

The couple married in 1957 but divorced in 1962. They remarried in 1972 and were together until Wood's passing. Wagner helped raise Gregson Wagner, and he and Wood had a daughter, Courtney Wagner, who also appeared in the documentary.
Natalie Wood and her daughter, Natasha Gregson Wagner, stand outside their home in Palm Springs, Calif., in 1973. (Getty Images)
"I am always blown away by his courage," Gregson Wagner told Fox News Digital at the time.

Actor Robert Wagner attends the inaugural Robert Osborne Celebration of Classic Film event at the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences in Beverly Hills, California, on Oct. 7, 2019. (Robyn Beck/AFP via Getty Images/Getty Images)

"As my dad and knowing him for basically my whole life, I know him to be such a courageous person. I was just so proud of him. I felt like he was so transparent, elegant, gracious, emotional, connected and present. He was everything that I know him to be, so it felt like an incredible experience to bear witness as his daughter. He's one of the great loves of my life. He moves me every day, and he deeply moved me on those days [of filming] for sure."
Gregson Wagner said she still has vivid, joyful memories of Wood.
Natalie Wood and James Dean goof off on the set of the film "Rebel Without a Cause" in 1955. (Getty Images)

"My mom made being a mom feel really effortless," Gregson Wagner said. "She loved it so much. She was always singing songs with us. We were always painting and reading. She was always there to talk to. I hear her voice a lot when I talk to [my daughter] Clover. Like, 'What are we going to do today? Are we going to take a walk?' Just the little mundane things. I can hear her voice in my ear when I talk to my own daughter."
Natasha Gregson Wagner attends the Tony Awards at Radio City Music Hall on June 9, 2019, in New York City. (FilmMagic,)

"My parents wanted their children to have that constant feeling of being loved and nurtured — the joy of childhood," she continued. "And that's what they did. Friends came over all the time and sometimes they went out. But the focus was really on us. I think we felt really safe in their world and around them. They were able to create just a bustling, joyful, jubilant kind of atmosphere for us to grow up."

Natasha Gregson Wagner attends the "Wonderland" premiere at Grauman's Chinese Theater in Hollywood. (FilmMagic)

At the time, Gregson Wagner said she hoped the documentary would give viewers a fuller picture of her mother. She said the special was ultimately a celebration of Wood's life and what she accomplished both in Hollywood and as a parent.

Natalie Wood (1938 –1981), is seen here in 1975. (Getty Images)

"I hope that audiences will get a very clear picture of this woman who was so strong, funny, joyful, empowered and courageous," she said. "She had a great life. It wasn't a long one, but it was the one she wanted to have. She was the architect of her own life."

title: Wynonna Judd admits helping daughter during meth battle ‘bit me in the butt'
summary: Wynonna Judd reveals she enabled Grace Kelley's meth addiction by giving her money for drugs, a painful realization explored on her album "The Hard Truth."
story: Wynonna Judd reflected on how her attempts to help her daughter Grace Kelley through her meth battle backfired and opened up about raising her granddaughter Kaliyah.
Wynonna Judd is reflecting on the painful lesson she learned while trying to help her daughter Grace Kelley through her years-long battle with methamphetamine addiction.

Kelley, 30, has struggled with drug addiction and faced a string of related legal troubles for more than a decade. She is currently serving a 15-month sentence at Rockingham County Jail in Harrisonburg, Virginia, after pleading guilty in June to a felony charge of driving with a suspended or revoked license.

During an interview with Fox News Digital, Judd, 62, who recently released her deeply personal album "The Hard Truth," candidly opened up about coming to the realization that some of her attempts to help Kelley only exacerbated her daughter's problems.
CUT OFF BY YOUR ADULT CHILD? PSYCHOLOGY RESEARCHER REVEALS WHAT PARENTS SHOULD DO NEXT

"I really lost myself with Grace and I enabled her, which comes down to basically giving her money for drugs," Judd admitted. "And here I thought I was buying her a car. And those things really bit me in the butt."
Wynonna Judd opened up about coming to the realization that she had been enabling her troubled daughter Grace Kelley. (Erika Goldring/Getty Images; Elmore County Sheriffs)
"And I'm still feeling, you know, some guilt and shame about that," she added.
LADY A'S CHARLES KELLEY SHARES BEFORE-AND-AFTER PHOTOS SHOWING HOW SOBRIETY TRANSFORMED HIS LIFE
The country star also shared what she would tell other parents struggling to help their children without enabling them.

"I would say work on yourself," Judd said. "That was one of the things that I was told. And working on myself, getting the peace, letting her see that she's attracted to that. Maybe she wants to get better herself. So let the light shine."
COUNTRY HITMAKER REVEALS HOW FAITH CARRIED HIM THROUGH SON'S MURDER — AND TOWARD COMPASSION FOR HIS KILLER

"Let your light shine through the cracks, that's how they see the light," she continued. "And hopefully she'll want the same thing that I have. Find someone whose recovery you love so much that you want to be like them and go and do it."

"The Hard Truth" is Judd's first solo studio album in more than a decade as well as her first time serving as a primary songwriter. The album explores heartbreak, healing, faith and survival while shining a light on some of the most painful chapters of Judd's life, including her complicated relationship with her late mother Naomi Judd and Kelley's struggles.
WATCH: WYNONNA JUDD SAYS HELPING DAUGHTER THROUGH METH BATTLE ‘BIT ME IN THE BUTT’
HAYDEN PANETTIERE DEFENDS GIVING UP CUSTODY OF HER DAUGHTER DESPITE INTENSE 'EMOTIONAL PAIN'
While speaking with Fox News Digital, Judd opened up about the hardest truth that she had to face while making the album.

"That there might be a chance that my daughter doesn't get clean, that she doesn't find the healing that she so desperately needs," Judd admitted. "As a mother, I'm devastated by her story, and I just had to let go."
‘NO CONTACT’ ON THE RISE: NEARLY 2 IN 5 AMERICANS CUT TIES WITH LOVED ONES
The six-time Grammy Award winner also reflected on her current estrangement from Kelley, with whom she said she has not spoken for a year.

"After all these years, the money ran out, and she did, too," Judd said. "And I just have to make peace with the fact that I did everything I could do. Including enabling, and I've had to deal with that. And just the pain of losing her to meth and realizing that there's absolutely nothing I can do to save her anymore."
Kelley is pictured in 2005 with Wynonna Judd, Maureen McGovern and Sutton Foster. (Bruce Glikas/FilmMagic)
'BAYWATCH: HAWAII' STAR BRANDY LEDFORD SAYS SHE 'WANTED TO TRULY CHECK OUT' BEFORE REHAB SAVED HER LIFE
Judd explained that her last conversation with Kelley was difficult since she had stood by her decision to stop enabling her daughter.

"Things were tense because I wasn't giving her money anymore and helping her to go back to rehab again and again and again, and again," Judd said. "And I just had to say, 'Sweetheart, you know, you're 30 years old. It's time to stop blaming your mom. And I want you to get the help that you need, and you're gonna have to do it yourself.'"
COUNTRY SINGER RUSTON KELLY COMMITS TO SOBRIETY AFTER RELAPSING ON DRUGS FOLLOWING FREAK GOLF CART CRASH
Judd told Fox News Digital that while she still has hope for a reconciliation with Kelley, there is one condition that would have to come first before they could begin rebuilding their relationship.

"Sobriety," she said. "You are not supposed to make any major decisions in your life, including relationships for a year after you get clean and sober. And I would ask her to go to rehab again, because I know that that's what worked for me."
Judd said Kelley has been in and out of jail since she was 17. (Morgan County Sheriff's Office)
CARA DELEVINGNE ADMITS SHE USED PARTY DRUG GHB DAILY BEFORE TERRIFYING SEIZURES FORCED HER SOBER

In 2006, Judd checked herself into the Shades of Hope Center of Headling in Buffalo Gap, Texas, where she underwent a 42-day treatment program to address her struggles with food addiction. She told Fox News Digital that her own time in treatment shaped the way she views recovery and the example she wants to set for Kelley.

"I'm gonna express that to her, of course, and you're not supposed to really go there. You want the person to want it themselves," Judd said. "But it would take some time because we've been apart a lot. She's been homeless and struggling for years and in and out of prison."

"And I have a song on the record called ‘Drive,’ which talks about me driving down to see her in prison back when she was incarcerated," she continued. "And I'm just gonna look forward to that day. I still have hope she's alive. There is still hope."
Judd shares Kelley and son Elijah, 31, with her first husband Arch Kelley III, to whom she was married from 1996 to 1998.
During a recent appearance on the "Shawn Ryan Show," Judd reflected on how her demanding career may have affected Grace differently than it did Elijah.
Naomi Judd, Ashley Judd, Elijah Judd and Grace Pauline Kelley attended the "Olympus Has Fallen" premiere at ArcLight Theatre in Hollywood, Calif in 2013. (Alamy Stock Photo)

"Grace was very jealous of my career because it took me away from her enough to where she was not satisfied," she said. "I think because she's the second born, I think it was important to her that I even spend more time with her because I had that with Elijah for a minute."
"He was more at peace about it," Judd continued. "She was the one that wanted to sleep with me, wanted my attention 24/7."
"So that was painful. That was hard. I was really hard on myself about that," she admitted.
Judd also spoke candidly about the toll of her daughter’s addiction, describing herself as "a mom in waiting."
"I'm waiting for my daughter to return from a nightmarish addiction to meth," she said. "And it has been quite a journey."
"And unfortunately, she's been incarcerated since … on and off since she was 17," she continued.

"I've made all the jokes about, 'I have one on parole. I have one on patrol,'" Judd added. "My son is a deputy. I've done all that, and now it's time to just tell my story as a mom who's constantly in this place between hell and hallelujah."
Judd said she hasn't talked to Kelley, who is currently incarcerated, for a year. (Elmore County Sheriffs)
Judd said setting boundaries with Kelley became one of the hardest decisions of her life, recalling how she struggled with refusing to help her daughter even when she reached out in desperation.
"I had to let go, and that means no more enabling," she explained. "And it about killed me because when your kid calls and says, 'I'm hungry,' what do you do?"
The "No One Else on Earth" singer said Kelley’s repeated incarceration and the dangers surrounding drug use made her realize that enabling her daughter could have life-or-death consequences.

"She's been in and out of prison and jail for so long that that's her way of walking through the addiction part in terms of what it costs her," Judd said. "We're also now dealing with fentanyl. So, there's that."
"I realized, 'Oh my God, it's possible that I could be part of the reason she dies. I'm loving her to death. Literally,'" she shared.
Judd said she believes that Kelley still carries resentment over the time her career took away from their relationship, as well as her decision to step in and raise her granddaughter Kaliyah.
Judd said Kelley is resentful that she took over care of her granddaughter Kaliyah. (Wynonna Judd Instagram)

"Grace is really mad at me right now," she said. "Because I had a career, and I was busy, and she didn't have enough of me in the beginning. I did the best I could. I've made a lot of mistakes, and she's really mad at me for stepping in with her child."
"Kaliyah has Type 1 diabetes," Judd continued. "There's no way she could have taken care of her. That's one thing. It's a 24/7 situation. I stepped in, and I took over, and she's mad at me."
"I understand that that's her journey," she added. "It's not mine. My journey is to raise this baby to be the healthiest and break the cycle."

Judd and her third husband, musician Cactus Moser, who she married in 2012, have been the primary caregivers for Kaliyah, 4, since her infancy and legally adopted her amid Kelley's addiction struggles and legal woes. The singer was previously married to former bodyguard D.R. Roach from 2003 until 2007.
Moser and Judd are currently raising Kaliyah on their 500-acre farm in Tennessee.
A post shared by Wynonna (@wynonnajudd)

When asked by Fox News Digital about how she balances protecting Kaliyah while leaving the door open for Kelley to be part of her life someday, Judd said her focus remains on giving her granddaughter a grounded childhood.

"I haven't answered that yet," she said. "I think I'm still in the part where I'm so hell-bent on keeping her out of the iPad and the phone and TV. We live on a farm, and she mucks stalls and does chores and she's a cowgirl. So I'm so centered on that. I haven't really given that a lot of thought and if and when that happens I'll answer your question."
Judd also shared a glimpse into her day-to-day life on the farm with Kaliyah and Moser.
Judd is raising Kaliyah with her husband Cactus Moser. (Wynonna Judd Instagram)

"Getting away with as much as possible without having to do anything, going on a side by side, ride down to the lake, taking her fishing, we do that a lot," she told Fox News Digital. "And being out in the woods, just being outside is just so heavenly."
Judd described their farm as a "peace place," noting that her life at home is much simpler than her life onstage.

"I have 40 animals," she said. "So I have chores as well. And I spend my time cooking. That's what I do."
The couple have cared for Kaliyah since she was an infant and legally adopted her. (Wynonna Judd Instagram)
"I'm known in our family as the cook, and I'm known as Nonie," Judd continued. "When I don't have on my lashes, I am known as Nonie."

Meanwhile, Kelley is believed to have welcomed a second child while incarcerated. During her appearance on the "Shawn Ryan Show," Judd said she learned about the baby through social media and knows little about the child’s circumstances.

"I just found out on TikTok that she's had another baby in prison, and I don't even know if it's a boy or a girl," Judd said.
The couple lives with Kaliyah at their 500-acre farm in Tennessee. (Wynonna Judd Instagram)

title: Olivia Dean song accused of ripping melody from Bill Withers’ ‘Just the Two of Us’

story: FOX Business’ Lydia Hu reports on the verdict in the Marvin Gaye copyright trial.
Olivia Dean’s music collided with a Grammy-winning classic in a new lawsuit accusing the singer of repeatedly copying the melody of Bill Withers’ "Just the Two of Us."

Dean's label was sued by Mattie Music Group, the publisher of Withers' catalog, Friday. Dean's 2025 song, "I've Seen It," and Withers' hit classic have "obvious and inescapable similarities," according to the lawsuit obtained by Fox News Digital.

"The number, character and arrangement of the shared musical features are so striking that they support an interference that the similarities did not result from coincidence, independent creation or reliance on common musical elements," the lawsuit claimed.
SUPREME COURT HANDS ED SHEERAN LEGAL WIN IN MARVIN GAYE COPYRIGHT FIGHT

After coming across the song in August 2026, Mattie Music Group hired musicologist Alexander Stewart, whose preliminary analysis allegedly found substantial similarities in protectable musical expression.
Mattie Music Group insisted Withers' original song was so widely disseminated that Dean and co-writers Bastian Langebæk and Max Wolfgang had a reasonable opportunity to encounter it.

title: Comedy stars lash out at Sebastian Maniscalco over SiriusXM shake-up
summary: Comedians like Patton Oswalt and Michelle Wolf are urging Sebastian Maniscalco to reverse a SiriusXM channel rebrand they say hurts working-class comics.
story: The comic is starting his nationwide It Ain't Right tour in July.
Sebastian Maniscalco has found himself in hot water with some comedians who are claiming that his new SiriusXM channel is taking away money and exposure from working-class comics.

Earlier this year, SiriusXM changed a long-running channel in its lineup called Raw Comedy that often featured lesser-known comedians to Sebastian Maniscalco's Comedy Radio. The new station more prominently features famous comedians now.

Stand Up for Stand Up, a nonprofit that supports comedians, recently wrote an article saying the rebranding has "drastically shifted from a wider pool of 800-plus comedians enjoying spins (and thus, royalties and exposure to the audience of listeners)" on the channel "to a narrower pool of comedians getting plays per month.

"And of those few hundred who are getting spins, over 75% of the plays are going to the top 50 artists, which results in a concentration of wealth among the top echelon, which is largely made up of big-name celebrity comics."
SEBASTIAN MANISCALCO IS A NO-NONSENSE FATHER, SAYS PARENTS NEED TO BE 'HALF-PSYCHOTIC' WITH THEIR KIDS
Sebastian Maniscalco is facing a backlash over a shake-up at SiriusXM. (Getty Images for Newport Beach TV Fest)

The nonprofit called the change "bad for comedians, and bad for the future of comedy," adding, "it hurts passive revenue, and discoverability, as well as the infrastructure that supports up and coming comedians."

Maniscalco addressed the criticism in an Instagram Story he shared Wednesday, saying, "This goes out to all my fellow comedians – I want to let you know that I hear you, I support you, I love you. I know how hard the grind is. Believe me, I've been there."

He said that he "had nothing to do" with removing the channel from SiriusXM, but assured fans that he's planning on working with the company to "highlight a variety of different voices in stand-up comedy," including newcomers, superstars and everyone in between.

"I just ask that you give me a little time, guys," he said. "I just got here, and I need a little time to build out the channel. I just wanted to let you know that I heard you, and give me a little time and be patient, and I think you'll like the result."
Before Maniscalco made his statement, several of his fellow comedians had been taking issue with his new channel.
Comedian Matt Ruby on his Substack page claimed the channel was "crushing middle class comedians who rely on payments from the company to pad income."

Liz Miele, another comedian, said in a video on her Instagram, "This year, the Raw channel on SiriusXM became Sebastian Maniscalco’s channel. Great. Fine. Celebrities have taken over channels before. Never been an issue. The problem is Raw went from playing 800 working-class comedians to now playing less than 300 celebrity comedians like Joan Rivers, Johnny Carson, Bob Hope, Norm Macdonald. Just dead comic, dead comic, dead comic, and then a plethora of very famous alive comedians that might not even know about this extra income that they’re about to receive."
She added that every "working-class comedian that has been kicked off the channel is quite aware" of the money they've lost.
Sebastian Maniscalco performs at the Ryman Auditorium. (Jason Kempin/Getty Images for Nobody Does This Tour)

title: Dolly Parton’s nephew erupted in profanity-laced tirade in emails days before her death
summary: Bryan Seaver's expletive-filled emails about Nashville hotel security surfaced in court documents filed just days before Dolly Parton's death.
story: Entertainment lawyer Jordan Matthews weighs in on the conflict involving Dolly Parton’s nephew and explains why disputes among relatives can intensify when a famous person leaves behind a valuable brand.

Dolly Parton’s nephew unleashed an expletive-filled tirade in an email exchange involving the country music legend just days before her death as tensions over security services boiled over, according to court documents obtained by Fox News Digital.

Bryan Seaver, Parton's nephew and longtime head of security, fired off the profanity-laced message Aug. 21, four days before Parton's death, in an email chain carrying the subject line "Fwd: Letter from Dolly."
"Hi Billy. Message received," Seaver began. "If you think my harsh language is too much for your failing vendors to digest, just wait until my lawyers start f---ing you up the a--."
DOLLY PARTON’S SISTERS PUSH BACK ON FEUD RUMORS AFTER NEPHEW’S LEGAL BATTLE WITH STAR'S ESTATE ERUPTS
Dolly Parton's nephew, Bryan Seaver, sent a slew of expletive-filled emails involving the singer just days before her death. (Getty Images; Dolly Parton's Instagram)
While it's unclear who Billy is, Parton’s longtime manager, Danny Nozell, and other members of her team were included in the email chain.
"I challenge you to bring spurious and feeble complaints. Let’s play ball you f---ing s---bag loser," he continued.
Seaver also blasted the progress of an apparent Nashville project, alleging the build-out was "late and worrisome" and subcontractors "continue to do drugs in our venue."
"Explain to your shareholders why your project is still failing and your building is unfinished, unoccupied and mired in violations," he wrote.

Dolly Parton's sister said the last thing the singer asked for from her was prayers. (Bridget Bennett/AFP via Getty Images)

"I encourage it. Go f--- yourself you f---ing weakling," he wrote. "Tell Mr. [redacted] to call me and we’ll talk man to man. Otherwise, your doom ensues."
The court exhibit does not reveal the contents of the apparent "Letter from Dolly" referenced in the subject line.
DOLLY PARTON’S SISTER REVEALS ‘LAST THING’ COUNTRY LEGEND ASKED OF HER BEFORE DEATH
The email came just two days after Seaver directly invoked his famous aunt while complaining about security arrangements at a Nashville hotel project.

"Your contract security company (Titan) you’ve hired in spite of me and Dolly’s request for service at the hotel has completely f---ed up and let an employee be assaulted," Seaver alleged in the Aug. 19 email.

"Let me know when you are ready to hand the security situation completely over to Dolly’s contracted service providers in Nashville and I will fix your problem," he added. "SAPS (Seaver’s Squadron Augmented Protection Services) is your answer."
Country music icon Dolly Parton died Aug. 25.  (Craig Sjodin/Disney General Entertainment Content via Getty Images)
The combative exchanges marked a dramatic shift from correspondence less than three months earlier.

On May 29, Seaver offered to help staff and train security personnel in Nashville. The recipient, identified as "Bill," thanked him for his "genuine care and concern" and said he hoped both teams would support "each other in success."
Parton died Aug. 25 at age 80 after a brief battle with cancer.

Seaver, who had served as Parton's head of security for more than two decades, was chosen by his aunt to publicly announce her death. Less than a month later, tensions between Seaver and members of Parton's business circle spilled into court.
As Fox News Digital previously reported, Parton's manager, Nozell, who runs She’s Alive, LLC, sought a restraining order against Seaver and his company, Squadron Augmented Protection Services.
She's Alive is an entity Parton created to oversee her business interests.
DOLLY PARTON LAID TO REST AS NIECE SHARES EMOTIONAL TRIBUTE TO ‘GRANNY’

A Tennessee judge granted a temporary restraining order, citing an alleged pattern of threats and demands for payment, along with Seaver's "claimed access to weapons, experience with violence, and intention to retaliate." The order barred Seaver and his company from entering She’s Alive properties, coming within 1,000 feet of its employees and business partners or contacting them.
Dolly Parton's sister has defended Seaver, saying there is "no feud within our family." (Jason Kempin/Getty Images)
She’s Alive alleged Seaver's communications continued to escalate after Parton's death.
In a Sept. 1 message included in earlier court filings, Seaver allegedly threatened to start a podcast aimed at damaging Parton's business relationships unless he was paid.

According to documents previously obtained by Fox News Digital, the alleged messages prompted several employees to resign, Parton's trust and estate attorney to step away and She’s Alive to hire private security to protect employees at work and at home. Seaver was fired Sept. 15 over what the company characterized as "terrorizing conduct."

"I've never threatened anyone," Seaver previously told ABC News, calling the restraining order "spurious and simply a publicity stunt."
Dolly Parton died after a brief battle with cancer. She was 80.  (Getty Images)
The newly surfaced emails show that tensions involving Seaver, Parton's business interests and security arrangements had been escalating even before the singer's death.
In an Oct. 5 filing, attorneys for She’s Alive specifically pointed to the communications, arguing that Seaver had not disputed sending them.

Dolly Parton was laid to rest shortly after her death, her niece confirmed. (Katherine Bomboy/NBC via Getty Images)

The filing also accused Seaver of attempting to evade service, claiming a process server tried three times to serve him. During one attempt, four vehicles were spotted in his driveway, but no one answered the door. title: Stomach-turning sexually transmitted infection is on the rise — and standard medicines are failing
summary: Shigella bacteria are becoming harder to treat as drug-resistant strains rise, and doctors warn Americans should be concerned but not panicked.
story: Speaking to Fox News Digital, Lenox Hill Hospital internist Dr. Michael Aziz discusses the increase in antibiotic-resistant shigella cases and explains why patients experiencing gastrointestinal symptoms should seek medical attention before taking over-the-counter medications.
A highly contagious gut infection that can spread during sex is becoming harder to treat as antibiotic-resistant strains become more common.

An April report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention tracked nearly 17,000 Shigella samples, which causes Shigellosis, which and can bring on diarrhea, fever and abdominal cramps, collected between 2011 and 2023. In 2023, 8.5% of Shigella samples with resistance data were classified as extensively drug-resistant, or XDR — resistant to all five antibiotics in the CDC’s definition — compared with none from 2011 to 2015.
The findings point to a growing resistance problem, not a surge in overall infections, noted Dr. Tyler Evans, a California-based infectious disease physician and CEO of Wellness Equity Alliance.
HIGHLY CONTAGIOUS STOMACH BUG SPREADS FAST, HITTING CERTAIN PATIENTS HARDEST
"The infection is not surging. The bacteria are changing," Evans told Fox News Digital. "Case counts can hold steady while the treatment options quietly disappear."
The percentage of Shigella isolates classified as extensively drug-resistant rose to 8.5% in 2023, according to the CDC. (Leonie Asendorpf/picture alliance via Getty Images)
There is no FDA-approved oral antibiotic for XDR Shigella, he said.
Shigella bacteria can spread when tiny amounts of stool reach someone's mouth, including through contaminated food or water, unwashed hands or sexual activity.
DANGEROUS DRUG-RESISTANT FUNGUS SPREADS ACROSS US, REACHING 27 STATES

"Shigella is not considered to be a typical sexually transmitted infection," Dr. Andi Toufexis, a Texas-based family medicine physician who specializes in sexual health, told Fox News Digital. "However, this gastrointestinal bacteria can be spread through sex when one partner comes into contact with the other's fecal matter."
Most patients with extensively drug-resistant Shigella in the CDC analysis were adult men. (iStock)
Shigella is not new, and sexual transmission has been documented since the 1970s, Toufexis said. What is changing is the growing share of tested samples classified as XDR.
MICHIGAN REPORTS 2 DEATHS IN RARE PARASITE OUTBREAK THAT HAS SICKENED MORE THAN 11,000

The CDC report found that most people with XDR Shigella were adult men. Sexual exposure data were not routinely collected, so the report could not establish exactly how each infection was contracted but previous research has found sexual contact among men who have sex with men as an important transmission route.

Eighty-six percent of XDR patients were men, with a median age of 41, and of those with a known HIV status, nearly half were living with HIV, Evans noted. People experiencing homelessness and those with weakened immune systems may also face heightened risks, he said.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Children younger than 5 are especially likely to get Shigella, according to the CDC, and many outbreaks in the U.S. have been linked to child care and schools. Earlier U.S. outbreaks primarily affected children and involved strains that were susceptible to antibiotics.
Washing hands before preparing food can help reduce the spread of Shigella.

According to the CDC report, 37.6% of patients with hospitalization data were hospitalized for the antibiotic-resistant infection. The CDC reported no deaths among the XDR cases analyzed and said infections may be undercounted because not all positive specimens were cultured or tested for resistance. Most patients with available travel histories reported no recent international travel, though travel information was missing for many.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Evans said Americans should be "concerned, not panicked" about the infection.
Most Shigella infections resolve on their own, Toufexis added, but severe illness may need treatment.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Dr. Michael Aziz, an internist at Lenox Hill Hospital in New York City and author of "The Perfect 10 Diet" and "The Ageless Revolution," urged people who suspect Shigella to seek medical advice before taking antidiarrheal medicine such as Imodium. "You want to flush out the bacteria, you want to get it out of your system," Aziz told Fox News Digital.
Experts advise people with Shigella not to take antidiarrheal medicines such as Imodium, which can slow the gut.

To reduce the chance of infection, doctors recommend washing hands, genitals and the anal area before and after sex, using condoms or dental dams, and cleaning sex toys after each use. If you or a partner has diarrhea, avoid sex and wait at least two weeks after symptoms end before resuming, Toufexis said.

"Feeling better does not always mean that an infection is completely gone," she said.
Deirdre Bardolf is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital.

title: One type of sleep linked to dramatically lower risk of dementia, Parkinson's and 81 other diseases
summary: Greater REM sleep was linked to 80% lower Parkinson's risk and 46% lower dementia risk in a major study of over 95,000 adults tracked for years.
story: Erin Palinski-Wade, a New Jersey-based nutritionist and author of ‘The Sleepdemic Solution,’ confirmed that household surroundings and ambient neighborhood conditions can directly interfere with restfulness.
Not all stages of sleep are equal in terms of benefits for the brain.
Greater amounts of rapid eye movement (REM) sleep were associated with lower risks of 83 diseases, including dementia, Parkinson’s disease and heart failure, new research has shown.
Additionally, greater amounts of deep sleep were associated with lower risks of seven conditions.
THIS ONE QUESTION MAY REVEAL WHETHER YOUR BODY IS GETTING THE REST IT NEEDS, STUDY FINDS

That’s according to a study of 95,559 adults who wore wrist accelerometers continuously for seven consecutive days and nights. Researchers in China used deep-learning algorithms to analyze REM sleep, deep sleep, light sleep, total sleep duration, wakefulness after sleep onset and sleep irregularity.
They then looked at health records to assess associations with more than 1,000 diseases over a nearly nine-year follow-up period.
Greater amounts of rapid eye movement (REM) sleep were associated with lower risks of 83 diseases, including dementia, Parkinson’s disease and heart failure, new research has shown. (iStock)
Greater REM sleep was associated with a significantly lower risk of several diseases, including Parkinson’s (80% lower relative risk), dementia (46% lower risk) and heart failure (26% lower risk).
Greater deep sleep was associated with lower risks of seven conditions, including Type 2 diabetes and major depressive disorder.
MORE NAPS, HIGHER RISK? RESEARCH LINKS DAYTIME SLEEP TO HEALTH WARNINGS IN AGING ADULTS

Sleep duration was also found to be highly linked to disease outcome. Six to eight hours per night was found to be the "sweet spot" associated with the lowest risk for 69 diseases. In contrast, sleeping fewer than five hours per night was linked to an increased risk of 37 health conditions.

The study also found that greater night-to-night sleep irregularity and more wakefulness during the night were associated with higher risks of several conditions, including anxiety and substance use disorders.
The findings were published Sept. 17 in the journal PLOS Medicine.
Disrupted sleep may sometimes be an early warning sign of disease rather than simply a cause, a sleep expert noted. (iStock)

"I think what is important is the total duration of sleep, and the percentage that REM takes up," Oki Ishikawa, M.D., pulmonary, critical care and sleep medicine expert at Northwell’s Northern Westchester Hospital, told Fox News Digital.
"The average percentage of REM sleep in this study population was about 20%, and generally 20-25% is considered normal per sleep cycle."
5-STEP SLEEP RESET COULD PROMOTE HEALTHY WEIGHT LOSS, NUTRITIONIST SAYS
Ishikawa, who was not involved in the study, said he does not believe that a higher amount of REM sleep alone will necessarily lower the risk.

"Normal sleep pattern and duration are associated with aspects like maintenance of good immune function and memory, so I think the important message here is to try and get a sufficient amount of sleep in general," Ishikawa sai.
Researchers used deep-learning algorithms to analyze REM sleep, deep sleep, light sleep, total sleep duration, wakefulness after sleep onset and sleep irregularity. (iStock)
Disrupted sleep may sometimes be an early warning sign of disease rather than simply a cause, according to Dr. Chelsie Rohrscheib, head sleep expert at Wesper, a sleep analysis company in New York.

"Conditions such as Parkinson’s disease, dementia and heart failure can begin affecting sleep years before they are diagnosed," Rohrscheib, who also was not involved in the research, told Fox News Digital.
"At the same time, poor sleep may contribute to disease progression, so the relationship likely works both ways."
DIETITIAN REVEALS SIMPLE EATING STRATEGY FOR BETTER SLEEP — AND ONE HABIT TO AVOID
The researchers noted some limitations of the study. Because it was observational, it could only show an association and could not prove that increasing REM or deep sleep directly prevents disease.
"Sleep was measured for only one week using a wrist device, which is less accurate than a clinical sleep study for identifying sleep stages," Rohrscheib said.
"Poor sleep may contribute to disease progression, so the relationship likely works both ways," an expert said. (iStock)
"Some health information was collected years earlier, medications that can affect sleep were not fully considered and some medical diagnoses may have been missed."

As the participants were all from the UK Biobank, the study population was also less diverse and generally healthier than the overall population, so the findings may not apply equally to everyone, Rohrscheib noted.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"Overall, changes in sleep may provide important clues about underlying health, but this study cannot determine whether poor sleep is a cause, an early symptom or both," she concluded.
Rohrscheib also cautioned that while wrist-worn sleep trackers are generally good at estimating sleep stages, they are not 100% accurate.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"Without a formal in-lab sleep study, it's impossible to know how much time the participants spent in REM and other sleep stages," she said.
More research is needed to determine whether increasing REM or deep sleep can help prevent certain diseases, the researchers said.
"If you get about seven to nine hours of uninterrupted sleep, you most likely have the opportunity to cycle through REM in a sufficient way."
Future studies could also explore whether the relationship between sleep stages and disease risk varies by age, sex, overall health and other individual characteristics.

Both experts recommended following general sleep hygiene practices, such as maintaining an optimal environment (dark, cool and quiet), keeping a consistent sleep schedule and avoiding sleep-disrupting substances such as alcohol and caffeine.

"If you have other sleep pathologies like sleep apnea … treating that would be a great way to optimize the amount of REM sleep," Ishikawa advised.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
While it can be difficult to measure REM sleep without a wearable, he said the best gauge is whether one feels refreshed upon waking and doesn’t feel sleepy during the day.
"If you get about seven to nine hours of uninterrupted sleep, you most likely have the opportunity to cycle through REM in a sufficient way."

title: Man loses 15 stubborn pounds after age 50 without giving up pizza or donuts
summary: Carl Daikeler lost 15 pounds by swapping breakfast for a 250-calorie shake and eating a big salad for lunch, then enjoying total dinner freedom.
story: Carl Daikeler, CEO and founder of BODi, shares how a simple breakfast, a hearty lunch, and the freedom to eat what he wants for dinner helped him lose 15 pounds and get into the best shape of his life at 63.
Maintaining weight loss in midlife doesn’t necessarily require strict dietary bans or extreme fasting protocols.
Carl Daikeler, co-founder and CEO of the fitness and nutrition company BODi, says a simple routine earlier in the day has helped him manage his weight while allowing more freedom at dinner.
Los Angeles-based Daikeler, 63, who has led the health brand formerly known as Beachbody for 28 years, openly admits that he doesn't have an affinity for healthy foods.
10-MINUTE FITNESS HABIT CAN HELP ADULTS OVER 40 MAINTAIN MUSCLE AND STAY STRONG
"I eat like a third-grader, okay? Pizza's a food group," Daikeler joked in an interview with Fox News Digital.
"I'm just constantly trying to figure out how can I hack my way without having to overturn my life to become one of those diehard health and fitness people, because I'm never going to become that."
The fitness CEO said he maintains long-term weight loss without strict dieting by eating structured, high-nutrient meals during the day to allow total freedom at dinner. (iStock)

When Daikeler turned 57, he found himself unable to lose 15 pounds he had gained around his waistline. Rather than adopting a strict diet, he adjusted two specific meals during the day while leaving his evening schedule unrestricted, he shared.
For breakfast, Daikeler replaced standard options with a nutrient-dense shake containing protein, fiber, prebiotics, probiotics and greens, totaling roughly 250 calories.
NIGHTLY GLASS OF WINE MAY NOT BE AS HARMLESS AS MANY PEOPLE THINK, STUDY SUGGESTS
"I got rid of breakfast, or I changed my breakfast to this shake that we've got called Shakeology," Daikeler said. "I put some spinach in there and I put a banana in there."
For lunch, Daikeler prepares a large salad loaded with baby spinach, carrots and chicken, mixed with toppings that mask the taste of the greens.
Replacing traditional breakfast with a 250-calorie nutrient shake provides essential greens, fiber and protein without requiring major cooking or dietary overhauls. (iStock)
"I hide it with some cheese, some nuts, some sliced strawberries, and it's delicious, and I put chicken in there ... I don't feel like I'm eating a bowl of vegetables, but I am."
By keeping breakfast and lunch relatively structured, Daikeler gives himself more flexibility at dinner.
BEER, WINE OR LIQUOR? MASSIVE STUDY REVEALS WHICH WAS LINKED TO LOWER DEATH RISK
"Now I've got a 'day pass' for everything else ... I eat whatever I want at dinner."
He does, however, follow a single guideline regarding alcohol intake. "I'm careful not to drink too much," he said.
"Now I've got a 'day pass' for everything else ... I eat whatever I want at dinner."
"Once I did that — Shakeology for breakfast, a big salad for lunch, total freedom for dinner, limited alcohol — the 15 pounds just got wiped out. And it stayed off."
Daikeler warns that overly restrictive nutrition plans are usually difficult to stick with long-term, leading many to abandon their health goals entirely.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"If you're trying to be too restrictive, I don't think that's life," he said. "The whole point is living ... So if it's too restrictive, it's going to break."
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Instead of completely banning indulgence foods, Daikeler recommends using portion control and mindfulness to enjoy without overeating.
The expert said he focuses on smaller portions rather than cutting favorite foods like pizza out entirely. (iStock)

"I love pizza. But I've learned that I can enjoy pizza without eating the whole pizza," he said. "I like doughnuts. I've learned that I can have literally a quarter of a doughnut and be like, that was delicious. But I get no additional satisfaction by eating the whole doughnut."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
For Daikeler, that balance is part of a broader focus on "health span" — prioritizing quality of life and the ability to stay active as he ages.

"Health span versus lifespan is all about quality of life," he said. "I'm all for longevity, but it's really about quality of life — a way to live and enjoy life that is balanced with maximizing your time on earth."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
While Daikeler said this approach has worked for him, weight-loss strategies are not one-size-fits-all.

According to the National Institutes of Health, different eating plans can support weight loss, but the most effective approach depends on a person's individual health needs, preferences and ability to maintain the habits long-term. Individuals are generally advised to consult a doctor or registered dietitian for personalized guidance.
